msContents.summary: A Catholic catechism in dialogue composed as a Virgilian cento.

editorialDecl.p: Diplomatic transcription of the collection copy: spelling, u/v and i/j, ligatures (æ, œ), abbreviations (q;, tildes) and accents are kept as printed; long s is transcribed s. Printer's misprints are kept as printed and noted. Pages are named by the collation of the copy. The English translation faces the Latin line by line; English may carry a word across a line break where the sense of the pair is kept.

Text establishment: two independent machine readings of every line from the page images, compared letter by letter; every divergence adjudicated against the image; corrections logged in editorial notes (type="editorial").

refsDecl.p: Verses are identified by page (collation name) and line number; each Latin verse has an xml:id, which the English line cites in @corresp.

category.catDesc: Printed marginal source tag naming the Virgilian model, resolved to a CTS URN.

handNotes.handNote: The Annotations layer distinguishes 82 printed authorial glosses from the copy’s later manuscript ownership marks. The printed notes explain Bavarius’s Christian reinterpretation of Virgil; the manuscript layer records Jean G. Smolderen and the Antwerp Jesuit professed house.

div.n: Dedicatory epistle (continuation leaf) — the tail of the prose dedication, with an interpolated verse couplet adapted from Horace, Satires 1.1.25–26; the page opens mid-sentence and ends mid-word ("Maro-/nis").
div.p: tem vario marmore incrustaui. Etiamne inquies, depontanum senem ad Permessi caput, & Parnassi culmen adrepsisse? Ecquis non iam illud è Varronis Satyrico, Δὶς παῖδες οἱ γέροντες; In gratiam Iuuentutis Christianæ, iuuenescere collibuit, & ad nuces, quod aiunt, redire. Nihil arduum reputat Charitas, quæ cùm non quærat quæ sua sunt, omnem propter electos formam induit, & vt paruulos lucrifaciat, quæ sunt paruuli, præter ætatem sapit. Denique doctrinam Christianam, quam profusa tua liberalitas, insigni posteris exemplo, per sacra munuscula, velut melimela quædam, tenerioris ætatis illicium promouet.

Eam ego Poëtæ magni versibus expressam, illustratam propono, quamquam Poëtico verborum inuolucro subinde tectam. Sed nucleum quærenti, comminuendum putamen, vt vulgatum habet adagium. Non potuit Musa Maronis

div.n: Author's preface to the reader (Ad lectorem benevolum praefatio)
div.head: AD LECTOREM BENEVOLVM PRÆFATIO.
div.p: Lector quisquis es, siste, in hoc limine paulisper te moror. Quod hîc damus, sacrum est, de spoliis profanorum. Dederunt ipsum ante me multi, sed à se, suisque verbis: ego sic malui alienis. Phrygium efformamus aulæum, pretiosis & variis aliorum telis, viliora rudis ingenij nostri fila interteximus, ne dissutum opus vndique diffluat. Centonem si dixeris, non penitus aberrabis; in quo mirari desine tam nostraesse omnia, quàm ferè nihil. A nobis sunt inuentio, & rerum ordo; versus, & hemistichia hausimus è Virgilio pleraque, hoc est, ex ipso fonte ornatæ Poëseos. Ac ne, quod aiunt, arenam sine calce afferremus, sparsas Poëtæ principis sententias, iam inter se commodè vinximus, iam verborum nostrorum quodam velut cæmento commisimus. Non poterit homini id ætatis vitio verti, cùm multa dixerit, à se pauca locutum esse: iam enim eorum in albo sum, quibus
vt tanto operi decenter elaborando, pares non sint. Quo factum est, vt conquisita aliunde ornamenta huc transtulerim, vt olim fabulosa Flacci cornicula, pennis

lg.l: AD LECTOREM BENEVOLVM PRÆFATIO.
——— tarda gelu, sæclisque effœta senectus
Inuidet auxilium, seræq; ad splendida vires;

div.n: Author's preface to the reader (Praefatio ad lectorem), continuation and end — with two embedded epigram-quotations; signed leaf A4
div.p: nis alienis nuditatem suam contexit; in illo tamen huic dispar, quòd, dum singula candidè in auctores suos refundo, alieni laboris fructum plagiarius impudens non decerpo. Nemo itaque mihi à tergo occinat illud Epigrammatographi;

Suum enim singulis corymbion fideliter remitto, contentus elegantiæ Virgilianæ, Christianæ fidei, pietatisque solidæ nectar affudisse; vt in ea, velut in artificioso Mentoris scypho, cum literarum ornatu veræ succum religionis inueniat & hauriat Iuuentus studiosa. Quàm nihil sit hoc præstitisse, post intermissa nouem lustris literarum studia, tu dispice. Quamquam enim suaue sit Pimplæis fontibus vuescere, tamen vbi iam annorum frequentia, earum, quæ prima inhæserant iuuentute, rerum obliuionem inuexit, labor hic, vel te iudice,

Sed amaritudinem hanc detersit planè, quem inde spero, fructus. Nonne enim magnum videri debet, si quæ fidei documenta, soluto sermone, Christiana Iuuentus semel imbiberit, velut saluti necessaria, ea tanti Poëtæ expressa versibus, altiùs inhæreant? Fruere, Lector, & emarcidi iam trunci malum insititium, explicata fronte deliba.

lg.l: Caluo turpius est nihil comato.
Plus aloës, quàm mellis habet.

div.n: Commendatory poem (Georgius Chamberlinus, Dean of Ghent) — "Ægidio Bavario ... Maronem conuersum gratulatur"
div.head: ÆGIDIO BAVARIO SOCIETATIS IESV PRESBYTERO MARONEM conuersum gratulatur
div.p: Georgius Chamberlinus Cathedr. Eccles. Gandauensis Decanus.

lg.l: ÆGIDIO BAVARIO SOCIETATIS IESV PRESBYTERO MARONEM conuersum gratulatur
Macte senex, cuius nitido de fonte Maronis
Musa repurgato gurgite sacra canit.
Macte iterum venerande senex, quem spiritus intus
Maior alit, plenum flamine fatidico.
Tu pandis Latij non vana poëmata Vatis,
Quæq; ignota dedit carmina, tu reseras.
Tu facis vt sanctos animent hæc flabra calores,
Et foueat flammam casta fauilla nouam.
Illa prius molli fluitabat vena susurro,
Solaq; nugaci murmure verba dabat:
Nunc sapit, atque animo melioribus ebria succis
Stillat diuinum nectar & ambrosiam.
Et quamuis solitos gestes mutata cothurnos,
Est alia, est eadem syrmate sub BAVARO.
Nempe salutiferum cultu variata priore
Nescia prædixit rel'igionis opus.
Dumq; incorrupto mens saga potentior æstro
Eructat sacris enthea verba modis;
Quas tulit illustres ab Apolline Mantua lauros,
Victa infert spoliis inclyta Roma tuis.

div.n: Commendatory poems (liminary verses): end of an elegiac poem in praise of Bavarius subscribed by Iustus Rycquius (Rijcquius); a distich "De Libro"; and a hendecasyllabic poem "Ad Auctorem" subscribed I.D.V., Theologus S.I.
div.head: De Libro,
div.p: Pos. L. M. IVSTVS RIICQVIVS.
I. D. V. Theologus S. I.

lg.l: Qualiter innumero depictum sidere cælum
Pandit formosas nocte silente faces:
Qualis Cecropias exspirans hortulus auras
Florifera vario messis honore nitet:
Qualis Erythræa multus nitet vnio concha,
Qualis ad Eoum plurima gemma mare:
Sic tua grandæua præstans virtute, BAVARI,
Ducta per Andinos mystica Musa modos,
Et quæ pulcra legens, quæ digna atque apta recondens,
Formosum æterno carmine vinxit opus;
Vt modò tot gemmas, florésque & sidera promas.
Quot tibi versiculos pagina quæque facit.
De Libro,
Hîc duo proueniunt libro portenta sub vno;
Et Maro Christicola, & factus Apollo senex.
Ad Auctorem.
Vis me plaudere, vis inusitato
Versu dicere res inusitatas,
Vis vt Theiologus Poëta fiam:
Maius prodigium, Poëta canus;
Sed ter maximum, ab inferis reuersus,
Et nunc Calicolûm Maro Poëta.
Nullum hîc prodigium; recanto versum.
Quid ni, si valeat, velitq; Phœbus
Vernans antea, nunc Apollo canus,
Gentilem priùs, esse Christianum,
Hæc res Theiologum petat Poëtam?
Sed cur canus Apollini capillus?
Hoc ætas dedit, vt velit Maronem
Gentilem priùs, esse Christianum.

div.n: Commendatory poems on the Virgil-cento (elegiac "In Virgilium ... ab Elysio reducem" + hexameter "Pollicetur Maro")
div.head: IN VIRGILIVM OPERA R.P. ÆGIDII BAVARII AB ELYSIO REDVCEM.

lg.l: IN VIRGILIVM OPERA R.P. ÆGIDII BAVARII AB ELYSIO REDVCEM.
Qua noua te Maro forma tegit? Samiusne figuram
Antiquam erudiit deposuisse sophos?
Aut quis ab Elysio retro vestigia luco
Ferre dedit? vacuum quis tibi pandit ebur?
Scilicet haud secto tibi porta nitens elephanto,
Sed tutum ad superos cornea monstrat iter.
Mercurio praeunte nouo hinc euadis ad auras,
Vt post Rura, Duces, Pascua, Sacra canas.
Pollicetur Maro iuuentuti dare Doctrinæ Christianæ bellaria.
Dum meliora Patres dant prima fercula mensa,
Quo victu reuocant vires, & plena reponunt
Pocula non fontis liquidi, sed vina ministrant,
Illiciis mihi fas iuuenum indulgere palato.
Instauro hîc epulas, & mensa grata secunda
Dona fero, cumuloq; oneratis lancibus aras.

div.n: Prelims: end of a commendatory poem, followed by the heading and opening of the author's verse preface (Praefatiuncula auctoris iubilearii annorum 70), with two authorial marginal glosses
div.head: Præfatiuncula auctoris iubilearij annorum 70.

lg.l: Corporis atque animi vires renouante, serena
Mente, Deo, est aquila parta iuuenta seni.
Audeat hac fretus, iuuenum concurrere Musis,
Septime, cui Phœbi voluitur orbe decas.
Sic tamen vt vegeta, viridi, florente senecta,
Personet Andinos nil nisi vena modos.
Vrgent iussa Dei, & sacra Virginis ora parentis,
Quæ visa est tales edere voce sonos:
Æneamne suum legat hoc in carmine Cypris,
Et meus in versu simpliciore fluat?
Ite modò, & vestrum, Musæ, reuocate Maronem,
Vt meus hoc ipso filius ore sonet.
Dixit; & Elysiis rursum Maro surgit ab oris,
Et canit ad iussus, maxima Virgo, tuos.
Præfatiuncula auctoris iubilearij annorum 70.
Mors matura seni veluti nox humida cælo
Præcipitat, suadentq; cadentia sidera somnos:
Tres tamen ipse velim luces mihi vita supersit;
Quin mihi tam longè maneat pars vltima vitæ,
In patriam vt rediens, fido comitatus Achate, †
Aonio mecum deducam vertice Musam,
Quæ quondam eximias retulit tibi Mantua palmas, *
Propter aquam tardis ingens vbi flexibus errat
Mincius, & tenera prætexit arundine ripas:
Huius enim tacitum pertentant gaudia pectus,
Quod modò non inuisa magis Cælestibus, auras
Vitales carpat. vitæ nam fluminis vnda
Lustratur, supplex diuinum Numen adorans,
Votorumq; memor iam aris imponit honorem:

div.n: Programmatic verse preface — the Muse of Maro declares her purpose (front matter, leaf A7)
div.head: Musa Maronis hîc animi sui propositum ob oculos ponit.

lg.l: Quin memorare parat (cùm non sit gratior vlla,
Quàm sibi quæ fidei præscribit pagina nomen)
Quæ fidei blandos fundent cunabula flores
Christiadum genti. Plausu studiisq; fauentum
Consonat omne nemus, vocemq; inclusa volutant
Littora, pulsati colles clamore resultant.
Spargite humum foliis, inducite frōdibus herbas,
O Vates; mandant fieri sibi talia Musæ.
Tu verò Latij pubes hanc aspice partem,
Ceu quædam aërij mellis cælestia dona:
Admiranda tibi leuium spectacula rerum;
Posthabuisse nefas tamen esset seria ludo.
In grauibus labor, at tenuis non gloria, si quem
Numina læua sinunt, auditq; vocatus Iesus.
En fidei responsa dabit tibi Musa Maronis,
Ipsius hîc tibi fas audire, & reddere voces;
Este animis faciles, intentiq; ora tenete.
Musa Maronis hîc animi sui propositum ob oculos ponit.
Illa ego, quæ quondam gracili modulabar auena
Carmen, & egrediens siluis vicina coëgi,
Vt quamuis auido parerent arua colono:
Gratũ opus agricolis. Post hæc horrentia Martis
Arma, virumq; dedi, Troiæ qui primus ab oris,
Italiam fato profugus, Lauinia venit
Littora: multum ille & terris iactatus, & alto.
Ast ex quo Christi leges his auribus hausi,
Vulnera dira, neces, atque horrida dicere mitto
Bella, acies, actosq; animis in funera Reges,
Tyrrhenamq; manum, totamq; sub arma coactam
Hesperiam: rerum maior mihi nascitur ordo,
Maius opus moueo, fidei cunabula nostra.

div.n: Close of the author's prefatory invocation — verse imploring the aid of the Blessed Virgin, Mother of God (with marginal gloss, printer's ornament, and catchword)
div.head: Implorat opem B. Virginis Deiq; matris.

lg.l: Implorat opem B. Virginis Deique matris.
Virgo, namque tibi diuûm Pater, atque hominum Rex,
Et mulcere dedit ventos, & tollere fluctus,
Decute vim ponto, mersamq; haud obrue puppim,
Sed me, quæso, moue, summum decus addita Diuis,
Da facilē cursum, atque audacibus annue cœptis,
Cantantiq; fauens adsis pede Diua secundo.

div.note: Implorat opem B. Virginis Deique matris.

div.head: Quid est fides?

lg.l: (Siluestrem tenui meditatus arundine Musam)
Carmina descripsit celeberrimus arte Poëta;
Sunt ea quæ paucis hic pagina nostra recludet:
Cana fides, spes certa poli, cui Numinis ardor
Iungitur, atque animæ septena arcana salutis,
Discite iustitiam moniti, & non temnere diuos.Aen. 6.620
His studiis ritè institui stet corde voluntas,

div.note: Per tribulas, trahas, rastra dentibus armata, quibus terra pungitur & conteritur, insinuandam duxi cordis nostri compunctionem, vt est prima pars pœnitentiæ. Per aratrum verò, & vomerem, quo terra aperitur, euertitur, & quasi euomitur, confessionem ipsam, quæ est secunda pars eiusdem Sacramenti, non incongruè intelligendam putaui, quatenus ipsa confessione nostram conscientiam Christi vicario aperimus, & sordes animi eruimus. Per mysticam denique vannum, qua purgatur frumentum, & à palea secernitur, vti etiam per tarda Eleusinæ matris voluentia plaustra, quibus seges in horreum inuehitur, satisfactionem intelligo, qua mouemur ad faciendos fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. Luc. 3.

Da rogo, Christe, meæ peragam sic tempora vitæ.

div.n: Colloquium B. Virginis. ad Musam Maronis.
div.head: Colloquium B. Virginis. ad Musam Maronis.

lg.l: Vt mora nulla obstet, quin mens ad amœna vireta
Fortunatorum nemorum, sedesque beatasAen. 6.639
Deueniat, lætosque locos, vbi sistere in æuum
Fas animæ detur potis es, ni velle recuses.
Qua ratione autem tam accensi pectoris ardor
Velle neget misero cælestia regna petenti,
Qui dedit inuitis, demulcens saxea molli
Corda sono? Deus, alme Deus, miserescito nostri,
Patrati sceleris quos maxima cura remordet:
Talibus ô quoties cælestis præmia regni,
Quin, pietate tua, primi redduntur honores?
Quòd si tanta igitur sunt præmia crimine victis,
(Dum te lapsorum miseret) quæ munera iustoAen. 5.354
Digna dabis, primam meruit qui laude coronam?Aen. 5.355 ; Aen. 5.355
Tunepater patrum quondam mitissime frustra?
Tantane, tam patiens cordis miseratio Christi,Aen. 5.390
Nos sinet in cassum veniam cælumque precari?
At tu diua parens, generis fiducia nostri,Aen. 4.365
Hanc sine nos spem ferre tui, te in vota vocantum,Aen. 9.291
Semper vbique tuos precibus fulcire sodales:
Ac cùm sis diuûm interpres, quæ Numina gnati,
Non tripodas, Clarij haud lauros, at sidera sentis,
Quæso canas, vocemque volens atque ora resoluas:Aen. 3.457
Eia age, namque omnē cursum mihi prosperadixitAen. 3.362
Relligio, & cuncti suaserunt numine Diui,Aen. 3.363
Elysium petere, & terras tentare repostas,Aen. 3.364
Pauca mihi è multis, (quo tutior hospita lustremAen. 3.377
Æquora, & ætherio possim consistere portu)
Expedias dictis, prohibent nam cætera ParcæAen. 3.379
Mortales scire, & fari vetat ætheris author.
Colloquium B. Virginis. ad Musam Maronis.
Hîc Genitrix. ô luce magis dilecta parenti,Aen. 4.31
Ne dubites: nam te maioribus ire per altumAen. 3.374
Auspiciis, manifesta fides: sic fata Deûm RexAen. 3.375
Sortitur, voluitque vices, is vertitur ordo.Aen. 3.376
Elysium verò quod tu iam rere propinquum,Aen. 3.381
Vicinosque ignara paras inuadere portus,Aen. 3.382
Longa procul longis via diuidit inuia terris,Aen. 3.383
Antè & Trinacria lentandus remus in vnda,Aen. 3.384

div.note: Colloquium B. Virginis, ad Musam Maronis.

div.head: MVSA.

lg.l: Et salis Ausonij lustrandum nauibus æquor,Aen. 3.385
Infernique lacus, Æææque insula Circes,Aen. 3.386
Quàm tuto possis cæli consistere portu.
Ne renue ambages, cursusq́ue horresce futuros,
Fata viam inuenient, aderitque vocatus Iesus.Aen. 3.395
* Dextra tibi tellus, & longo dextra petanturAen. 3.412
Æquora circuitu: læuum fuge littus & vndas:
† Læuum Scylla latus, læuum implacata CharybdisAen. 3.420
Obsidet; atque imo barathri ter gurgite vastosAen. 3.421
Sorbet in abruptum fluctus, rursumque sub aurasAen. 3.422
Erigit alternos, & sidera verberat vnda.Aen. 3.423
Præstat Trinacrij metas lustrare PachyniAen. 3.429
Cessantem, longos & circumflectere cursus,Aen. 3.430
Quàm semel informem vasto vidisse sub antroAen. 3.431
Scyllam, & cæruleis canibus resonantia saxa.Aen. 3.432
Hæc tibi ne qua moræ fuerint dispendia tanti,Aen. 3.453
Et quo quemque modo fugiasque ferasque laborē;Aen. 3.459
Expediam, cursusque dabo venerata secundos.
Hæc sunt quæ nostra liceat te voce moneri:Aen. 3.461
Perge modò, & qua te ducit via, dirige gressum;Aen. 1.401
Hac etenim puppesque tuæ, pubesque tuorum,Aen. 1.399
Aut portum tenet, aut pleno subit ostia velo.Aen. 1.400
MVSA.
Stat monitis parere tuis, mihi certa voluntas,Aen. 4.125
Magna Dei genitrix, mihi iussa capessere fas est,Aen. 1.77
Quo tandem detur dextræ coniungere dextram,Aen. 8.164
Ac Superûm faustas audire ac reddere voces.
O fortunati, quorum illic mænia surgunt:Aen. 1.437
Conditio at melior, quibus est fortuna peractaAen. 3.493
Iam sua. Nos alia ex aliis in fata vocamur:Aen. 3.494
Illis parta quies, nullum maris æquor arandum;Aen. 3.495
Arua neque Elysij semper cedentia retroAen. 3.496
Quærenda. Interea felix, bis terque beatus,
Qui simul istius fastigia suspicit vrbis,Aen. 1.438
Acceleratque viam, gressumque ad mænia tendit;
Quem Deus obscuro gradientem tegmine sepsit,
Et multo nebulæ circumdans fudit amictu,Aen. 1.412
Cernere ne quis eum, nec quis contingere possit,Aen. 1.413

div.note: * Per dexteram tellurem, viam mandatorū Dei intellige, quæ ducit ad vitam æternam.
Per læuum latus, via perditionis insinuatur, quæ consistit in transgressione legis diuinæ.

lg.l: Moliriúe moram, aut veniendi poscere causas.Aen. 1.414
Infer me precor hac nebula Deus optime septam,
Vt nisi diuinum maneat mihi mente repostum;
Namque animus meminisse horret genus omne profanum:Aen. 2.12
Vna Dei subeat cari genitoris imago,Aen. 2.560
Vnius & Christi crudelia fata reuoluam;
Multa viri virtus animo, multusque recursetAen. 4.3
Laudis honos, sedeant infixi pectore vultus,
Is mihi vita, salus, dux vitæ, vera salutis
Semita sit; posthac nil me mortalia tangant,
Sitque mori lucrum cælestia regna tuenti.
Iam pridem mundo effœta, vt quid inutilis annos
Demoror? Ah patrio tuta vt modò limine sistar.
Sit labor extremus, longarum hæc meta viarum.Aen. 3.714
En nos immensum spatiis confecimus æquor,Geo. 2.541
Et iam tempus equûm fumantia soluere colla;Geo. 2.542
* Hinc nos digressos faustis Deus applicet oris.

div.head: ORATIO:

lg.l: ORATIO:
ANIMA CHRISTI SANCTIFICA ME.
Mens Christi instaurans animas, collapsaque corda,
Pectoris accelera lapsi sarcire ruinas,Geo. 4.249
Numine me complens, vacuum per inane vagantem,
Excolar Astræa, & reliquo virtutis amictu:
Cùm sese agglomerent summi decora alta Parentis.
CORPVS CHRISTI SALVA ME.
Teter abundauit cordis liquor, omniaque in se
Ossa minutatim morbo quassata trahuntur;Geo. 3.485
Quin furit, atque intus de pascitur arida febrisGeo. 3.458
Viscera tosta siti: varius dolor occupat artus.
Quid reliqui est? medicas sectabor Apollinis artes
Is ferat artis opem? Nihil hunc tentasse iuuabit.
Sit medicans tua, Christe, caro mihi causa salutis.
SANGVIS CHRISTI INEBRIA ME.
Congressus peto, Christe, tuos & amœna tuorum.
Concilia, Elysiosque agros: huc casta cruentis
Vina tuis ducunt, deprompto sanguine, venis.
Dulcior ipsa mero, rosei mihi fluminis vnda
Christe tui: hi calices quem non fecere disertum?
Ite procul Bacchi fœdantia pocula mentes,
Dummodo melliflui hæc hilarent me vina cruoris.
AQVA LATERIS CHRISTI LAVA ME.
Pure latex Christi lateris de vulnere manans,
Lethiferæ labis de cordibus elue fæces,
Nulli etenim maculæ patet alti ianua Regis.

div.note: Insinuatur hic virtutum inter se concatenatio.

lg.l: Passio Christi FORTIFICA ME.
Cruda flagella, truces inflictæ cuspidis ictus,
Christe, tuæ carni, toto cuî corpore nullum
Verber inane datur, valido me robore firment.
MORS CHRISTI VIVIFICA ME.
Mors tua, vita mihi, vt bello sit viuida virtus,
Vndique Cocyti dum circumfundimur armis;
Nostra, Pater, molire tuas in pectora flammas,
Nos face, nos ferro, nos vulnere, victor, eodem
Confice, da sobolem caro comitem ire parenti.
Ibimus optato, duce te, data victima letho;
Dummodo vitales tua mors mihi proferat orsus
O BONE IESV EXAVDI ME.
O gregis alme tui custos, mitissime Iesu,
Summe ouium Pastor, cui sunt tot ouilia curæ,
Quæ nunquam surda pietas tua præterit aure,
Ne mitis renuas in voces ire precantum.
INTRA VVLNERA TVA ABSCONDE ME.
Vulneribus latuisse tuis sit facta potestas,
Præsertim in roseo traiecti limine cordis,
His etenim semper versabor tutus in oris,
Donec triste nefas lacrymarum fonte luatur.
ET NOLI ME SEPARARE ABS TE, SED PONE ME IVXTA TE.
Tanto sim tecum nexu constrictus amoris,
Auelli vt nequeam patriis amplexibus vnquam,
Quolibet aut casu, aut quouis discrimine rerum,
Dum mihi vita comes, dum spiritus hos reget artus,Aen. 4.336
Ac tua me pietas maturum poscet Olympo.

div.n: VT CVM ANGELIS, ET SANCTIS TVIS, &c.
div.head: VT CVM ANGELIS, ET SANCTIS TVIS, &c.

lg.l: VT CVM ANGELIS, ET SANCTIS TVIS, &c.
Fas vbi sit demum mihi sceptra resumere regni.
Proque suis donis, sua reddere iura Tonanti,
Aligerûm ritu, citharis fidibusque sonoris,
Et vocum innumeris concentibus atria cæli
Complere ac lætoster Io, ter dicere Pæan,
Insertosq́ue choris Superûm, tria Numinis ora
Cernere, lustratos diuini lumine vultus.
Felicem is sed enim censetur ducere vitam,
Qui mentem expleri nequit, ardescitque tuendoAen. 1.713
Id genus obtutus; stans hoc defixus in vno,Aen. 1.495
Quo datur æternùm cælesti sorte potiri.

div.n: MAGNIFICAT ANIMA MEA DOMINVM, ET EXVLTAVIT SPIRITVS MEVS, &c.
div.head: MAGNIFICAT ANIMA MEA DOMINVM, ET EXVLTAVIT SPIRITVS MEVS, &c.

lg.l: MAGNIFICAT ANIMA MEA DOMINVM, ET EXVLTAVIT SPIRITVS MEVS, &c.
Fas Superûm Regi grates persoluere dignas,Aen. 1.600
Inque Deo exultare animis, pro munere tanto,
Quo sua nos pietas dignatur, grata salutis
Dona ferens, propriam sobolem cùm destinat aræ.
QVIA RESPEXIT HVMILITATEM ANCILLÆ SVÆ.
Qui vilem famulæ sortem despectat ab alto,
Atque humiles habitare casas, vterique latebras
Haudquaquam horrescit, nouus at fit sedibus hospes
Virgineo partu, intemerato flore pudoris,
Me facere instituens diuina prole parentem,
Hinc Genitricis ego non munere fungor inani.
ECCE ENIM EX HOC BEATAM ME DICENT OMNES GENERATIONES.
Inde hominum omne genus me terq́ue quaterq́ue: [turnover line] beatam
Esse feret, mihi dans æternum in sæcula nomen:
In freta dum fluuij current, dum montibus vmbræAen. 1.607
Lustrabunt conuexa, polus dum sidera pascet,Aen. 1.608
Semper honos, nomenq́; meum, laudesq; manebūt.Aen. 1.609
FECIT MIHI MAGNA QVI POTENS EST.
Tu das alme Pater (cui summa potentia rerum)
Sim magnæ Heroûm Isacidæ non infima stirpis
Gloria, virtutem vt non vnica pagina claudat
Certè magna nimis mutatæ est gratia sortis,
Dum satis est famulæ, si laudis honoribus ornes

div.n: ET SANCTVM NOMEN EIVS, ET MISERICORDIA EIVS A PROGENIE, &c.
div.head: ET SANCTVM NOMEN EIVS, ET MISERICORDIA EIVS A PROGENIE, &c.

lg.l: ET SANCTVM NOMEN EIVS, ET MISERICORDIA EIVS A PROGENIE, &c.
Iure tibi sanctum debetur Numine nomen,
Cùm tua, Rex, pietas sese diffundat in omnes.
Insignes pietate viros, in quidquid vbique est
sanctorum gentis, magnum quæ sparsa per orbem,Aen. 1.602
Quosque feret, tuleritq́ue ætas, queis mascula còrdi
Insedit virtus, Domini quibus addidit alas
Ipse timor, spumantis equi calcaribus armos
Dum sodit, atque asptos cogit decurrere calles.
FECIT POTENTIAM IN BRACHIO SVO, DISPERSIT SVPERBOS, &c.
Dextra potens Domini, magniq; ipsa agminis instar
Dispergit tumido turgentia pectora fastu.
Quam multi Libyco voluuntur marmore fluctus,Aen. 7.718
Sæuus vbi Orion hybernis conditur yndis;
Vel quot sole nouo densæ torrentur aristæ,Aen. 7.720
Aut Hermi campo, aut Lyciæ flauentibus aruis:Aen. 7.721
Colla superborum tot fulua sternit arena,
Verè Marte potens supremi Numinis ira,
Scuta sonent, pulsuque pedum tremat excita tellus,Aen. 7.722
Aratæque micent peltæ, micet æreus ensis;
Nequidquam in Superos insurgent arma tumentum.
DEPOSVIT POTENTES DE SEDE, ET EXALTAVIT HVMILES.
Qui facit excelsas descendere montibus ornos,Aen. 4.491
Non poterit regni sublimia sceptra tenentes,
Illustri solio detrudere corde superbos?
summissos animo contrà, super æthera ferre?

div.n: ESVRIENTES IMPLEVIT BONIS, ET DIVITES DIMISIT INANES.
div.head: ESVRIENTES IMPLEVIT BONIS, ET DIVITES DIMISIT INANES.

lg.l: ESVRIENTES IMPLEVIT BONIS, ET DIVITES DIMISIT INANES.
Non potis esuriem vacuæ compescere mentis,
Vt sit adempia fames, & amor compressus habendi?
Nec virtute leuare sitim sitientis auari?
Mittere nec dites poterit rerum omnium egenos,
Qui quondam fuerant multa ditione potentes?
Mille tuæ Siculis errant nunc montibus agnæ,
Lac tibi non æstate nouum, non frigore defit,Ecl. 2.22
Nudatumque bonis fors te lux crastina cernet.
SVSCEPIT ISRAEL PVERVM SVVM, RECORDATVS MISERICORDIÆ SVÆ.
Pôst tot millenos, reuolutis mensibus, orbes,
Promissi memor ipse sui, & pietatis auitæ,
Qua voluit mundi commune refellere crimen,
Felici partu sub luminis editur auras,Aen. 7.660
Infantis ritu, Isacidûm de sanguine cretus.
Huc ades; ô formose puer; tibi lilia plenisEcl. 2.45
Ecce ferunt Nymphæ calathis, tibi candida NaisEcl. 2.46
Pallentes violas, & summa papauera carpens,Ecl. 2.47
Narcissum & florem iungit bene olentis anethi,Ecl. 2.48
Tum casia, atque aliis intexens suauibus herbis,Ecl. 2.49
Mollia luteola pingit vaccinia caltha:Ecl. 2.50
Ipse ego cana legam tenera lanugine mala,Ecl. 2.51
Castaneasque nuces, quoniam hæc dileximus ipsi:
Et vos, ô lauri, carpam, & te proxima myrte;Ecl. 2.54 ; Ecl. 2.54
Sic positæ quoniam suaueis miscetis odores.Ecl. 2.55
SICVT LOCVTVS EST AD PATRES NOSTROS, ABRAHAM, ET SEMINI EIVS, &c.
Patribus vt nostris fuerat Deus ore locutus,

div.n: GLORIA PATRI, ET FILIO, ET SPIRITVI SANCTO.
div.head: GLORIA PATRI, ET FILIO, ET SPIRITVI SANCTO.

lg.l: Magno Abrahæ, ſobolique eiuſque nepotibus olim.
Sic grauiter Vates ceu fatis ora resoluunt,
Mittimur huc lapsis quæsitum oracula rebus.Geo. 4.449
GLORIA PATRI, ET FILIO, ET SPIRITVI SANCTO.
Mente sedet magno sua reddere iura Parenti,
Par simul est soboli, ob partos de morte triumphos,
Quantū opis est nostræ, meritos dare laudis honores,Aen. 1.601
Atque etiam manans vtroque à Numine Numen
Consimili celebrare modo, stat corde voluntas.
Musa Maronis paraphrasticè canit Hymnum
VENI CREATOR SPIRITVS, MENTES TVORVM VISITA.
Spiritus alme veni, cælo demissus ab alto,
Da nouus his nostris succedas sedibus hospes:
Namque humiles habitare casas, & sordida rura,
Pauperis & tuguri congestum cespite culmen,
Numine magnus aues, præsepia grata Tonanti.
IMPLE SVPERNA GRATIA, QVÆ TV CREASTI PECTORA.
Sit tuus iste labor, cæli Spirabile Numen:
Inspirare animis, quos dextera flaminis auræ
Condidit è nihilo, certantibus arma tuorum,
Dona & habere humeris, & vertice figere cristas,Aen. 10.701
Gratiæ vti clypeo gestare insigne paternum.
QVI PARACLETVS DICERIS.
Tu potis es mœstos animi lenire dolores,
Solando verbis factisque auertere curas,
Mens pietate potens, longum seruata per æuum,
Non ignara mali, miseris succurrere prompta.Aen. 1.630
DONVM DEI ALTISSIMI.
Tene vocem donum, ac rebus melioribus æquem?
Non tibi par sceptrum, Iliene quod gesserat olim,Aen. 1.653
Maxima natarum Priami, colloque monileAen. 1.654
Baccatum, aut duplex gemmis auroque corona;
Munus es immensum Patris omnipotentis Olympi.
Munera nulla putem Iliacis erepta ruinis,Aen. 1.647
Ornatus Argiuæ Helenæ, quos illa Mycenis,Aen. 1.650
Pergama cùm peteret, inconcessosque Hymenæos,Aen. 1.651
Extulerat, matris Ledæ mirabile donum.Aen. 1.652

div.n: FONS VIVVS, IGNIS, CHARITAS, ET SPIRITALIS VNCTIO.
div.head: FONS VIVVS, IGNIS, CHARITAS, ET SPIRITALIS VNCTIO.

lg.l: Hisce addas palam signis auroque rigentem,Aen. 1.648
Et circumtextum croceo velamen acantho:Aen. 1.649
Nil hæc cuncta vni dono collata Tonantis.
FONS VIVVS, IGNIS, GHARITAS, ET SPIRITALIS VNCTIO.
Tu fons es viui laticis, salientis in altos
Caelicolum montes, vis ignea, flammeus ardor
Mentis amore Dei succensæ; atque vnctio fragrans
Quæ tibi odorato referat sudantia ligno
Balsama, quæ baccas semper frondentis acanthiGeo. 2.119
Partibus innumeris vincat: tu denique Numen
Crederis æternum, cæli cui sidera parent.Aen. 10.176
TV SEPTIFORMIS MVNERE.
Tu genus vsque tuum doni septemplicis ornas
Eximio cultu: magni decora alta parentis,
Regia Maiestas soboli communia fecit.
DEXTRÆ DEI TV DIGITVS, TV RITE PROMISSVM PATRIS, SERMONE DITANS GVTTVRA.
Tu Patris es dextræ digitus, tu rite Tonantis
Promissum, ditans cælësti guttura verbo.
ACCENDE LVMEN SENSIBVS, INFVNDE AMOREM CORDIBVS.
Lumen age æthereum accendi da sensibus imis,
Vt sapor indicium faciat manifestus, & oraGeo. 2.246
Tristia tentantum, sensu crucientur amaro,
Sicque suas discat fraudes auersa Deo mens,
Pareat inde dolis, non auersata, repertis.
Vt cornix plena pluuiam vocat improba voce,Geo. 1.388

div.n: INFIRMA NOSTRI CORPORIS VIRTVTE FIRMANS PERPETI.
div.head: INFIRMA NOSTRI CORPORIS VIRTVTE FIRMANS PERPETI.

lg.l: Et sola in sicca secum spatiatur arena,Geo. 1.389
Vt varias pelagi volucres,& quæ Asia circumGeo. 1.383
Dulcibus in stagnis rimantur prata Caystri,Geo. 1.384
Certatim largos humeris infundere rores,
Nunc caput obiectare fretis, nunc currere in vndas,Geo. 1.386
Et studio in cassum videas gestire leuandi;
Haud secùs optandum flammarum incendia mitti
In gelidas hominum mentes, quæ sidera lambant,
Attollantque globos, liquefactaque corda sub auras.
Ergo age, cor nostrum vehemēti hoc turbine perfla,
Eructansque ignes, rorantia flamina misce.
INFIRMA NOSTRI CORPORIS VIRTVTE FIRMANS PERPETI.
Da Pater attritos defessi corporis artus
Robore firmari, vt redeant in prælia vires.
Hostibus obruimur: mihi ferreus ingruit imber:Aen. 12.284
Arduus armatos mediis in mœnibus astansAen. 2.328
Fundit equus: portis alij bipatentibus adsunt,Aen. 2.330
Millia quot magnis numquam venere Mycenis,
Obsedere alij telis angusta viarumAen. 2.332
Oppositi: stat ferri acies, mucrone corusco,Aen. 2.333
Stricta parata neci. Quis, cæco Marte, resistat?Aen. 2.334
Nemo queat; nisi quos diuûm Pater atque hominum RexAen. 1.65
Flaminis afflauit ventis, & contigit igni.
HOSTEM REPELLAS LONGIVS, PACEMQVE DONES PROTINVS, DVCTORE SIC TE PRÆVIO VITEMVS OMNE NOXIVM.
Hostiles acies procul hinc, procul arma repelle:
Præferimus dextra vittas ac verba precantum,Aen. 7.237
Paciferæque manus ramum prætendit oliuæ.Aen. 8.116
Fædera iungantur, pacem te poscimus omnes,Aen. 11.362

div.n: PER TE SCIAMVS DA PATREM, NOSCAMVS ATQVE FILIVM, TEVTRIVSQVE SPIRITVM CREDAMVS OMNI TEMPORE.
div.head: PER TE SCIAMVS DA PATREM, NOSCAMVS ATQVE FILIVM, TEVTRIVSQVE SPIRITVM CREDAMVS OMNI TEMPORE.

lg.l: Quæ sit nixa Deo, firmataqúe Numinis aura,
Qùa non omne malum miseris, nec funditus omnesAen. 6.736
Corporeæ excedant pestes: at saucia noxis
Corda instaurentur, lethali labe remissa.
PER TE SCIAMVS DA PATREM, NOSCAMVS ATQVE FILIVM, TEVTRIVSQVE SPIRITVM CREDAMVS OMNI TEMPORE.
Te duce, fas Patrem noscendi, sitq́ue serenum
Diuinæ vultum sobolis, quæ hunc legibus orbem
Fundauit, nobis cernendi facta potestas.
Teque ab vtroque omnes teneant Spirabile Numen.
Immotæ id fidei est: dubiis absiste moueri.
GLORIA PATRI DOMINO, NATOQVE QVI A MORTVIS SVRREXIT, AC PARACLETO IN SÆCVLORVM SÆCVLA. AMEN.
Laus tibi nate Deo, qui victa morte triumphas,
Vi propria excedens tumulo, Stygiaque palude;
Multa tuum meritis sustentet fama trophæis
Nomen, in orbe tui maneat bona gratia facti,
Sit simul immenso par laus, & gloria Patri,
Siq́ue ab vtroque suum mananti in sæcula Numen,
Par iubar, & decus, & splendor, par culmen honoris.

div.n: Quod in re diuina de Spiritu sancto proximè Euangelio præmitttitur, & Sequentia vocatur.
div.head: Quod in re diuina de Spiritu sancto proximè Euangelio præmitttitur, & Sequentia vocatur.

lg.l: Quod in re diuina de Spiritu sancto proximè Euangelio præmitttitur, & Sequentia vocatur.
VENI SANCTE SPIRITVS, ET EMITTE CÆLITVS LVCIS TVÆ RADIVM.
Numinis aura veni, patriæ cælestis ab oris,
Atque tuæ lucis vibratus ab æthere fulgorAen. 8.524
Cum sonitu veniat, terris fragor intonet ingens,
Agnoscantque homines summi promissa parentis.
VENI PATER PAVPERVM, VENI DATOR MVNERVM.

div.n: Dedicatory epistle: opening address and first paragraph of the dedication to Jacobus Boonen, Archbishop of Mechelen
div.p: There comes to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, most vigilant Prelate, something or other from an exhausted breast; whether I should call it a miscarriage or an offspring, I am in doubt: this one thing I know, that if it has any life, it is not owed to me, from whom, already devoted to death, nothing vital could proceed. But that it may live, perhaps the dignity of the subject matter will bring it about, and likewise the authority of the Bard whom I have plundered: for nothing has flowed from the rich vein of Maro that is not worthy of eternal memory. This work, with his fragments snatched here and there, like some clay wal-

lg.l: TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST REVEREND LORD, LORD JACOBUS BOONEN, ARCHBISHOP OF MECHELEN.

div.n: Dedicatory epistle (continuation leaf) — the tail of the prose dedication, with an interpolated verse couplet adapted from Horace, Satires 1.1.25–26; the page opens mid-sentence and ends mid-word ("Maro-/nis").
div.p: -tem I have inlaid with varied marble. Will you even say that a superannuated old man has crept up to the source of the Permessus and the summit of Parnassus? Who does not now recall that line from Varro's Satire, 'Old men are boys twice over'? For the sake of Christian youth, it has pleased me to grow young again, and to return to the nuts, as they say. Charity considers nothing difficult; since she does not seek her own, she puts on every form for the sake of the elect, and to win over the little ones, she savors the things of a little one beyond her years. Finally, Christian doctrine, which your lavish generosity, as an outstanding example to posterity, promotes through sacred little gifts, like certain honey-apples, an enticement for a more tender age,

This I set forth, expressed and illustrated by the verses of the great Poet, although from time to time concealed by a poetic wrapping of words. But for one seeking the kernel, the shell must be broken, as the common adage has it. The Muse of Maro could not

div.n: Author's preface to the reader (Ad lectorem benevolum praefatio)
div.p: Reader, whoever you are, halt; I delay you for a little while on this threshold. What we offer here is sacred, from the spoils of the profane. Many have offered the same before me, but from themselves, and in their own words: I have thus preferred to do so in the words of others. We are fashioning a Phrygian tapestry; into the precious and varied webs of others, we have interwoven the cheaper threads of our own unpolished intellect, lest the unstitched work fall apart on all sides. If you call it a cento, you will not be entirely wrong; in which cease to wonder that everything is as much ours as almost nothing is. From us come the invention and the order of things; the verses and half-lines we have mostly drawn from Virgil, that is, from the very fountain of ornate poetry. And lest, as they say, we should bring sand without lime, we have at times conveniently bound together the scattered thoughts of the prince of poets, at times joined them with a sort of cement, as it were, of our own words. It cannot be turned into a fault for a man of that age, though he has said many things, to have spoken few from himself: for I am already on the register of those, to whom

so that they are not equal to elaborating so great a work fittingly. Hence it came about that I transferred hither ornaments sought from elsewhere, just as once the fabled little crow of Flaccus, with feathers

Begrudges help, and strength too late for splendid deeds;

div.n: Author's preface to the reader (Praefatio ad lectorem), continuation and end — with two embedded epigram-quotations; signed leaf A4
div.p: ers of others covered its own nakedness; yet in this I am unlike it, that, while I candidly return each item to its authors, I do not, like a shameless plagiarist, pluck the fruit of another's labor. Let no one therefore chant behind my back that line of the Epigrammatist:

For I faithfully return to each his own hairpiece, content to have poured the nectar of Christian faith and solid piety upon Virgilian elegance; so that in it, as in an artfully crafted cup of Mentor, studious Youth may find and drink the essence of true religion along with the ornament of letters. Consider for yourself how trifling a thing it is to have accomplished this, after literary studies had been interrupted for nine lustres. For although it is sweet to be moistened by the Pimplean springs, nevertheless when the multitude of years has already brought on a forgetfulness of those things which had taken root in early youth, this labor, even in your judgment,

But the fruit which I hope for from it has completely wiped away this bitterness. For ought it not to seem a great thing, if those teachings of the faith which Christian Youth has once imbibed in prose, as necessary for salvation, should take deeper root when expressed in the verses of so great a Poet? Enjoy, Reader, and with an unfurrowed brow taste the grafted fruit of a trunk now withered.

div.p: George Chamberlain, Dean of the Cathedral Church of Ghent.

lg.l: He congratulates Aegidius Bavarius, priest of the Society of Jesus, on the converted Maro
Well done, old man, from whose clear spring of Maro
the Muse sings sacred things with a cleansed stream.
Well done again, venerable old man, whom a spirit within
greater nourishes, full of prophetic breath.
You lay open the not idle poems of the Latin Bard,
and the unknown songs he gave, you unlock.
You bring it about that these breezes enliven holy ardours,
and that a chaste ember fosters a new flame.
That vein formerly flowed with a soft whisper,
and gave only words with a trifling murmur:
Now it is wise, and in its mind, drunk on better juices,
it distils divine nectar and ambrosia.
And although, changed, you wear the accustomed buskins,
she is another, she is the same under the robe of Bavarius.
Truly, altered from her former dress, the health-bringing
work of religion she unknowingly foretold.
And while the prophetic mind, more powerful with uncorrupted frenzy,
pours forth divinely inspired words in sacred measures;
The illustrious laurels which Mantua won from Apollo,
renowned Rome, conquered, adds to your spoils.

div.n: Commendatory poems (liminary verses): end of an elegiac poem in praise of Bavarius subscribed by Iustus Rycquius (Rijcquius); a distich "De Libro"; and a hendecasyllabic poem "Ad Auctorem" subscribed I.D.V., Theologus S.I.
div.p: Justus Rycquius placed this gladly and deservedly.
I. D. V., Theologian of the Society of Jesus.

lg.l: Just as the heaven, painted with countless stars,
spreads forth its beautiful torches in the silent night:
just as a little garden, breathing Cecropian breezes,
shines with the varied glory of a flower-bearing harvest:
just as many a pearl gleams in the Erythraean shell,
just as many a gem by the Eastern sea:
So, Bavarius, excelling in age-old virtue, your
mystic Muse, led through Andine measures,
and gathering what is beautiful, storing up what is worthy and fitting,
has bound a beautiful work in everlasting song;
so that you now bring forth as many gems, and flowers, and stars,
as each page makes little verses for you.
On the Book,
Here two portents come forth within a single book;
both a Christ-worshipping Maro, and Apollo made an old man.
To the Author.
You want me to applaud, you want me in unaccustomed
verse to tell of unaccustomed things,
you want me to become a theologian poet:
a greater prodigy, a white-haired poet;
but thrice the greatest, returned from the underworld,
and now Maro, poet of the heaven-dwellers.
There is no prodigy here; I recant the verse.
Why not, if Phoebus is able, and willing,
previously blooming, now a white-haired Apollo,
formerly a pagan, to be a Christian,
should this matter call for a theologian poet?
But why white hair on Apollo?
Age has given this, that he wills Maro,
formerly a pagan, to be a Christian.

div.n: Commendatory poems on the Virgil-cento (elegiac "In Virgilium ... ab Elysio reducem" + hexameter "Pollicetur Maro")

lg.l: ON VIRGIL BROUGHT BACK FROM ELYSIUM BY THE WORK OF THE REVEREND FATHER AEGIDIUS BAVARIUS.
What new form covers you, Maro? Did the Samian your shape
ancient teach you to lay aside, the sage?
Or who from the Elysian grove your steps backward
granted you to bear? Who opens the empty ivory to you?
Doubtless, not the gate gleaming with sawn ivory to you,
but the gate of horn shows a safe path to the world above.
With a new Mercury leading the way, you escape from here to the upper air,
so that after the Countryside, the Leaders, the Pastures, you may sing of Sacred things.
Maro promises to give the youth the sweetmeats of Christian Doctrine.
While the Fathers serve the better first courses at the table,
with which food they restore strength, and set out full
cups, pouring not water from a clear spring but wine,
it is right for me to indulge the palate of the youth with enticements.
I renew the feast here, and at the second course pleasing
gifts I bring, and I heap the altars with loaded platters.

div.n: Facultas R. P. Provincialis (Jesuit Provincial's printing licence, signed by Antonius Sucquet, Antwerp, 15 October 1621)
div.p: Since four theologians of our Society, to whom this was entrusted, have examined the Maronian Catholic Muse of the Reverend Father Aegidius Bavarius, and have approved that it may be published, by the power granted to me by our Very Reverend Father Mutius Vitelleschi, Superior General of our Society, I grant to Martinus Nutius, printer of Antwerp, permission to print it. In witness whereof I have issued these letters, signed with my own hand and sealed with the seal of my office, at Antwerp, October 15, in the year 1621.
Antonius Sucquet.

lg.l: Permission of the Reverend Father Provincial.

div.n: Prelims: end of a commendatory poem, followed by the heading and opening of the author's verse preface (Praefatiuncula auctoris iubilearii annorum 70), with two authorial marginal glosses

lg.l: Renewing the strength of body and mind, with a serene
mind, with God, an eagle's youth has been gained for the old man.
Relying on this, let him dare to vie with the Muses of the young,
O seventh one, for whom a decade is rolled in Phoebus' circuit.
Yet in such a way that, in a vigorous, green, and flourishing old age,
his vein may sound forth nothing but Andine measures.
God's commands urge him on, and the sacred lips of the Virgin Mother,
who seemed to utter such sounds with her voice:
"Shall Cypris read of her Aeneas in this song,
and my own Son flow in simpler verse?
Go now, Muses, and call back your Maro,
so that my Son may sound forth from this very mouth."
She spoke; and Maro rises again from the Elysian shores,
and sings at your commands, greatest Virgin.
A little preface of the jubilarian author of 70 years.
Ripe death for the old man, just as the damp night from the sky
falls headlong, and the setting stars urge sleep:
yet I myself would wish that my life might survive for three days;
nay, that the last part of my life may remain for me so long,
that returning to my homeland, accompanied by faithful Achates, †
I may lead down the Muse with me from the Aonian peak,
who once brought back outstanding palms to you, O Mantua, *
near the water where huge in slow windings wanders
the Mincius, and fringes its banks with tender reed:
for joys thrill her silent breast,
because now, no longer hateful to the Heavenly ones, the breezes
vital she draws. For by the wave of the river of life
she is purified, a suppliant adoring the divine Godhead,
and mindful of her vows she now places her offering on the altars:

div.note: That is, with the guardian Angel.
A description of the Muse of Maro.

div.n: Programmatic verse preface — the Muse of Maro declares her purpose (front matter, leaf A7)

lg.l: Nay, she prepares to recount (since there is none more pleasing,
Than the page which inscribes upon itself the name of faith)
What gentle flowers the cradle of the faith will pour forth
For the race of Christians. With the applause and zeal of those favoring,
Every grove resounds, and the enclosed roll the voice along
Shores, the struck hills echo with the shout.
Strew the ground with leaves, cover the grass with foliage,
O bards; the Muses command such things to be done for them.
But you, youth of Latium, look upon this part,
Like certain heavenly gifts of airy honey:
Marvelous spectacles of slight things for you;
Yet it would be a sin to have set serious things below play.
The labor is in weighty matters, but the glory is not slight, if anyone
The hostile powers allow, and Jesus hears when called.
Behold, the Muse of Maro will give you the answers of faith,
Here it is lawful for you to hear and return her very words;
Be favorable in your minds, and hold your faces intent.
The Muse of Maro here places before the eyes the purpose of her mind.
I am she, who once played on a slender reed
A song, and departing from the woods I compelled the neighboring
Fields to obey the farmer, however greedy:
A work pleasing to farmers. After these things, the bristling of Mars
Arms, and the man I gave, who first from the shores of Troy,
Exiled by fate, came to Italy and the Lavinian
Shores: he having been tossed much both on lands and on the deep.
But ever since I drank in the laws of Christ with these ears,
I cease to speak of dire wounds, deaths, and horrid
Wars, battle-lines, and kings driven by their passions to death,
And the Tyrrhenian band, and all gathered under arms
Hesperia: a greater order of things is born for me,
I set in motion a greater work, our cradle of faith.

div.n: Close of the author's prefatory invocation — verse imploring the aid of the Blessed Virgin, Mother of God (with marginal gloss, printer's ornament, and catchword)

lg.l: He implores the aid of the Blessed Virgin and Mother of God.
O Virgin, for to you the Father of the gods and King of men
has granted both to calm the winds and to raise the waves,
strike the violence from the sea, and do not overwhelm and sink my ship,
but stir me, I pray, added as the highest glory to the heavenly ones,
grant an easy course, and nod assent to my bold undertakings,
and be present, Goddess, favouring me as I sing, with propitious step.

div.note: He implores the help of the Blessed Virgin, Mother of God.

div.n: MVSA CATHOLICA MARONIS, SIVE CATECHISMVS MARONIANO CARMINE EXPRESSVS.

lg.l: THE CATHOLIC MUSE OF MARO, OR THE CATECHISM EXPRESSED IN MARONIAN VERSE.
CHAPTER I.
On faith and the Symbol of faith.
GUIDE.
Who is to be called a Christian and a Catholic?
MUSE.
He who, amid the foaming sea, like a crag in the salt spray,
is drenched by the sacred surge of the life-giving water,
and of the eternal offspring of God (whom a royal virgin
in a happy birth brought forth into the breezes of light)
holds the laws and the faith, the rite and custom of the sacred worship
of the Roman Father, where there is a safe anchorage for ships;
and seeks out and hears the records of earlier men,
seeking the heavenly fatherland, as he takes his descent from the upper air.
With God the Father showing the way, following the given fates,
himself unknown, destitute, wandering through the deserts of the world,
rejects mouths discordant in sound from the mouth of the mother,
and whatever the supreme Latins have swept away from the sacred shrines.
For these are set as a boundary, by which a dispute over the fields is settled.

div.note: In baptism the Christian man is sprinkled with water seasoned with salt, so that he may remember that he, like a rock, is exposed to all the storms of the fierce sea of this world.
The Latins here are said to be the Supreme Pontiffs, whose task it is to settle controversies of faith.

lg.l: On the sign of the Christian man.
GUIDE.
What signs do the Christ-worshippers bear? What is the watchword of war?
You know the ancient custom of Ausonia, antiquity is known to you:
Tell me, when the fathers' resolve for battle sits fixed,
Does not, in the Quirinal robe and the Gabine cincture,
Distinguished, the Consul unbar the creaking thresholds?
Or is there need that the Queen, gliding down from the sky, the lingering
should herself with her hand thrust open the lingering gates, and, the hinge turned,
Heavenly force should burst the bolted doorposts of war?
MUSE.
For the Christ-worshipper, as I have learned, the watchword does not go thus in this war.
But the threefold God with his voice, the three faces of the Godhead
He sounds sweetly, and with the sign of the cross sends himself into battles:
This funereal sign of the Master's golden-leafed tree,
Sacred by religion, and by the dread of fierce Mars,
Tertullian, On the Soldier's Crown.
Has ever belonged to the Christ-born race, which the right hand onto the forehead
Imprints, fashioning it, which more frequent use wears down,
This calls to battles, then the rest of the youth follows,
And the brazen horns blow together with hoarse assent,
Ausonia burns, unroused and immovable before.
GUIDE.
To what does the sign of the Holy Cross contribute?
MUSE.
If it is not granted to enter the dark places of the earth before
Than someone has plucked the golden-leafed shoots from the tree,
(Just as the vain poets once taught us)
It is more fitting, so that you may be able to look upon the vaults of heaven,
To direct your steps into the groves, where the rich one shades the fertile
Ground, the branch of the cross, so that thus now with gleaming arms
You may be as if equipped, and girded with a weapon against the enemy:
For under the auspices of the cross we have for war brave
Hearts, we have courage, and youth tested in action.
On the sum of the catechetical matter.
Tell me, in what things must be instructed in its boyish years,
The youth, the flower of Latium, whom the care of the soul vexes?
The distribution of the work into six chapters.
Bend your twin eyes hither now, and drink in with your ears.
What sort of things they are, which recently on the green bark of a beech tree,
(Having practised the woodland Muse on a slender reed)
The poet most celebrated for his art wrote down the songs;
These are the things which our page will here reveal in a few words:
Hoary Faith, sure hope of heaven, to which the ardent love of God
Is joined, and the sevenfold mysteries of the soul's salvation,
Learn justice, being warned, and not to despise the gods.
Let the will stand firm in the heart to be duly instructed in these studies,
Whether when the eighth year has not yet taken you,
Or when first youth clothes your cheeks with its bloom,
Or when a strengthened age has now made you a man.
GUIDE.
What is faith?
MUSE.
Hoary faith is a gift, and a distinguished paternal light,
Which protects the people under the ancient religion,
A star trailing a torch, which has run its course with abundant light,
Coming to show oracles for fallen affairs,
And sure oracles for things to come, sent from heaven through the shadows.
He who is surrounded by this great cloak of light.
Does not plant stumbling footsteps on the trodden ground,
But with firm and unmoved faith, having followed the sacred gifts,
Holds stored in his mind the more hidden things of our faith,
And what the first parents taught in the sacred shrines,
Whether those things be entrusted to the light leaves of papyrus, b
(Which fly scattered as playthings for the swift winds)
Or transmitted of old by the hands of the Fathers to their descendants.
Preserved through many years by solemn religion.
Thus the tree which has raised itself from scattered seeds, c
Comes slowly, about to make shade for late descendants.
Let him know these things, unrolling the monuments of ancient men.

div.note: Here the twofold duty of Christian Justice is suggested.
Through the shadows: because faith by its very nature includes obscurity.
b The Catholic faith relies not only on sacred Scripture, but also on the pure traditions of our ancestors.
The traditions of the Fathers, by their late use, are likened to a tree, which, after seeds are sown, has at last raised itself on high, about to make shade for late descendants.

lg.l: THE MUSE TO HER OWN.
A brief exhortation to men of doubtful faith, and even straying from the Catholic Religion.
Faith herself, all that which now, drawn over you as you look,
dulls your mortal sight, and dank all around
gathers in darkness, she will tear away the cloud, and bring back the sun.
Therefore, troubled by portents, the oracles of Faunus
cease, of the prophetic Seer, and the groves beneath lofty
to consult, Albunea, which, greatest of the woods, with its sacred
spring resounds, and, shadowy, breathes out savage Mephitis.
In doubt seek answers here; hither also let the priest gifts
bring, and of slaughtered sheep, under the silent night,
let him lie down upon the spread fleeces, and demand sleep,
that he may hear the heavenly voice, and enjoy the gods'
converse, and be able to know by certain signs,
uncertain whither the fates may lead, where it is granted to settle.
THE GUIDE.
Recite now the twelve articles of the faith.
THE MUSE.
This is my certain faith, and I cease to be moved by doubts.
The first article of the Creed, I BELIEVE IN GOD THE FATHER, etc.
The almighty Father, who has supreme power over things,
in the beginning the heaven, the lands, and the liquid plains,
and the shining globe of the Moon, and the Titanian stars
founded from nothing, and, infused through the limbs,
a Mind animates the whole mass, and mingles itself with the great body:
thence the race of men and beasts, and the lives of flying creatures,
and the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface.
Fiery is their vigour, and heavenly their origin.

div.note: We are taught here that, while the mind is in doubt, so that we may be strengthened in the Catholic faith, we must in no way resort to vain superstitions, but rather earnestly take refuge in Christ the Lord through frequent and repeated prayer, and various mortifications of the body, offering to him the sacrifice of the immaculate Lamb, and of the slaughtered sheep, the holy Martyrs: wearing a hairshirt, spending sleepless nights in goatskins and sheepskins, so that we may be visited by God, and illuminated by his divine light.

div.n: Artic. 2. De Filio Dei, quatenus est Deus.

lg.l: Article 2. On the Son of God, insofar as he is God.
Offspring born to God, who the affairs of men and of gods
rules with eternal commands, and terrifies with the thunderbolt,
the only one of the supreme Father, his own great power, strength:
a power equal to God, an equal force matched with the Thunderer.
At length time has brought this to us who longed for it,
the help and the coming of God: when first a woman,
bearing the face and garb of a virgin, wondrous to tell,
brought forth a boy neither of our race nor of our blood.
For thus the prophets sang with an awe-inspiring omen,
that a man was approaching, proud over peoples and lands,
from heavenly seed, who would seize the world by his might,
who would bound his empire by the Ocean, his fame by the stars.
Article 3. On the incarnation and nativity of Christ the Lord.
And now the promised day was at hand, at which time first
the origin of the divine lineage raised his sacred face,
sent under command, and power came forth from the body
mingled with God, the image of the dear Father appeared.
Whence the Prophet thus begins with Sibylline witnesses:
The last age of the Cumaean song has now come,
now the Virgin too returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return,
a royal progeny is sent down from high heaven,
offspring of the eternal Godhead, through whom the iron race first
ceased, and a golden race will arise in the whole world:
Chaste Lucina, show favour, my Jesus now reigns.
When ten months had brought you no weariness.
O Mary, with this fair offspring he made you a parent,
God himself: with the fruitful showers of the holy breath,
he descended into the lap of the joyful Virgin, and the lofty
Great One, mingled with the holy body, nourishes the offspring.
The Muse professes the integrity of the Blessed Virgin.
Meanwhile, destined to resemble God the Father in face and shoulders,
you remain an undefiled virgin, but also yourself a beautiful

div.n: Artic. 4. PASSVS SVB PONTIO PILATO, CRVCIFIXVS, MORTVVS ET SEPVLTVS.

lg.l: The offspring gives you flowing hair, and the light of youth
Radiant, and had breathed joyful graces upon his eyes.
The very cradle pours forth charming flowers for you,
The serpent too perishes, and the deceitful herb of poison
Perishes; Assyrian amomum will spring up everywhere.
"Run, such ages," they said to their spindles,
The Parcae, in accord with the steadfast will of destiny.
Article 4. SUFFERED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE, WAS CRUCIFIED, DIED, AND WAS BURIED.
Thirty great circles, as the months rolled round,
The Radiance of the high ether kept itself enclosed in the dwellings;
The royal offspring, so long submissive to a parent,
To submit his neck to the yoke, and inglorious to the whole world
The Ruler of highest Olympus chose to live:
Until at last, driven by heavenly commands,
He came forth into the midst, so that he, than whom no other was more excellent
At rousing men with his mouth, and kindling minds with his word,
Might cure wounded breasts with healing words,
Just as for the viperous race, the heavily breathing hydras,
He who was able to scatter sleep, both by song and by hand,
Might soothe their angers, and relieve their bites with his mouth.
But not to heal the blow of the spear of envy
Did he prevail, nor did those songs help them against their wounds,
Sleep-bringing, and the herbs sought in the Marsian mountains:
The ungrateful offspring of the Solymi perished in their hatreds;
They sharpen their angers against the physician with various rumors:
Whom, by a kind of hideous death, to be bound to a high beam
They urge, alas, pierced in his arms and soles,
Nay, even bound about his temples with a thorny band,
He falls as a slain victim, a priest celebrating new sacred rites,
And reddening, unadorned. Thus the grape hung on the briars,
And the hard oaks sweated dewy honey.
By this death, if any traces of our sin remain,
Rendered void, they will free the lands from perpetual fear.
Meanwhile, the lifeless body, pierced through the breast,
The nourishing Parent did not endure it to be left without the honor of a tomb.
The Governor grants whatever solace of burial there is.
Some, warm waters, and bronze cauldrons bubbling with flames,
Make ready, and they wash and anoint the body of the cold one:
A groan arises, then they lay the wept-over limbs on a bier,
And over them purple garments, the familiar coverings,
They cast. Some took up the huge bier,
A sad service: nay, here are sought heaped-up
Sabaean incense for God: finally the corpse is veiled;
Soon, laid to rest in a hewn rock, not in cheap earth,
He is buried by the holy ones, to whom fragrance is dear,
To join sweating balsams to the scented wood.
Article 5. HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.
Holy love conquered the harsh journey, and the unlovely to the living
Realms to seek, and by his command to break the brazen gates
Drove him, when he wished from the dark cave of the prison,
And from the lake of Cocytus to lead forth the souls of the Saints.
How great a love for us, O how great a desire for souls!
Soon the cave, and the vast uncovered of Limbo appeared
Palace, and the shadowy caverns lay open deep within;
Not otherwise than if by some force the earth gaping utterly open
Should unlock the infernal dwellings, and reveal the realms
Pale, hated by the gods, and from above the immense abyss
Should be seen, and the shades should tremble at the light let in.
ON THE THIRD DAY HE ROSE AGAIN FROM THE DEAD.
Scarcely had the third Dawn brought back her saffron risings,
When, retracing his step, he returned to the upper air:
Then suddenly before their eyes the tomb of immense bulk,
Where the lifeless body was laid, neither the barriers, nor the very
Guards are able to withstand, and torn from the rocks
They see the rocks, the tight joints of the sides being loosened:
A sound arises, the earth is shaken by a massive weight.
Dread everywhere, and at the same time the very silences terrify their minds.
Article 6. HE ASCENDED INTO HEAVEN.
On the fortieth day, he parts the breathing shadows
Through the yielding air, and borne along in the open sky,
He left mortal sight in the middle of his speech,

div.n: Artic.7. INDE VENTVRVS EST IVDICARE VIVOS ET MORTVOS.

lg.l: He brings himself in, enclosed in a cloud (marvelous to tell),
And him, on a throne, the glory of the starry heaven
Receives, and he holds an eternal name through the ages.
Article 7. FROM THENCE HE SHALL COME TO JUDGE THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.
And at last an age will come as the years glide by,
He will appear with the full majesty of the Thunderer,
Resting upon a high throne, and with gleaming arms
Surrounded by winged ones, so that as Judge he may dispense justice,
About to give to each according as his own virtue and life have brought;
Trojan and Tyrian shall be treated by him with no distinction.
Article 8. I BELIEVE IN THE HOLY SPIRIT.
Just as the almighty Father, and the Offspring coeval with the parent,
The affairs of men and of gods, and the whole world which he founded,
Rules with eternal commands, far and wide all around,
Beyond the paths of the year and the sun, where heaven-bearing Atlas
Turns on his shoulder the axis studded with burning stars;
Not otherwise the breathable Deity sent forth to the lands,
Not unequal in any steps to the eternal Father,
Has extended his empire, and as all adore his deity,
And load his altars with various gifts,
so let me match him with the Begetter in equal praises.
I believe in one God, and at the same time three persons of the Deity:
There is the almighty Father, who has the highest power over things:
The Royal offspring gathers himself to the side of the Begetter,
And from both, from the flowing Deity, there is its own Deity,
To whom belong radiance, and glory, splendor, and an equal peak of honor.
Article 9. THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.
As much as Rome has raised its head among other cities,
And as much as cypresses are wont to rise among the pliant viburnums,
So much does the form of the sacred flock, whose name is the Church,
Raise its head to the world above the rest of the sheepfolds of men,
Which extends its empire to the Ocean, its fame to the stars.
He looks up to her, if anyone the farthest land by the overflowing
Removes by the Ocean, and if any the stretched-out of the zones
The zone of the harsh sun separates in the midst of the four,
Here where the rising East first breathed with panting steeds,
Or where reddening Vesper kindles his late lights,
And where for you the golden sun rises toward the Scythian citadels,
And where the same sun, sloping downward, sinks toward the shores of Libya.
She rules with her command the peoples, both mothers and men,
Spirits long sluggish, and unaccustomed hearts,
And the Mother pities the idle, ignorant of the way,
Demanding back that all things be turned and ruled under Christ.
THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.
O fortunate beyond measure, if they knew their own blessings,
Romans, lords of the world, and the toga-clad nations,
Ancient Ausonians, to all of whom God also granted
That there be one city for the Heavenly ones, and for those departed from the earth,
And for men to hold the gate in a common station;
And to call upon a common God willing to give wine!
For whom it is lawful that peoples be mingled, and covenants be joined,
Between the Heaven-dwellers, and us, who feed upon the air
Ethereal, and among those now already laid to rest in the earth,
Whom they call shades, and thin lives without a body.
However things shall fall, there is one and a common danger,
One salvation for the peoples joined by this allied covenant.
Christ himself among the foremost, of surpassing form,
Moves holding arms, and is above them by a whole body;
A cloud of winged ones follows, and shielded
Columns are massed in all the plains: there stands in flashing light
A drawn line of steel, and finally with the weapons of vows,
It is certain that battle is joined from all sides, both on earth and in the sky,
For the help of the Ausonian faith, and the Latin race.
But their own are not lacking to those deprived of the vital light
Aids: besides the funeral offerings, which to the Shades
The pious race of Christians destines, there are also the sacred words of those praying,
Or the prayers of the funeral rite, gifts given to the needy;
cruel scourges, hunger, and harsh fasts on behalf of the fallen,
And a varied kind of penance, and nameless penalties,
By which, while the wrath in heavenly minds subsides,
Soon the banks seething with pitch and a black whirlpool
They evacuate the souls from the shades and from the Acherontian flame,
And they snatch them from dreadful punishments, and to be placed in heaven
The supreme piety of the highest Parent grants.
Therefore come, cease from fear, pious nation, and sad dread
Dismiss, you whom cruel horror first surrounded;
The city will be bereft of fear, when the world has come into the city. c
Article 10. THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS.
I believe that orders are given, with iron and tight joints,
Of closing the gates of Cocytus, with the stain forgiven,
By the power of the Ones Above, with the ministering key bestowed upon Peter.
Let the wickedness of Erebus cease; let impious Frenzy, within,
Sitting upon cruel arms, and bound by a hundred brazen
Knots behind his back, let him roar, horrid with bloody mouth.
Article 11. THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH.
Once the earth, shaken by a harsh-sounding tremor,
Resounded with a groan, and, roused, with its tombs torn open,
Sent forth phantoms. But to few was this given of things
Condition, to few to return to the lights of life
Was it granted. But there will be a time, when the heavenly with hoarse
Bellowing the trumpet will shake the world, and when suddenly
All bodies will rise far and wide through all lands,
You will see these very things returned into their old shape.
Look at the world nodding with its convex weight,
And the lands, and the tracts of the sea, and the deep sky,
Look how all things rejoice in the age to come.
Article 12. LIFE EVERLASTING. AMEN
Then the harsh ages will grow mild, with wars laid aside,

div.note: a The Romans are by the best right called lords of the world, because in the possession of the Roman and Apostolic Church herself are all the spiritual treasures of the Christian religion. b Christ the Lord wished to give us wine in the sacrifice of the Mass, which brings forth virgins.
Christ the Lord wished to give us wine in the sacrifice of the Mass, which brings forth virgins.
That city, which is the Church of God, will be utterly bereft of fear, when all the elect, gathered into one heavenly Jerusalem, have happily come together.

lg.l: Nor will the trumpet give a terrible sound with sonorous bronze
Any longer, but the rewards of eternal life will be rendered,
Where there is deep peace, where there is supreme rest, where there are the joys of heaven.
The Ruler of Olympus will give an empire without end,
And he will set no bounds of space nor limits of time for his own.
GUIDE.
What is the Church?
MUSE.
Of the Christ-worshipping race (which, joined by the covenant of faith,
Is guided by divine commands, and through the great world
Is divided by vast tracts of lands) a large
Assembly it designates, which adores the Divinity of Christ:
Concerning which the Prophets once wrote, that this would be in war
An outstanding nation, and easy to sustain through the ages.
GUIDE.
Who is the supreme Shepherd of the Church of God?
MUSE.
To her is given an outstanding Shepherd by divine gift,
The supreme one who by dying restored the state to the lands,
hope of the heavenly flock, to whom he has granted the citadels on high:
It is of his office, both to impose custom upon peace,
To spare the subjected, and to vanquish the proud.
Rightly he will always be a God to me; his altar
A tender lamb from our sheepfolds will often stain.
O too happy flock, with this Master feeding it.
GUIDE.
Does Christ not have his vicar on earth?
MUSE.
Happy too are those whom the first after him feeds,
And to whom God thunders from his mouth that his own role has passed.
You, Roman Shepherd, remember to rule this flock,
By feeding them in empty glades, and along full
Rivers, where there is moss, and a bank most green with grass.
And let caves shelter them, and let a rocky shadow project forward.
Nor let the care of dogs be last for you, but together
The swift hounds of Sparta and the fierce Molossian
Feed with rich whey; never, with those as guards,
The nocturnal thief in the stables, and the attacks of wolves,
Or the unpacified Iberians from behind will you dread.
It is necessary to obey the orders and commands of God:
To feed his sheep and lambs, your greatest care,
Let that be your labor, this is the certain will of the Lord,

div.note: In the absolute sense, the supreme Shepherd of the Church is Christ the Lord himself.

lg.l: Joyfully obey the command, and unmoved will remain
the endeavours of your faith which it holds established.
GUIDE.
Is it enough for this flock that good Shepherds preside?
MUSE.
Provision will not be sufficiently made for the flock, and for the flock's master,
unless, shaking off sleep, the people of God resolve to keep watch:
Keep watch in haste, men; a snake lies hidden in the grass;
Let this fixed resolve to keep watch stand in the mind for the saints.
And no light harm has he done to those whom this vigilance has escaped.
Rise, come, let the way be by force. Relentless toil conquers all:
Stir up wars, and to set troops in the midst against the wolves,
lest they join the camps of the sheep, let it be your next care.
For just as a wolf lies in ambush against a full sheepfold,
when he growls at the pens, having endured winds and rains,
past midnight: the lambs, safe under their mothers,
keep up their bleating: he, fierce and relentless in his wrath,
rages against those out of reach; the gathered craving of eating
from a long time exhausts him, and his jaws dry of blood.
Not otherwise, when the Furies of Erebus see the
closed thresholds of this flock. And the sheepfolds are a care to the Shepherd,
their wrath kindles, and resentment burns in their hard bones,
by what method they might attempt approaches, and by what way the enclosed
lambs they might shake out from the stable, and pour them out through the fields.

div.note: In the empty glades of fasting and abstinence, the sheep of Christ find rich pastures; there too the rivers are full of water springing up into eternal life, from the fountains of the Saviour. Here by 'muscus' I understand something of another kind than that which is produced either from the earth or from animals: rather, an odor of sweetness, which proceeds from the fame of a good name. The bank greenest with grass is the barrier of chastity. And let caves shelter Monks and Anchorites under the shadow of the wings of Christ the Lord, which, because of the strength of its defense, may be called rocky. By the dogs, the whelps of Sparta, and the fierce Molossian, understand preachers, who ought to be steeped by the Apostolic See in the rich whey of sacred doctrine, so that they may teach others what is profitable for salvation.

div.n: Qui sunt prorsus ab Ecclesia alieni?

lg.l: Who are wholly estranged from the Church?
GUIDE.
As they keep the drones, a lazy herd, from the hives,
MUSE.
the busy bees, when they fill the honey with sweet nectar,
so must be kept far from the sheepfolds of the Lamb by me,
the faithless race of Solyma, the Gentile, the shipwrecked crowd
of abandoned faith, from whom the light is entirely taken away;
then those infected by the heretical plague, who seem to follow our
camp, while they boast themselves with a great name:
meanwhile the flooding error of a blind mind lies hidden,
they nourish wounds in their veins, which they do not open without war.
But they would rather fall to a cruel fate sooner,
than revoke their false faith, or the monsters of profane
perfidy by warning, and tame their proud arrogance.
There are those who entirely tear themselves away from the body itself,
like the brothers who conspired to tear down heaven,
and attempted to thrust Jove down from the realms above,
while they fiercely wished to drive out the Master of the flock
from his seat; thus they willingly departed from the stables,
separated from the rest, with common peace rejected.
To their side gathers a fierce crowd of wicked men,
whom heavy impiety, conscious of wicked guilt,
like some stormy Orion rising with the flood,
has carried into blind shallows, and deep within by the insolent South winds,
both through the waves, with the sea overcoming, and through impassable rocks,
has scattered into the Scylla of avenging censure; the unjust men,
Hence, snatched far from the folds and sheepfolds of the kindly
Shepherd, in vain to call the Gods to their vows,
and to use the accustomed altars of the divine service.
And according to their custom, to recline at the tables of the gods
they strive, in vain to rejoice in the merits of the pious,
which they sought for themselves, and the common words of those praying,
for, excluded, they are despoiled of these just laws:
Such power has been granted to man by the Highest.
A prayer to God, to avert such a great plague from the minds of men.
Almighty Father, whom the stars of heaven obey,
MUSE.
this I ask of thee, which is bound by no law of fate,
I entreat for Latium, for the majesty of the Thunderer,
That the native Latins not change their ancient name,
Or may you allow them to become heretics, or be called schismatics,
Or the men to change their speech, or alter their dress:
Let Latium be, let there be Alban kings through the ages,
Let the Roman offspring be powerful, by the virtue of Christ,
If no nation has equally celebrated your honors.
Let the Sect fall, and grant that it has fallen, along with Schism,
Lest the evil contagions of a neighboring flock do harm,
And lest the marsh cover the pastures with muddy rush,
For unaccustomed fodder would afflict the pregnant flock.
Let the plagues subside, and the custom and rites of sacred things
Adding, may you make all Latins of one voice.
Nourishing Parent of things, if you are bent by any prayers,
Look upon us, this only: and if we deserve by our piety,
Then grant your help, Father, and confirm all these things.
GUIDE.
By what means are heretics distinguished from Catholics?
MUSE.
The Teucrians had changed their shields, and the insignia of the Danaans
They had already adapted for themselves, when the walls of Troy were falling;
But suddenly, behold, the deceits and the lying weapons the Danaans
Recognize, and mark their mouths discordant in sound.
Thus a wolf, changed in spoils and face, of a sheep
If clothed in a wool-bearing fleece, in a beastly manner,
Should fill all things around with horrific howls.
In vain does the harmless wool feign love.
And the bleating flock, which discordant anger provokes.
A heretical man is easily distinguished from a Catholic by his very speech.
It belongs to the spirit of the Christians, of the faith or of the ancestral stock,
To proclaim the highest honors to the Supreme Pontiff.
(Just as it belongs to faith itself to help in doubtful matters)
At the same time for ambiguous matters to be thus resolved by a fatherly mouth,
So that faith may be certain: that by a divine mind have come together,
The Fathers, harmonious by the stable power of the fates,
Not ignorant of the sacred law, to whom an inspired ardor
Went, and granted to go to the stars with an uplifted face.
They say that by the honor of praise it deserved to be raised to the stars,
The see, sacred by religion in the Roman name,
Which God, with the exceptional gifts of the divine breath,

div.note: A heretic is easily told from a Catholic by his very speech.

lg.l: He enriched her, and from then on protected her from her very origin:
They wish whatever she teaches to be held to have weight,
A column resting on God, as on firm and solid adamant;
Which no force of men, nor they themselves to destroy in war
Would the Tartarean troops be able, nor a thousand phalanxes.
What fates await these men, I pray, do not seek to be taught,
And what death may one day engulf the guilty, in a burning tomb,
With God as witness, who deceive the wishes of so great a parent.
Should the Prophetess not be to you the surest messenger of truth,
To whom God Himself wished to entrust His own thoughts?
Cease, fool, to hope that God is swayed by praying,
So that you yourself may be able to enjoy the embraces of God the Father,
Turned away from this prophetic Seer, for whom will remain unmoved
The fates for her from her spouse, whose promises to be torn away
Will by no means be able. What opinion has turned you,
While such great weariness of a pious mother has seized you?
Is this the reward of piety? Thus do you wish to be restored to the sceptre
You are deceived, O race hateful to God, ignorant of the truth.
But rewards worthy of your deeds will be paid back to you,
Unless your hard heart melts like soft wax;
For this, this very honor of mortal life,
Which scarcely the skillful guarding of crops and flocks
Had forged for you trying all things, you will leave behind with your mother,
Nor will the Father be gentle to you, but an unjust stepmother.
Therefore come, turning your counsel for the better, believe me.
Behold, already he fulfills his words, and of the sea lay down the fierce
Hearts, God willing, and the land of Holland receives a quiet
Spirit towards the Latins, and a kindly mind,
Bringing its counsel for the better, and at last will cherish
The Romans, lords of the world, and the toga-clad race.
GUIDE.
Is the Church of God likened only to a sheepfold of sheep?
It is also likened to a fertile field.
MUSE.
It is like a rich field, which never, with the Deity offended,
Golden Ceres looks upon in vain from high Olympus;
A joyful field, with no cultivation does Moesia so much herself
Boast, and Gargara which marvels at its own harvests.
And as he who breaks the sluggish clods with mattocks
And drags the wicker hurdles, helps the fields of the farmer,
And he who, once the plain is broken up, the ridges that he raises,
breaks through again crosswise with turned plough,
and constantly works the earth, and commands the fields:
Thus God, this his field of rich earth,
while he allows it by the rakes of swords, and by the dark
to be worked, and to be carried off by violent death,
adorns it with more splendid cultivation. We marvel at the ears of corn
heavy with manifold offspring: what harvests do the plains
return from a richer bosom, with how much interest?
Unless a grain of wheat has died, it alone
remains; but if it has died, it brings forth much fruit.
CHAPTER II.
On Christian Hope, which is the anchor of salvation.
GUIDE.
What is Hope?
MUSE.
It is a virtue by which God thus sounds with a calm mouth
to heavenly minds, to whom there is confidence of the kingdom
infused from heaven, and the soul's sure hope of salvation:
O companions (for neither are we ignorant of prior evils)
O you who have suffered heavier things: God will give an end to these too.
You have approached both the Scyllaean rage, and the deeply sounding
crags: you have also experienced the Cyclopean rocks,
call back your courage, and send away sorrowful fear;
perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even these things.
Through various misfortunes, through so many hazards of things,
we make our way to our homeland, where the fates quiet resting places
show, there it is right to resume the scepters of the kingdom:
Endure, and save yourselves for favorable circumstances,
so that this anchor of the homeland may bind you with its hooked bite.
Press on, burning for the work, some to build walls,
