and to construct a citadel, and to roll up rocks with their hands:
some to prepare a place for a dwelling, and to enclose it with a trench.
Just as the bees, in early summer through the flowery countryside
toil busies beneath the sun, when the grown of the race
offspring they lead out, or when the liquid honey
they pack, and swell the cells with sweet nectar:
or they receive the loads of those arriving, or, forming a column,
they drive the drones, a lazy herd, from the hives.
The work glows, and the fragrant honey smells of thyme.
From where do we learn the manner of praying, and the practice of hoping? GUIDE.
From the Lord's Prayer, which is divided into 7 petitions.
MUSE.
What this manner of praying is, I shall first tell in order.
1st Petition. OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN: HALLOWED BE THY NAME.
Kindly Parent of things, who fill heaven with your divine presence,
May your honour, and your name, and the praises of your people always
resound through all the mouths of men far and wide around the towns,
just as the pathless thickets resound with tuneful birds:
May very many temples rise to you, to you may a thousand, with Sabaean
incense, altars grow warm, and breathe with fresh garlands.
2nd Petition. THY KINGDOM COME.
Us, your offspring, to whom you grant the citadel of heaven,
restore, brought back, to the sceptres of our lost empire.
3rd Petition. THY WILL BE DONE, etc.
No differently than in heaven, on earth may your sure will
stand unmoved by its own fates, to be heaped with triumphs.
4th Petition. GIVE US THIS DAY OUR DAILY BREAD.
May no Dawn bring forth her risings hither for us,
without supplying the pleasing gifts of toiled-for Ceres.

div.note: * With what zeal and industry we ought in this life to restore the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem.

div.n: 5. Petitio. ET DIMITTE NOBIS DEBITA NOSTRA, &c.

lg.l: 5. Petition. AND FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS, etc.
The wrath of no slight Deity pursues me,
great guilt has been committed: I pray that for me the tight
bonds be lifted, bid it so, and the monstrous offences dissolved by your Spirit;
even as we, wronged by our fellows, slacken the reins of pardon.
6. Petition. AND LEAD US NOT INTO TEMPTATION.
A hostile force rushes on, a crueller foe assails us,
whose aim is to wrap us, submerged, in Stygian flames;
Ensure that he does not drive us, once seized, to monstrous shores.
7. Petition. BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL.
But us, covered by the spreading shelter of your protection,
Protect us as we struggle, driven by so many misfortunes of life. Amen.
GUIDE.
Recite the Angelic Salutation:
HAIL MARY, FULL OF GRACE.
MUSE.
O how shall I name you, Mary? O offspring of Jesse?
Virgin full of God, of the fruits of the long-lived olive?
Be blessed, and may your honours be celebrated everywhere.
THE LORD IS WITH YOU.
The eternal Creator, whom the stars of heaven obey,
dwells with you as offspring; himself in that breast
He hides himself to refute the shared charge by an infamous
death, while he resolves to do so (this remains stored deep in his mind);
for your Son has struck these covenants for you with himself.
BLESSED ART THOU AMONG WOMEN.
Hence deservedly, before all others, you are three and four times blessed,
you shine bright in your childbearing: no mother is to be equalled to you,
great Mother of God. What ages so joyful bore you?
What parents so great begot one such as you?
The brightest lights of mothers are darkness (kindly one, in your sight),
and whatever glory of womanly praise exists anywhere,
and whatever belongs to my lot, becomes unequal to your honours;

div.n: ET BENEDICTVS FRVCTVS VENTRIS TVI, IESVS.

lg.l: By this one travail of birth you have embraced countless descendants,
all the heaven-dwellers, all who hold the lofty heights above.
AND BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF YOUR WOMB, JESUS.
And blessed are the offspring of your fruitful childbearing,
the fruit of a virgin womb, heavenly gifts,
the one salvation for the vanquished, the hope bestowed, gentle Jesus.
HOLY MARY, MOTHER OF GOD, etc.
Supreme parent of the heavenly ones, we the guilty call upon you in our prayers,
let it not displease you (while things proceed by the gentle nod of a mother)
to obtain by entreaty peace for your own, and the promised kingdoms,
lest, deprived of sweet life, by an ill-omened death
the black day carry us off, and plunge us in bitter death.
CHAPTER III.
On Charity.
Charity depicts herself in her own colours.
I am she who is the Queen and glory of the virtues,
kindling the marrow of the soul, like a gentle flame,
I nourish a wound in my veins, and am scorched by a hidden heat,
when the image of the dear Father comes to mind:
the great virtue of God keeps returning to my mind, and the great
honour of his praise; his face clings fixed in my breast,
and his words; nor does care grant peaceful rest to my limbs.
While this silent wound lives beneath my breast,
all the mockeries of the vain world delight me not at all,
since I deem nothing great, which does not equal you, O Godhead:
You are to me life, father, mother, and brother, and sister,
bridegroom strong in love; you, the nourisher of the holy heart,
giving the sacred cakes of wrought Ceres, of salvation,
and to the thirsting soul the gifts of heavenly Lyaeus.
What you allow me to will, grant by your divine will that I may be able to merit;
grant that I may more fully recognize the traces of the old flame,
and may the gratitude for so great a deed stand well with one who remembers;
and may I know neither sweet children, nor the rewards of Venus,
May I only be the daughter of so great a Father, to be joined in the triumphs
of the heavenly fatherland, destined to come beneath the vault of the Gods above,
while it is settled in my mind to fall to a heavier fate,
O God, before I violate you, and break your laws.
bursting the breathing-places of the soul with a deadly wound.
My mind moves me to hope for the sure salvation of life;
For it is my delight to undertake your holy commands,
and with kindled spirits to extend virtue by deeds.
By these things may I deserve to be deemed worthy of your favor?
Or to be called the daughter of the highest Father and invoked in prayers?
Or to be joined in stable wedlock, and dedicated as a spouse?
Or is it perhaps a sin for me to hold forth such marriage torches?
No: for your loving kindness has entered into these covenants with me,
and gave hope to my doubting mind, nor is your will changed.
Another care is mine (as our order demands)
For that is my labor, to run to the aid of my companions' affairs,
lest your offspring, whom you demand for the Olympus of heaven,
who is tossed about so much on all sides on land and on the deep;
piercing the ribs of the soul with mortal sin,
should collapse, and at last fall from the heavenly fields.
To me is given the power to kindle breasts with flames,
by which they may duly pay their dues to God the Parent.
But it is not in our power to cut out the wicked plague
of heretical fraud, and to subdue proud nations,
and the evil of perfidy, by which the conquered power of Kings
has lain prostrate on the ground, for so many gliding years now.
It does no good to have held out against it two thousand Camilli,
swift with the javelin, and superior to the rest by much skill.
Grant, Father, that this disgrace be abolished by our arms,
Almighty One. Not the spoils, or the trophy of repulsed
heresy, or any booty do I seek: to you let other
deeds bring praise; while this dire plague by my wound
falls repulsed, I shall return inglorious to my native seats.
Come then, great Parent, of this vow to succeed
grant a part, at the very least, lest the hostile force approach,
and it be seen by us as much more worthy of a triumph.
God first of all, then our neighbor as ourselves

div.note: * The order of charity consists in this, that we love ourselves for the sake of

lg.l: GUIDE.
How many are the precepts of Charity?
MUSE.
These two commandments chiefly through the swift breezes
the Messenger of the gods brought down, sent by the Father on high.
GUIDE.
What is the first and greatest commandment?
On the love of God.
MUSE.
Let your mind be wounded by this one sweet care;
let it nourish this one wound in its veins, and in the deepest recess
of the heart, so that the burning love of the divine Godhead boundlessly
may grow, driving its flames, and gather strength as it goes,
and, with the hiding places of the soul laid open, the heat may fly to the breezes,
pondering nothing else with itself, with inflamed heart,
than duly to pay its rightful dues to God the Father:
By this path let us hasten to Christ with wondrous love.
Thrice I pray that she may obtain by entreaty this great fire for me in my bones,
and inflame my kindled soul with greater love,
the exalted Mother of God, and lest my foolish mind resist her,
may she grant that I recognize more the traces of the old flame.
Scarcely had I said this, when the Virgin, with snowy arms on this side and that,
fondles the praying one in a soft embrace, and suddenly
he received the accustomed flame, and the familiar heat
entered his marrow, and ran through his melting bones,
not otherwise than when sometimes, burst by flashing thunder,
a fiery crack, gleaming, runs through the storm-clouds with light.
GUIDE.
What is the second, similar to this?
On the love of neighbor.
GUIDE.
What is the second commandment? THOU SHALT LOVE THY NEIGHBOR AS THYSELF.
MUSE.
Just as Nisus, to join Euryalus to his greatest deeds,
did not shun his companion, while he sent himself into battles,
following great-hearted Aeneas, and the utmost fame;
not otherwise, go far from us, you profane goads
of envy; let the unhappy man fear the furies, and the harsh river
of Cocytus let him fear, and the twisted circles of Ixion,
and the monstrous wheel, and the insurmountable stone:
Let this plague be banished from my mind, O best Father of things,
let no glory be sought for my deeds without you,
and grant that I may embrace my companions with a love equal to my own.
GUIDE.
By what sign does Charity towards God reveal itself?
MUSE.
That fiery vigor, by which for the friendly Deity supremely
we burn, is a certain heavenly origin of the soul.
A flaming force of ardor driving into the breast of lovers,
so that they thirst for nothing more than to uphold the laws of the Gods.
By this the faithful love of children towards the Deities reveals itself,
this one thing, I say, is the certain sign, if they undertake the commands:
For thus the very Wisdom of the highest Father teaches.
He who keeps my words, fulfilling the commands of the parent,
he bears witness to his true love for me.
GUIDE.
By what certain sign does Charity towards one's neighbor reveal itself?
MUSE.
The flaming force of companions, if the heat has kindled any
of the eternal Deity, to produce various for the mind
effects is accustomed, as the Apostle clearly begins with these words:
The fiery force of brothers is patient and benign to the harsh,
despising its own, it is not envious of another's praise:
It shudders at wicked things, nor swollen with tumid pride
does it allow itself to be puffed up, by repressing proud minds,
it holds the scepters, and softens minds, and calms angers,
and the untamed movements of the mind, with the ruling of the Thunderer's
command it represses, and curbs with chains and a prison:
No fickle ambition, no glory steeped in false paint
sits in its heart, nothing of vanity lingers in this seat;
nor does the gentle one rashly flare up into heavy angers,
it never turns over anything wicked in its heart concerning its companions,
It despises all wickedness, it is mindful of right and wrong
that God is the avenger: just as immortal to the just
worthy rewards it will bring, until the final of life shall have come
line: moreover it is devoted to the pursuits of true honor,
With ethereal strength the weapons of sinister fortune,
the madness of the winds, and the sounding storms
Joyful in mind she endures, nay, she suffers all hardships:
Even though at times she may be sick with immense cares,
She feigns hope on her face, she represses deep sorrow in her heart,
Turning over immense courage in her narrow breast.
Why are the ten commandments set forth?
GUIDE:
It is pleasing that those things be said more fully, which more concisely by mouth
Were said before, so that the obscure matter may become clear.
MUSE.
He sent down ten golden commands from high Olympus,
With the heavenly trumpet blaring, and with sonorous clarions,
The Almighty Father, whom the stars of heaven obey:
Overcome this yoke, he says, my fixed will for you,
Joyfully obey the command: for it will be pleasing to have fulfilled it:
He orders Moses to bring these mandates to the ears of the people.
The first commandment of the Decalogue, where in the name of the great God, Moses speaks thus to the people.
With such words the Almighty, who has the supreme power over things,
Begins: as he speaks, the lofty house of the gods falls silent,
And the earth is shaken from its foundation, the lofty ether is silent,
Then the Zephyrs settled, the sea stills its placid waters.
I myself am the Lord, the Ruler of great Olympus,
You shall by no means worship alien things, fashioning for yourself the divine powers of gods:
Let not your right hand form images of false gods:
For less will the deadly gift of unwed Minerva
Harm the Trojans, when Troy falls from its height,
With its walls overthrown, than the Mulciber of the golden calf
Will have harmed the Solymi: there remains stored deep in the mind
The judgment of the Israelite, and the injury of the spurned worship
Of the eternal name, and then of the ancestral religion.
What unattempted deed does vain superstition not contrive?

div.note: What is said here about the golden calf must be taken by anticipation, which is very familiar among the Prophets.

div.n: II. Præceptum. NON ASSVMES NOMEN DOMINI DEI TVI IN VANVM.

lg.l: The Second Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT TAKE THE NAME OF THE LORD THY GOD IN VAIN.
It is lawful for no one to swear by my Godhead, and thus deceive it:
That ancient race of Earth, the Titan brood,
Did not bear it unpunished, soon felt the wrath of the Godhead,
Cast down by the thunderbolt, they are rolled in the lowest abyss.
Behold Salmoneus paying cruel penalties,
While he attempts to deceive the mind, which is incapable of being deceived;
While, having imitated the flames of the Gods above, and the sounds of Olympus,
He went exulting, and demanded for himself the honor of the gods,
Madman, when the storm-clouds and the inimitable thunderbolt
He would simulate with bronze and the running of horn-hoofed horses:
But the almighty Father, among the thick clouds, his weapon
Hurled (not firebrands he, nor smoky from torches
Lights) and drove him headlong in a dreadful whirlwind.
Thus I would wish all to remember, that it is not to be borne unpunished,
The supreme name, to which you can equal none in praises,
To be attacked with a sacrilegious mouth. Though the wrath of the Gods above be rather slow,
Enraged at last, they demand penalties with blood.
The Third Commandment. REMEMBER THAT THOU KEEP HOLY THE SABBATH DAY.
This is the command of the Father, which it is wicked not to obey:
With such friendly words he addresses his offspring:
Let the seventh day, my progeny, be a care to you,
And celebrate all festivals favorably with pious devotions,
The annual ones, which it is a sin to postpone, as if from the mouth of a mother
They are proclaimed to the world: for neither have these solemnities upon you
A vain superstition, ignorant of false gods,
Imposed, but by the warnings and the Godhead of the gods,
Instructed you act, and you renew the deserved honors.
Not as once the Arcadian King undeserved honors
Brought to the boxer son of Amphitryon, and unworthy,

div.note: I thought indulgence should be granted to the neophyte Muse of Maro, so that at each of God's commandments she might cite profane examples of her own race, since the rationale of this my design demands that we hear him speaking in his own manner, as far as it can be done.

div.n: IV. Præceptum. HONORA PATREM ET MATREM, &c.

lg.l: Before the city in a grove. With him his son Pallas,
together all the foremost of the youth and the poor senate
were offering incense, and the warm blood smoked at the altars.
Then chosen youths, and the priest of the altar, eagerly
bring the roasted flesh of bulls, and load in baskets
the gifts of toiled-for Ceres, and serve Bacchus.
Let these things be far from ours; go far away, you profane
rites; let her be far from here, roused by the shaken sacred emblems,
the Thyiad, when, Bacchus being heard, the triennial spur her on,
orgies, and nocturnal Cithaeron calls with a shout.
Let us not suffer even the slightest mark to be branded upon the sacred rites
of the Christians, but let them be worthy of God, and pleasing to the saints,
and let nothing of disgrace touch our altars.
Let the festal day be veiled with festal foliage throughout the city,
The august, huge temple, sublime with a hundred columns,
let fill, with the immense zeal of ancestral piety,
the race devoted to God, and let it heap the altars with gifts.
IV. Commandment. HONOUR THY FATHER AND MOTHER, etc.
Let just honour be given to the worthy, and to both parents.
By the command of God, let this will be fixed in the offspring,
of a renewed mind to bring aid to the paternal roof,
and to relieve the family with help, and to add strength to the overcome,
which will be a matter of piety, to help with money and resources,
and for their own, to expose their head to heavy perils.
Thus once Aeneas, having followed the laws of piety,
desiring to carry his parent out of the Trojan flames,
utters such things with his voice, walking through weapons, through enemies;
Come then, dear Father, place yourself on our neck,
I myself will support you on my shoulders, nor will that labour weigh me down.
However things shall fall, one and a common peril,
one salvation shall there be for us both; to me little Iulus
let be a companion, and let my wife observe my footsteps from afar,
You, Father, take the sacred objects in your hand, and the ancestral household gods.

div.note: Here the manner of celebrating festivals in the custom of Christians is described more in particular.

lg.l: Having spoken thus, his broad shoulders and bowed neck,
covered over with a garment and the skin of a tawny lion,
he goes beneath the burden, and little Iulus to his right hand
entwines himself, and follows his father with unequal steps,
his wife comes up behind, hastening through the very dark places.
The Fifth Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT KILL.
It is lawful for no one to destroy life with cruel iron:
Excepted is the Judge, the avenger of wicked crime,
the champion of justice, to whom full power has been given
of removing the guilty from our midst by a violent death.
Hence he shall fall before his day, and unburied in the middle of the sand,
he who to overcome his unwary companion secretly with the sword
has dared, so that his offenses are atoned for with a far different punishment.
And although the crimes themselves can be hidden for a long time,
it happens nevertheless that the hidden wickedness cannot be kept secret forever.
Pygmalion, more monstrous in wickedness than all others,
pretending many things for a long time, deceived his sister with wondrous art:
But the very ghost of the unburied came in her sleep,
husband, lifting up his pale face in wondrous ways,
and the cruel altars, and his breast pierced with iron
he laid bare, and uncovered all the blind wickedness of the house.
Thus also the murder of Polydorus was betrayed by portents,
and made known was, of the twice and thrice unspeakable Thracian King,
the impiety, and the hunger for gold, by which the innocent is destroyed.
Shall I speak out? Or shall I be silent? A tearful groan from the bottom
of the mound is heard, and a voice returned is brought to my ears:
Why do you tear a wretched man, Aeneas? Spare now the buried,
spare to defile your pious hands; me to you Troy
bore no stranger: this blood does not flow from the wood:
Alas, flee the cruel lands, flee the greedy shore;
For I am Polydorus: here an iron covered me pierced through,
crop of weapons, and grew over me with sharp javelins.
Thus although wickedness hides itself in a concealed cave,
it is betrayed, so that it may pay the deserved penalties.
The Sixth Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT COMMIT ADULTERY.
To violate the rights of another's bed, and the marriage torches,
the eternal law forbids, to which the Julian law deservedly yields,
Which is set apart for Venus, and for the mighty weapons of Cupid.
Hence you, joined to a husband by the shared pact of the bed,
May you look upon the daughter of Tyndareus, hiding in a secret seat.
She, the Teucrians hostile to her on account of overthrown Pergamum,
And the punishments of the Danaans, and the wrath of her deserted husband,
Fearing, the common Fury of Troy and of her homeland,
Had hidden herself, and was sitting, hated, at the altars:
Here let it please to remember that a just husband does not endure,
A wife joined in wedlock to dissolve the shared laws,
But to be her own mistress, to hold forth blameless marriage-torches.
Fires blazed up in my soul, anger arises, the fallen
Consort to avenge, and to exact penalties for her wickedness.
Shall she, forsooth, unharmed, these roofs and her accustomed household gods
Behold? and will she go, joined to her injured husband?
And will she see her marriage and home, fathers and sons?
Accompanied by a crowd of mothers and by her father's servants?
Not so: for although no memorable name
Is in the punishment of a woman, nor does the victory have praise,
Yet to have extinguished the abomination, and to have exacted the deserved
Punishments I shall be praised, and it will please to have filled my soul
With avenging flame, and to have satisfied the ashes of the unspeakable
Crime, and to have averted this plague from the marriage bed.
But does not compel mortal breasts, virginal
By his command, the almighty Father, to preserve modesty.
Hence those whom, prone to Venus, fiery heat urges on.
The sacred laws release these to be joined in stable wedlock.
But you shall pay your vows to God, and shall abide by your word:
For faith must be kept with the Powers above, and chastely let the priest
Tend the sacred rites, and celibate let him mingle his hands with the altars.
The 7th Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT STEAL.
Sweet thefts are mixed too much with sad bitterness;
For wealth acquired by a thieving hand flows away of its own accord.
And thus hope, slipping backward, is wont to be carried away by theft.

div.note: Marriage is permitted to the free, not commanded. For, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 7: It is better to marry than to burn. But chastity must be kept by those who have bound themselves to this vow.

div.n: VIII. Præceptum. NON LOQVERIS CONTRA PROXIMVM TVVM FALSVM TESTIMONIVM.

lg.l: The sadder end of Cacus teaches this. He, by plunder
While he considers he must live, so that he may be rich and abound,
Four bulls of outstanding body from the stalls
He drives off, and as many heifers of surpassing beauty.
Meanwhile, when now he was moving the well-fed from the stalls
The son of Amphitryon the herds, and was preparing his departure,
At their departure the cattle began to low, and the whole grove
To be filled with complaints, and the hills to be left with a clamour.
One of the cows returned the call, and beneath the vast cave
She lowed, and, though guarded, cheated the hope of Cacus.
For at this there had blazed up in fury of Alcides with black
Gall the grief, he seizes arms in his hand, and heavy with knots
The oak club, and at a run seeks the steep heights of the airy mountain,
And Cacus, vomiting vain fires in the darkness,
He seizes, clasping him in a knot, and clinging fast he chokes
His squeezed-out eyes, and his throat dry of blood.
Immediately the black house is opened, its doors torn away;
And the stolen cattle, and the plunder he had forsworn
Are shown to the sky, and by the feet the shapeless corpse
Is dragged forth; hearts cannot be sated with gazing at
The terrible eyes, the face, and the shaggy with bristles
Chest of the half-beast, and the fires extinguished in his jaws.
The Eighth Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT SPEAK FALSE WITNESS AGAINST THY NEIGHBOUR.
To this are reduced insults, abuse, and the other sins of the tongue.
It is a great wickedness a comrade's reputation, and name, and honour
To harm, and to scatter ambiguous words among the crowd,
By which very often harsh hatreds are wont to be stirred up for many.
How many did the elder Drances, with his tongue, and hatreds, and accusation,
Hostile to the youth Turnus, stir up horrid wars?
While mothers, and wretched daughters-in-law, while the dear of sisters
Hearts of the mourning, and boys bereft of their parents
Curse the harsh war, and the marriage of Turnus;
They bid him himself to decide it with arms, and himself with the sword,
Who demands for himself the Kingdom of Italy, and the first honours;
Fierce Drances aggravates these things, and that he alone is called
he testifies, that Turnus alone is demanded for the combat:
He rises, and burdens him with these words, and heaps up wrath.
The contest of Drances' tongue against Turnus.
A matter obscure to no one, nor needing our voice,
you consult upon, O good King; all confess that they know
what the fortune of the people brings, but they hesitate to speak.
Let him grant the liberty of speaking, and let him relax his arrogance,
on account of whose unlucky auspices and sinister ways,
(I will speak indeed, though he threaten me with arms and death)
we see that so many lights of our leaders have fallen, and the whole
city has sunk in grief, while he attacks the Trojan
camp, trusting in flight, and terrifies heaven with his arms.
Turnus' equally bitter invective speech against Drances.
Would not violence swell in Turnus, inflamed by such words?
He gives a groan, and breaks forth these words from his inmost breast:
Ample indeed always is your abundance of speaking, Drances,
then when wars demand hands, and when the fathers are called,
you are the first present: but the senate-house is not to be filled with words,
which fly abundantly for you in safety, while it keeps the enemy at bay
the rampart of the walls, and the trenches do not overflow with blood.
We go against the foe. Why do you delay? Or will your Mars
in your windy tongue, and in those fleeing feet
always be? Will your right hand always be cold for war?
Am I defeated? Or will anyone justly, you most foul man, that I am defeated
claim? who the swollen Tiber to rise with Trojan
blood, and will see the whole of Evander with its offspring
house to have fallen, and the Arcadians stripped of their arms?
Not thus did Bitias and huge Pandarus experience me,
and the thousand whom I sent down to Tartarus as a victor in a day.
IX. Precept. THOU SHALT NOT COVET THY NEIGHBOUR'S WIFE.
He who is consumed by a blind fire for another's wife,

div.n: X. Præceptum. NON CONCVPISCES REM PROXIMI TVI?

lg.l: He nourishes a wound in his veins. Although into these pacts never
he may have entered: this man is guilty of having broken the marriage bed.
But indeed the will of the mind must be reckoned as a deed.
To this one fault Dido could have yielded.
But no diligence more shapes their strength,
Than to turn away Venus, and the goads of blind love;
And therefore they banish the bulls far away and into lonely
Pastures, behind an opposing mountain and across glad rivers,
Or keep them shut inside at full mangers:
For she gradually consumes their strength, and burns them as they gaze,
The female, and allows them to remember neither the groves nor the grass.
The Tenth Commandment. THOU SHALT NOT COVET THY NEIGHBOR'S PROPERTY?
Let ill-advising hunger and the dire desire of possessing be
driven far away from the moderate threshold of your heart.
Lest you steal anything belonging to another, draw in the sails
of your desire entirely, and blunt the wishes of your mind,
retaining nothing with burning desire, nothing in your heart
that is unjust; not the roof of a house, not fields, or a yoke,
you shall not take a lowly manservant, or a lesser maidservant,
not the hide of an ox, not the fleece of a slow ass,
in short, none of the things which the great world contains.
How much blood the pursuit of another's stag cost the Ausonians, under Ascanius.
While the Cocytian virgin sudden madness to the dogs
casts, and touches their nostrils with the familiar scent,
so that burning they might hunt the stag: was this the first of the evils
cause, and did it kindle the rustic minds to war?
There was a stag of outstanding beauty, and huge with its antlers,
the boys of Tyrrhus, which, snatched from its mother's udder,
and father Tyrrhus were rearing; to whom the royal
herds obey, and the custody of the plain far and wide is entrusted;
accustomed to commands, their sister Silvia with all care,
weaving them with soft garlands, used to adorn its antlers,
and she would comb the wild beast, and wash it in a pure spring,
He, submitting to the hand, and accustomed to his master's table,
He used to wander in the woods, and again to the familiar threshold
he himself would betake himself home, however late at night.
Him, wandering far off, the swift hounds of hunting Iulus
roused, when by chance down the stream
he was floating, and relieving the heat on the green bank.
He himself too, inflamed with the love of outstanding praise,
Ascanius, directed his arrows from his curved bow.
Nor was chance absent from his erring right hand, and driven with a loud
sound, the reed came through his belly and through his flanks;
But the wounded four-footed beast fled back within the familiar house,
and moaning entered his stalls, and bleeding, with his complaint,
and like one imploring, he filled the whole house.
The sister Silvia first, striking her arms with her palms,
calls for help, and summons the hardy rustics:
They (for the fierce plague lies hidden in the silent woods)
are on the spot unlooked-for: this one armed with a fire-hardened brand,
this one with the knots of a heavy club; whatever was found by each
as he searched, anger makes a weapon. Tyrrhus calls the troops,
as by chance, with driven wedges, an oak split in four
he was cleaving, breathing monstrously with his snatched axe.
Nor is the discord finished for you in sad war,
which bespattered the Teucrians with so much Ausonian blood.
Epilogue of the Decalogue.
The fates wished you to lead your life under these, their own
auspices, not by your own will to settle your cares:
Therefore execute the commands of God; let this be your greatest care:
And just as ants a huge heap of spelt
when they ravage, mindful of winter, and store it in their home,
the black troop goes through the plains, and their booty through the grass
they convey on a narrow path, some push the large
grains of corn, straining with their shoulders, some marshal the troops,
and chastise delays: the whole path seethes with the work.
Thus he whom the great glory of the highest things moves,
he himself moreover undertakes labor for his own praise;
he burns to depart in flight, and to leave the sweet lands,
and to expose his intrepid head to a thousand dangers,
astonished by so great a warning, and by the impulse of the Thunderer,
there is one love in his heart, to seek the heavenly kingdoms,
Let it delight to prepare arms, and to lean on strong oars:
To this one love it is right for you to submit your spirit.
Let fierce fear drive them headlong, whithersoever the ropes
To shake out, and to stretch the sails to unfavourable winds,
Between either way of death, Scylla and Charybdis,
Unless they hold their course, it is resolved to turn the sails back.
Loose the sails swiftly: a God sent from the high ether
To hasten flight, and to cut the twisted cables,
Behold, again he urges: I ask you, let no delay hold you back.
On the precepts of the Church.
GUIDE.
How many are the precepts of the Church?
MUSE.
Such as was once the Queen to the Sabaean peoples
Amazed at the words of him holding the sceptres of the kingdom of the Solymi;
Or such as she, ruling over her own, bore herself joyfully,
Through the midst, urging on the work and her paternal realms,
When at the doors of Saba, in the middle vault of the temple,
Enclosed by arms, and resting high on her throne, she sat,
She gave rights and laws to men, and the labour of works
She equalized in just parts, or perhaps relieved it;
Such is the bride of God. With a crown of winged ones surrounding her,
Who, enclosed by virgin choirs, bound with a tiara,
In sublime adornment hiding her head among the clouds,
Gave five commands to the flock, and to her reborn offspring.
GUIDE.
What is the first? On the observance of feast days.
MUSE.
She wishes to keep these feast days, by approved custom.
Not temples of solid marble to Phoebus and Trivia
To be established, and a sacred day from the name of Phoebus,
Where the fire is in the middle and companions crown the bowl,
and, pouring libations, call upon Lenaeus; then Menalcas
Sets up contests of the swift javelin on an elm,
And strips very hard bodies in the rustic wrestling-place:
This rite the ancient farmers once held.
But the nourishing mother Church, with pious duties,
Orders these days to be observed and interrupted things to be stopped,
She wishes the works and play of the exempted one to hang suspended, and the threats
Huge, of the walls, and the ramparts equalled to the sky.

div.n: II. Præceptum. SACRVM MISSÆ OFFICIVM DIEBVS FESTIS REVERENTER AVDITO.

lg.l: And the hands of craftsmen to cease, with labor laid aside,
So that his people may ponder heavenly gifts in their mind.
Yet it is lawful to perform certain things on feast days,
Which pious laws allow: to lead down the streams no
Religion has forbidden, to stretch a hedge before the crop,
To contrive snares for birds, to burn the brambles,
And to plunge the bleating flock in the healthful river:
He has given the remaining suns in order as fortunate for works.
II. Precept. HEAR THE SACRED OFFICE OF THE MASS REVERENTLY ON FEAST DAYS.
If once the Aeneadae, called from a great name,
Were offering sacrifices to the Dionaean mother, and to the gods
As patrons of the works begun (if it is lawful to believe it)
And a varied bleating flock, and to the High One a shining
Bull they were accustomed to sacrifice, to the King of the heaven-dwellers;
And if once Alcides won his own sacred rites by merit,
Antiquity stands as a great witness in all lands,
While Cacus, vomiting vain fires in the darkness,
He seizes, embracing him in a knot, and clinging to him, chokes
His squeezed-out eyes, and his throat drained of blood:
If from that time the honor has been celebrated, and joyful descendants
Observed the day, and Potitius, the first founder,
And the Pinarian house, guardian of the Herculean rite,
Set up a great altar in the grove; what is the glory of the deed?
Who will relate how much better it is that his sacred rites to the Thunderer
Be duly celebrated, and the altars be loaded with gifts?
And to call upon the common God, by whose vengeance, of Dis
The dark house is immediately opened, its doors torn away?
And the drawn-forth fathers, and the foresworn plunder
Are shown to heaven, while the dragon gnashes dreadfully?
III. Precept. OBSERVE THE FASTS DECLARED ON CERTAIN DAYS, AND ABSTINENCE FROM CERTAIN FOODS.
Of praiseworthy Hippolytus, and Epidaurus, tamer of horses,
Who press on with various pursuits, as the time approaches, and all

div.n: Dulta ab equis similitudo hominibus applicatur.

lg.l: They devote their care to swelling him out with dense fat,
the one they have chosen as leader and named husband of the herd;
and they cut flowering grasses, and supply him with streams,
and grain, lest he prove unequal to the pleasing labor,
and lest weak offspring reproduce the fasting of their fathers:
But the mares themselves they purposely thin down with leanness,
And when known pleasure now the first mating
provokes, they deny them leaves, and keep them from the springs:
often too they shake them with running, and weary them in the sun,
when the threshing-floor groans heavily with the shorn crops, and when
the empty chaff is tossed to the rising west wind.
They do this, lest by too much luxury the dulled use
be for the generative field, and clog the sluggish furrows.
Each group is duly prepared by such a distinction.
The analogy drawn from horses is applied to humans.
Not otherwise, intent in mind like a provident mother,
the Bride of God wishes different people to be bound by different laws.
Those whom hard labor exercises, lest the grim break them,
gripes of a barking stomach, for these she relaxes her reins,
nor does the pious mother keep the weary flock from the mangers.
Boys and tender girls rejoice in an equal lot,
the woman in labor, the one having brought forth offspring, and the one nursing at the breast,
and feeble old men, and the throng of beardless youth,
and those who drag broken joints and exhausted limbs.
But for those whose age is blooming in youthful years,
(Each best day of life for wretched mortals
although it flee first, and fierce diseases approach,
and labor and the harshness of hard death wear them down)
these she knows how to restrain, just as she knows how to give loose reins to the wretched:
The feasts which by custom they are accustomed to tear with a greedy
tooth, the parent denies and forbids, zealous for their salvation:
The roasted flesh of an ox, or a boar, and fat venison,
and every kind of meat, nor is it lawful to feed on eggs
for a barking stomach, and for one bearing in the belly a rabid
wolf, a grim thing for the stables; while there is a wondrous desire to chew, / until hunger is taken away, and the love of eating is suppressed.

div.n: IV. Præceptum. PECCATA TVA SACERDOTI PROPRIO, &c. SINGVLIS ANNIS CONFITETOR.

lg.l: Let it please them to remember the Corycian, to whom a few of abandoned
acres of land there were, and those not fertile for bullocks,
nor a crop suitable for flocks, nor convenient for wine,
he matched the wealth of kings in spirit: and returning late
at night to his home, he loaded his tables with unbought feasts.
For he had sparse greens among the brambles, and around white
lilies, and planting vervains, and the slender poppy,
yet he banished little greens greased with fat lard.
Imitate this old man, O youth, whose virtue is vigorous,
and let it stand in your mind never to break the laws of the fast
maternal, and let it come to mind that it is beautiful to die in this
pursuit of virtue, thus you will not despise common things.
IV. Precept. YOU SHALL CONFESS YOUR SINS TO YOUR OWN PRIEST, &c. EVERY YEAR.
A gentle bridle is the sorrow of a bruised breast, and
the annual confession of the committed stain into the ear
of your own pastor, brought forth from the bottom of the heart.
And, lest by chance to your Cupentus the fierce monsters of your crimes
you refuse to reveal, lest thus you offer exposed to the iron
your breasts to the glowing, you whom savage fires terrify,
lest shame hinder your freedom to confess dreadful deeds,
It is granted to you by lot to present yourself at a faithful throne,
and you choose the ear of those who supply the place of the shepherds;
for this is the right granted to the guilty, by received law.
Who, I pray, with this bridle, will drive bloody foam from his mouth?
Would that it might please us to bind ourselves more frequently with this thong:
But that indeed is a matter of counsel; yet our offenses once every year
to wash away, we are bound by the command and warning of heaven,
when the year next after the eleventh has now taken us.
and it is granted to touch the fragile branches from the ground.
Unless you do this, let your mind be, by a heavier blow of the wound
wounded, indeed to be cured by no potent herbs.

div.note: This is to be understood not of just any fast day, but only in Lent, at which time the use of eggs is forbidden until Easter day.

div.n: Docet hic Musa Maronis, quòd Confessio nos grauiori peccatorum pondere exoneret.

lg.l: Here Maro's Muse teaches that Confession unburdens us of the heavier weight of sins.
Never does the keeper, the driver of the slow little ass, with oil,
or with cheap fruit load it, and, returning, a stone
hammered out, or a lump of black pitch bring back from the city,
without sometimes unburdening the beast, its labor relaxed,
for several spaces of hours: for, as the poet witnesses,
What lacks alternate rest is not lasting.
Is there any respite, is there any rest for one pressed by a heavier crime?
What does it profit this man, for great cycles, with the rolling months,
to be weighed down in vain by the mass of such great crimes?
To unburden yourself, wretched one, a sweet relief for you in your weariness,
if it pleases, is at hand; it remains to confess your offenses:
Then I, if it pleases, will lead you to the full mangers.
Lest to turn over the bristling field with broken clods
be burdensome, I will scatter the hiding places and recesses of the soul.
The Fifth Precept. THOU SHALT RECEIVE THE MOST HOLY EUCHARIST AT LEAST ONCE A YEAR, AND THAT AROUND THE FEAST OF EASTER.
The horses of the Sun bring back the sacred feasts of Easter in their four-horse chariot,
The very offspring of God presents himself at the holy altars,
Standing, he invites the people, and proclaims honor for the temples,
And he wishes that his own people, rejoicing among themselves, attend to the banquets,
While he especially gladdens the new dishes with abundant wine,
Pouring heavenly wines from bowls as a new nectar,
The gifts and the joy of God. Then all these things are free:
For to him there is no value in a price, he gives each thing unbought.
Behold, the inner house, splendid with royal luxury,

div.note: Confession is a sweet bridle, suitable for restraining sensuality, by which one may be led away from sinning.
If one is held by the guilt of mortal sin, just as even at a younger age we can be conscious of a graver sin, as St. Gregory witnesses in his Dialogues.
Lest it be difficult for anyone to examine his conscience, the priest promises him his help in drawing out sins.

lg.l: It is prepared, and banquets lie open in the middle of the temples;
Garments worked with skill, and of proud purple,
There is massive silver on the altars, and chased in gold
The brave deeds of the fathers, a very long series of events.
Many gather, bidden to recline on painted
Couches of varied flower, with fragrant garlands on all sides.
Servants give water for the hands, and bread from baskets
They serve, and bring napkins with shorn nap.
CHAPTER IV.
On the Sacraments.
GUIDE.
How many Sacraments are there?
MUSE.
Just as, renewed by a sevenfold kind of things, is nourished
The life of men on earth, so that which is the one for mortals,
Seen as the salvation of the soul, rightly demands for itself seven
Mystical gifts from the sacred shrines, which cure wounded
Hearts: let antiquity be as a great witness of the faith.
Let not the Shepherd, to apply healing hands to the wounds,
Refuse, and burden God, demanding better omens:
For the fates preserve this man, and he feeds on the air
Ethereal, and never lies dead in the cruel shades,
(Even though the mind be covered in vices, very close to death)
If only, groaning much, he wash himself with that draught
Diligently, and take these cups of medicine for the soul.
It will not be the way of death, however much, fiery, in the veins
Driven through all, thirst has burned up the wretched limbs:
He will not die like a calf in the joyful grass,
And he will not yield his sweet soul at the full mangers,
These things, on the contrary, are destruction itself to the wolves, and revived by furies
They will burn, and they themselves, their own, now under a sick death,
(May fate grant better things to the pious, and that burning to the enemies)
Will tear torn limbs with bare teeth.

div.note: Here is designated the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, as it is received in the divine service.
The table of communion is destined for the great supper.
The servants give water in the sacrifice of the Mass.

lg.l: Not the shades of lofty groves, not the heavenly can
meadows move the mind; nor the stream which, rolled over the rocks,
purer than amber, seeks the plain; but the lowest
flanks are loosened, and a stupor weighs upon sluggish eyes,
and the neck droops to the earth with its downward weight.
GUIDE.
What are those seven things necessary for temporal life?
MUSE.
Here is unrolled the sevenfold order of nature's aid:
First of all, at the rising of the light we are brought forth into the breezes.
But scarcely has this fleshly mass, drawn out by a sorrowful birth,
come forth into the light, but suddenly it desires the beginning of the body
to be strengthened on all sides with gathered strength,
to grow, and to be increased until firm bones and muscles
it puts on, and exercises the great joints of the limbs.
So that the body may then be able to stand firm on its own sinews,
hunger must be taken away by feasts, and at the same time the mouth must be moistened
with a bowl of foaming Bacchus, unless perhaps through the heat
to quench thirst with a leaping stream of sweet water,
be better for the thirsting mouth, or custom so require.
And since by disease, a pitiable storm of the sky frequently
arises, laying waste to all things far and wide around;
Nor does a whirlwind driving a storm rush so thick over the sea,
as the many plagues of cattle, and suddenly of men,
seize the bodies and the whole race from its origin:
Hence Iapis, beloved by Phoebus before all others, is sought,
who, an old man girt in his cloak in the manner of a physician,
may fearlessly try to help whichever panting one he can.
Nor is it enough for physicians to shut out the causes of diseases,
unless with aids the strength broken by the whirlwind of disease
you restore, driving away the remnants, strengthening the vigor.

div.note: By the wolves are designated the heresiarchs, who despise and repudiate the Sacraments of the Church.

These things are to be understood allegorically concerning the refreshments of the sheep of Christ, of which heretics, since they are not of the number of those sheep, but rather ravenous wolves, by the just judgment of God, are entirely deprived.

lg.l: The more their strength is exhausted, the more fiercely they all
press on to repair the ruins of the fallen race.
Now a twofold restoration of our race remains:
One part proclaims the laws of the forum, and human rights;
And the other part opens the homes of Astraea and of Heaven.
that both estates be fostered, the secular as well as the Ec-
An apostrophe to the Church of Christ.
Nurturing mother of Christians, resting on the pillars of faith,
Since you are joined in stable marriage, and dedicated to Christ,
come, bearing children, supply offspring for both these courts.
To add special honors to the leaders themselves,
Make it your care, and to foster the life of the skilled,
Who preside over the rest; both those who handle civil affairs,
(Whence they bear their temples shaded with the civic oak)
Pondering the laws, as well as those who handle heavenly things, by the command
Of the eternal Deity, fill the benches by their office.
Application of these seven to the Sacraments of the Church.
Now I will teach, pay attention, how these seven correspond to souls. MUSE.
The first Sacrament is Baptism.
First of all, the soul has its own beginnings of life,
But bathed in the purifying wave of salty sprinkling,
As if just born we draw the vital air;
And the mind, weighed down by the heavier burden of Adam's stain,
Previously buried in death, is called back from sad Orcus,
And purified by the rays of justice, is reborn innocent.
For as soon as the body, with a sacred descent to the breast,
The power of heavenly water touches, the old shadow perishes,
And a new light arises, just as when a smoky cloud
Is sometimes lifted high into the ethereal breezes,
It first kindles with the flashes of the sun; then
Driving away the smoke, it is clothed in light, and gleams far and wide;
Finally it becomes, with radiant flames, a rival of the Sun.

div.note: * For the restoration of the Christian Republic it is necessary that both estates be fostered, the secular as well as the Ecclesiastical.

lg.l: The second is Confirmation.
Thence the fiery vigour of the divine breath within
strengthens the powers with might and supplies courage,
by which you may be able to conquer, or to fall in brave death.
There is no need for Achates to strike a spark from flint,
and catch the fire in leaves, and dry things around
bring as nourishment, and catch the flame in the tinder:
Immediately the devouring fire to the highest rooftops by the wind
is rolled, the flames rise above, the heat rages to the breezes
of the intent breast, the breaths of heavenly life
in the zeal of catching. Just as the companions strained,
formerly, the twelvefold cohort of Christ; and kindled with cares
their breasts, like offspring bereft of a lost parent:
For twice five days they kept silent, they stand at the closed threshold,
and they pray of one mind, and demand the promises of the Lord;
When suddenly the heavens thundered, and to be moved with a great
they seemed, as if once by the whirlwind of an approaching wind
the heights of the roofs, and the dwelling to be filled with terror:
While they fear, more and more the huge sky thunders
with manifold flame, then a tongue with flashing rays
frequent, in the manner of snow, scatters sparks of fire.
Immediately they were astounded in their minds, and the promised gifts
submissive they acknowledge, nor do they so much greet the sent-down
signs from the sky with eager shout, as fervent with silent
vows in fear they double: no less does it roar in the ether,
and flaming fleeces glide from the high sky;
By this the more the sounds were heard, while with much lightning
in divided order, and harmless with a soft touch
a flashing tongue of fire sat on the head of all:
The crown burns on the head. Then the holy fills the breasts,
Spirit, and breathing gently the breeze embraces
ethereal the senses and entwines fire in the minds.
This way must be entered by us, this sea must be plowed,
so that it may be permitted to rejoice in the favorable breath of the breeze.
The third is the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist.
It is certain that by the food of the soul strength increases for the living,
And that strength is increased within for brave deeds. But what
nourishments fill men with bold spirits?
Than which better things cannot be given from the fruits of the high
Deity to the human race, as a gift of the gods.
O Father, O boundless goodness, best God, with what
food do you restore souls? How sumptuous to the palate
does it please you to have given wines to ours, with which the mysteries of the sacred
sober, of Bacchus we may celebrate, in the manner of our ancestors?
For your Bride lives thriving, your pledges, O Christ,
And having embraced your body, having embraced your blood,
having embraced the feasts and cups of the divine table,
your gifts, O Christ, and the monuments of your cruel pain.
But indeed when we place gifts on the incense-burning altars,
that the meager bread is changed into the limbs of the body
of the immense one we believe: but also this, wonderful to say,
(forbear to shake faith) that the sacred liquids shine,
and the seen wines to turn themselves into rosy blood.
On the fruit of this great Sacrament.
What flames in the mind, what fires in the bones does it entwine,
O Son of the highest Father, my great power, my strength,
the ample virtue of your supper, and of the rosy blood,
among the heavenly tables, and the Bacchic liquid?
Who would deny that by this food strength is recalled to battle?
And the bronze-clad battle-lines of sad Avernus to be broken?
And immense courage to be drawn in, while with bloody slaughter
the hostile force rages, while the innocent is destroyed by the sword?
Come, tell, what is the appearance of things? How great a change
has brought things back for the better? What correction of morals,
where these sacred rites thrive, and there is more frequent use of this
fruitful chalice? O you for whom, untouched by age,
the blood courses, and whose solid strength is in its own vigor,
let it not displease you to say, whom have they not made eloquent,
these divine liquids, with a great love of piety
kindled: alas, why still to be foul to our palate
do we suffer the delights of the Lord, known above the ether!
O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts,
whom to violate with the hand, and with bold jaws the disc
of changed bread into the limbs of the divine body,
And instead of sacred banquets, to use rustic fruits;
Impiety has compelled, and the forgetfulness of ancestral faith.
Woe at the same time to those whom, with an unclean breast, to turn their bites b
Against this kind of fruits, the lack of eating has driven.
Woe also to the faithless faithful, whom, driven by laws, c
It is right to be compelled by force, to recline at the tables of the gods.
I would like these to remember that they are true Latins,
The race of Christians, righteous not by bond, nor by laws,
Of its own accord, holding itself by the custom of the eternal God.
As the Trojans, their feast consumed, to turn their bites
Extreme want compelled against the scanty Ceres,
And not to spare the fateful crust, the broad squares:
Hey, we are even consuming our tables, said Iulus,
Joking no more, that heard voice, of labors
First brought an end, and first from the mouth of the speaker
The father snatched it up, and astounded by the divine will, checked it:
Immediately: Hail, land owed to me by the fates,
And you, he says, O faithful household gods of Troy, hail:
Here is our home, this is our country, for my father such things to me
(Now I recall) Anchises left as secrets of the fates:
When hunger, son, you, carried to unknown shores,
Shall compel, your feast being diminished, to consume your tables.
Then, exhausted, remember to hope for homes, and there,
to set your first dwellings with your hand and fortify them with a rampart.'"
You are deceived, Aeneas, you are greatly deceived, guest:
That was not the hunger, which awaited you as the final one,
To put an end to your ruins; but the spelt cakes,
Now known to the sacred rites of Christians, and of the poured blood
The abundant streams of the Lamb, about to bring an end to labors
The holy monuments of God teach. Therefore let there be immense shame
And a great impiety for you, brought forth by better fates
O race, by the compelling command of the great parent of the Gods
And by his authority to be driven to these dishes of so great a table
Let force not have to be applied to you, but rather may you be carried of your own accord:
Let the seasonings for you, stimulating a sluggish taste,
Be piety, and hoary faith, and the fervor of love:
For the manifest flavor will give proof, and the mouths
Of those trying the sweet things, it will soothe with a friendly sensation,
And at the same time you will be satisfied with the rich delights of the Lord,
And you will begin to be moved alike by the pure wine and by the gifts,
And you will fulfil the great love of the true Father.
The fourth is the Sacrament of Penance.
Will medicine for the soul be lacking to sick mortals?
Shall hearts, then, O Christ, languish under grievous disease,
And will you not pity bruised souls and shattered fortunes?
If Venus, shaken by her son's undeserved pain,
Plucked, as a mother, dittany from Cretan Ida,
A stalk with downy leaves, and crowned with a flower
Of purple (those are not unknown to wild goats
Grasses, when winged arrows have lodged in their backs)
If Venus, her face veiled in a dense cloud, this
Brought down: with this the dark water in gleaming basins
She tinctures, secretly medicating, and sprinkles the healthful
Juices of ambrosia, and fragrant panacea:
With that water aged Iapis bathed the wound,
Unknowing, and suddenly from the body fled all
The pain indeed, all the blood was stanched deep in the wound,
And now, following the hand, with no one forcing it, the arrow
Fell out, and fresh strength returned for the battle.
What is it fitting that the Father, sprung from the Godhead, could do?
What to have willed at the same time, in curing the wounded of the mind
Wounds of his children: let not Apollo, the founder, of the medical
Presume to be held of this art: to potent herbs
Nature gave no way; but Jesus alone
Cures every kind of disease, and the deeply gaping
Wounds of his beloved offspring: to confess every crime
He willed the guilty meanwhile, then their breasts with their palms
To beat, and to heave a mighty groan from the depth of the heart,
Thus at last to be loosed from their bonds, by the ministering key,

div.note: First are designated the heretics, who violate this sacrosanct Sacrament with sacrilegious hands and with profane mouth and heart.
Of the second kind are those who communicate only out of necessity and fear of death.
Noted are the cold Catholics, who, were they not bound by law, would scarcely approach this holy table once a year.

div.n: De tribus partibus pœnitentia, videlicet contritione, confessione, & satisfactione, que variis agrestibus instrumentis assimilantur, quibus siluescentem mentis agrum excolimus.

lg.l: Which God instituted for the sake of removing the death
Of the prostrate mind, by the lethal blow of a wound.
On the three parts of penance, namely contrition, confession, and satisfaction, which are likened to various rustic implements, with which we cultivate the wild-growing field of the mind.
Ceres first mortals to turn the earth with iron
Instituted, when already the acorns and arbutus berries of the sacred
Woods were failing, and Dodona was denying sustenance.
Yet unless you pursue the earth with constant harrows,
Prune back the shadows with a sickle, and call upon the rain with vows,
Alas, in vain will you await another's great heap;
And you will console your hunger in the woods by shaking an oak.
Thus labor is added to the earth of the mind, so that baneful the stalks
Blight might eat, and the lazy might bristle in the fields
Thistle: the crops perish, a rough wood comes up,
Both burrs and caltrops, and among the shining cultivated lands
The unlucky darnel and barren wild oats dominate.
Hence the mind has its own weapons, just as for rustic gifts,
The plowshare, and first the heavy oak of the bent plow,
And the slow-rolling wagons of the Eleusinian mother,
And threshing-sledges and drags and harrows of oppressive weight,
Besides the wicker-work of Celeus, and cheap equipment,
Arbutus hurdles, and the mystic winnowing-fan of Iacchus.
These three parts supply weapons to you, having confessed;
Especially when many predictions of former Prophets
Terrify with dreadful warning: a cry strikes the upper air.
You are beaten, and you feel cares deeply in your tamed breast;
Just as the mourning nightingale under the poplar shade,
Laments her lost offspring, which a harsh plowman
Observing them, dragged them unfledged from the nest: but she
Weeps through the night, and sitting on a branch, her pitiful song
Renews, and fills the places far and wide with mournful complaints,
Dripping with a shower. Truly tears are not rolled down in vain,
The mind remains unmoved in good: and it is settled in the heart to have atoned for offenses, until the dregs are conquered by grief.

div.n: Quintum Sacramentum, quod est, Extremæ vnctionis.

lg.l: of greater crimes, which one is then not ashamed to confess;
so that a most holy life, although late, may follow,
so that, with committed sins sent into dark Tartarus,
Astraea, returning bright from heaven, may revisit the earth,
bringing back the ancient examples of the saints' virtue.
The Fifth Sacrament, which is of Extreme Unction.
But the compassion of Christ, to soothe the grieving soul
desiring by consoling, and to turn away cares with prayers,
groaning much, and shaken in mind by great grief,
to these another help for the mind (when the final of life
threads the Fate draws out, while the hostile force approaches)
added, ordaining this, that a priest in pure vestment
should come forth, and bearing bowls with sacred oil,
should touch the sick man, with prayers poured out to the stars,
that he may take away the remnants of sin; so that life and health,
and new strength may return to the languishing man as before.
On the twofold remedy of the Sacraments for preserving the Christian Commonwealth.
But now the ruin of the fallen race to be repaired
is twofold: a double medicine has been granted to these for salvation.

div.note: By the threshing-sledges, drags, and harrows armed with teeth, by which the earth is pricked and crushed, I considered that the compunction of our heart should be suggested, as it is the first part of penance. But by the plough, and the ploughshare, by which the earth is opened, turned over, and as it were vomited out, I thought that confession itself, which is the second part of the same Sacrament, should not incongruously be understood, insofar as by confession itself we open our conscience to the vicar of Christ, and root out the filth of the soul. Finally, by the mystic winnowing fan, by which the grain is purged and separated from the chaff, as also by the slow-rolling wagons of the Eleusinian mother, by which the crop is carried into the barn, I understand satisfaction, by which we are moved to produce fruits worthy of penance. Luke 3.

lg.l: The sixth Sacrament is Matrimony.
Hence, lest anyone contemplate a secret love,
and call it marriage, and cloak his fault with this name;
lest this evil creep more widely, the divine powers
the social pacts of the bed in stable wedlock,
have granted to be confirmed by law in a solemn rite:
let it be pleasing to lead solemn processions to the shrines.
And since the bonds of marriage are a care to God alone,
with Juno excluded, and Phoebus, and the Lyaeus of Erebus,
and law-giving Ceres, as they call her, and the migrating shades,
we burn deserved honors to Christ alone,
renewing the day with gifts, at the altars of the Deity.
The seventh Sacrament is that of Holy Orders, which is the second aid for preserving the Church in her state.
To holy Orders deservedly are appointed honors
special: for upon these the leaning house rests,
the mystical house of the Christians. To repair the ruins of the fallen
race of priests, and the temples ravaged of ministers,
is given to these by lot, and the full power to restore them;
they create the whole race of sacrificers, who may appease the divine powers.
These, standing, heap the altars with heavenly bowls,
and the chalice of the bloody liquid, and the implements of Ceres
they make ready in the holy sanctuaries, and the consecrated fruits.
What of the fact that Holy Order also strength to us for brave deeds
supplies, moving our inner parts with the favorable blowing
Zephyr of the eternal Deity, which it bestows by its gift?
But in full assembly, who else is more excellent
to rouse men with his mouth, and to kindle Mars with his word,
than the pious priest, relying on his Order, unlocking his lips?
With Orders dismissed, who the due rights to the Father,
would be able to render, sacred offerings to God, at the smoking altars?
Why is the woolen headband surrounded by a snowy fillet?
Thence, neither do the altars burn with the placed entrails,
nor can the consulted Prophet return answers;
in vain does the suppliant place honor upon the altars.
Vain superstition is too hostile to the Thunderer.
Thus he who will present himself as a Priest by a counterfeit Order,
When he prepares to deceive, by offering feigned sacrifices to the Heavenly ones,
Will not carry it off unpunished: but for such daring deeds
He will feel that he has paid for his offenses with no ordinary penalty,
Making known to all that the guilty man has paid for his crime.
CHAPTER V.
On the first duty of Christian Justice, which consists in this, that we turn away from evil.
GUIDE.
How many are the duties of Christian Justice?
MUSE.
Learn Justice, being warned, and not to slight the Deity:
By this twofold kind of duty let us be borne on high;
By this to retrace our steps, and escape to the upper air,
If it is a toil, on the other hand the descent of Avernus is easy,
With the difficult is mixed Hyblaean honey, but with the easy, bitterness,
And instead of a heavy and grim yoke, you bring back one that is light and sweet.
GUIDE.
Can man avoid sin, and do good, or fulfill justice?
MUSE.
That is not in our power by our own strength, but under Christ's auspices,
What a world, I pray, will you see this to be, what kingdoms to arise
With such support? With the accompanying arms of Christ,
With what great deeds will martial glory exalt itself?
Greatest Guide of the Christians, while you are safe, never
Will I confess the affairs of our soul or our kingdoms to be defeated.
For us, for help in war, in proportion to the divine power of the gods,
Our strength is meager: on this side we are surrounded by arms,
On that side madness torments us, and within are a thousand fears:
But for you I mighty peoples, and rich in kingdoms
Prepare to join camps: the salvation which unexpected fortune
Shows; by the fates' demand you bring yourself hither.
If you allow yourself to be added as a guide to these thousands,
The matter is safe; with you as guide, we shall rule the stars of heaven.
A race hostile to you sails the Lethean sea,
Bring it about, for you have the power, that it does not land on our shores,
Strike force into the winds, and sink and overwhelm their ships.
How many kinds of sin are there?
There are said to be twin plagues, surnamed the Dirae,
Whom, along with Tartarean Megaera, dead of Night
Bore in one and the same birth, and bound with equal
Coils of serpents, and added windy wings.
Hence I resolve that there is a twofold kind of human stain;
One which is drawn from our first origin.
The first parents of the human race offended.
When they consumed the forbidden foods: but the grim poison
Ignorant posterity, subject to another's fault,
Drank in, and the sons reproduce the contagions of their fathers.
Hence that first stain of evil, hence the wicked plague
Settled in the veins, and flowed abundantly with gore,
Infecting men: hence the joyless wound
Was inflicted on the soul, which no power to heal
Nor any art of men could: but it spreads by its tinder,
The deadly touch, it descends through the whole body,
The furious evil of the serpent, and its hidden powers
It insinuates into the silent senses, and grows as it goes.
From the occurrence of the stain, this draws its name from the origin.
On the second kind of sin, which is actual.
How many kinds of actual sin are there?
In an inauspicious birth, she nourishes twin offspring at her breast:
For she is an unhappy mother with a deadly crime,
On the fifth Moon, unless I am mistaken, when pale Orcus,
And the Eumenides were born, when Earth in an unspeakable birth,
Creates both Coeus and Iapetus, and savage Typhoeus,
And the brothers who conspired to tear down heaven,
Who tried to place Pelion under Ossa,
And indeed to roll leafy Olympus upon Ossa.
There is another offspring to her, a heap of venial fault,
Which, although it does not render the Deity unfriendly to us,
Yet minds defiled by these dirts, after death,
Are soon disciplined with punishments, and of their old evils
They pay the penalties; for some, beneath the vast whirlpool,
The imported crime is washed away, for these it is burned out by fire.
By what steps are we led down to sinning?
O faith of Gods and men, a second Mezentius,
Supreme despiser of the gods, more cruel than he,
Who once used to join dead bodies to the living,
Putting together hands with hands, and mouths with mouths,
(A kind of torture) and dripping with gore and putrefaction,
In a wretched embrace, he thus killed them with a lingering death.
Harsher than this, I say, with loose reins pours itself forth
The madness of sin, mixing all things widely around,
While wretched minds, deprived of vital light,
It joins to living bodies, by a deadly crime.
When the weary citizens this enemy, raging unspeakable things,
Wish to surround, having slipped away into the fields of his allies,
He flees for refuge, and is defended by the arms of a threefold host:
For he who suggests shameful things arms this one's party,
When with Stygian blasts the breezes of the human breast
He infects, spreading poisons from his foul mouth.
Vicious Pleasure joins herself as an ally of crimes,
Leading out feminine troops with crescent shields,
For whom, like a consuming fire, and a soft flame the marrows
We must beware with skill lest she devour the inner parts of the mind:
For Cytherea turns over in her breast new arts, new
Counsels, that Cupid, changed in face and features,
May come instead of sweet Christ, and with gifts the raging
May inflame minds, and entwine fire in their bones.
Third proceeds from the camp the worst beast, by her nod,
Before the rest, strengthening the scepters of so dire a Tyrant:
For to what does dire assent not compel mortal breasts?
Therefore let all boldness, rising with just furies,
Demand the King for punishment in present war,
And prepare to bear the standards. O chosen youth of the Gods above,
Flower of the ancients, and valor of men, whom just against the enemy
Grief bears, and the impious King inflames with deserved anger,
Arms, men, bear arms in hand, let reason supply the arms;
For we see the hostile battle-lines standing on this height,
Here a sudden cloud gathering with black dust:
We comrades look out, and darkness rising on the plains,
First from the opposing mound Caicus shouts out;
What mass, O citizens, is rolling in black gloom?
Bring the sword quickly, hand out weapons, and mount the walls:
The enemy is here: to draw up a battle line, and entrust ourselves to the plain,
Is not now advisable: we see what our fortune is:
Therefore let us guard the camp, and the walls made safe by a rampart.
On the seven capital sins.
THE LEADER.
How many, of what kind, how great the leaders of this host
Have brought themselves out from the gates of the rampart, declare, Calchas?
CALCHAS.
I have twice approached this camp of crimes as a scout;
And I have surveyed the battle lines, and I will reveal the secrets I know:
It is right to hate the men, and to bring all things into the open air,
If they hide anything, lest I be bound by any laws of crimes.
The foremost leader of the war, who wields the reins,
Boasts himself by the unjust title, by the name of Lucifer,
For he is a horrendous, huge monster, whose light has been taken away.
That he is excluded from the empyrean kingdom, from the fated fields,
And that his scepter is transferred to a mortal settler,
Impatient in his mind, he stirs up the fires of the Furies.
It was not enough to have sharpened his first furies against heaven,
And to have wished the council and the whole house of the Thunderer
To overturn in vain: but to involve this race of ours
In the punishments of Erebus he desires: hither he brings all his zeal,
And his attempts, thither his thunderbolts of war
He directs in vain (as is our hope) while the fates resist.
Yet confidence does not cease for the audacious defeated one:
Of his own accord he raises spirits with his words, and of his own accord rebukes
The sevenfold battle lines, which he leads out on the open plain:
Then raging in his mind, while he fluctuates with the tide of his anger,
Gnashing his teeth, he thunders these things with a truculent mouth:
Shall pious fates help the Christ-worshippers? The hostile mind of God

div.note: The madness of sin is here called a great Tyrant, whose side is fostered by Suggestion, Delight, and Consent.

div.n: Describuntur hîc septem peccata capitalia, sub nomine Ducum partis aduersa.

lg.l: He has snatched from them their accustomed help: neither weapons, nor fires
of ours will they escape: the seas are impassable to Christ himself,
nor is there any hope of flight: the other half of things is taken away.
But the land is in our hands, so many thousands of the heretical
race bear arms. The fated things do not terrify me at all:
if they boast of any responses of the Thunderer on their own behalf,
Enough has been granted to the fates and to Mary, that so many thousand ruins
they have restored to the kingdom of heaven: and there are my own opposing
fates for me, to cut down with the sword the accursed race
Catholic without delay. Darkness, and the cowardly thefts
of the Palladium, with the guards of the topmost citadel slain,
let them not fear: nor shall we be hidden in the blind belly of a horse:
Openly in daylight it is resolved to surround the walls with fire;
I shall see to it that not with Danaans, and Pelasgian youth, business for themselves
they say there is, whom Hector held off into the tenth year.
Their spirits roused by these words, the cohorts to advance,
and to join battle, and to charge farther forward dare:
and the seven chief Leaders once more into the fray
descend, and send their lives into open dangers;
A shout goes up along all the walls, across the ramparts;
they bend their keen bows, and whirl their throwing-thongs:
The whole ground is strewn with missiles, then shields, and hollow
helmets give a sound from the blows, a fierce battle rises:
As great as, coming from the west with the rainy Kids,
a rainstorm lashes the ground, with as much hail as storm-clouds
plunge into the shallows, when Jupiter, bristling with south winds,
whirls a watery tempest, and bursts the hollow clouds in the sky.
Here the seven capital sins are described, under the name of the Leaders of the opposing side.
Matters at last settled, with the tumult ceasing,
Calchas continues his discourse, and of his own accord added this:
Has anything by word of mouth perhaps reached your ears,
about these seven Leaders, the sinews and strength of the
opposing side? You may know for certain that they exist, but also by renowned fame?
Whether perhaps by their counsels any name and honour,
or outstanding praise they have earned by brave deeds?
An example is set forth of a proud and puffed-up man.
Pride is depicted.
Avarice.
Lust.
Or they can sound forth their forefathers, and of their grandsires the ancient
Names, and a whole lineage traced through Latin kings.
Nay rather, their very origin turns to their own disgrace.
Begotten of Vice as father, they betray themselves by the work of their crimes:
For it belongs to the first to attempt a way, by which he can
Raise from the ground, and flit victorious on the lips of men,
To trample the ground, and gather his proud steps.
Thus straightway before you with vast strength raises
His face Dares, and lifts himself amid a great murmur of men;
He who alone was wont to contend against Paris,
And the same man, at the tomb where greatest Hector lies,
Victorious Butes of immense body (who
Bore himself as coming from the Bebrycian race of Amycus)
He struck down, and stretched him dying on the tawny sand:
Thus, I say, with swollen mouth Dares extols himself with praises,
And displays his broad shoulders, and tosses his alternating
Arms, stretching them forth, and lashes the air with blows,
So that he may betray the arrogance of his breast, and his haughty mind.
But ill-counselling hunger, and the dread lust of having,
Avarice gives to this one; let him be called by the infamous name
Pygmalion, more monstrous in crime than all others,
Who secretly with cruel sword slew the unwary Sychaeus;
Or, equal to the Thracian, who, seized by a like love,
Breaking all divine law, butchers Polydorus, and the gold
Takes possession of by force. To what do you not compel mortal breasts,
Accursed hunger for gold, and most harsh in the pursuits of gain?
The foul plague of Venus bestows an ignoble lineage on another,
Who invaded his daughter's chamber, and forbidden nuptials,
Whose limbs roving lust shamefully devours.
Unhappy Dido burns with this, and wanders through the whole
City raging, like a hind struck by an arrow,
Which, unwary, from afar amid the Cretan woods has pierced
A shepherd hunting with darts, and has left the flying steel in her
Unknowing; she in flight ranges the forests and glades
Of Dicte, the deadly shaft clings to her side.
But Envy, that her flanks may burst, as the fourth monster,
Torments herself with the swollen ulcer of an inflated crime.
Drances once felt this, whom the glory of Turnus
Agitated with sidelong envy, and bitter goads.

div.note: An example is given of a proud and boastful man.

lg.l: Wrath.
The fifth, whetting war, with what great wrath does he rouse himself?
By what furies is he driven? Look, from the whole face of the blazing one
sparks fly off, fire flashes from his fierce eyes:
Just as when a bull, for his first battles, bellowings
terrifying raises, and tries to throw his wrath into his horns,
pushing against the trunk of a tree, and assails the winds
with blows, and rehearses for the fight with scattered sand.
Or as with Alcides, when frenzy and wrath his mind
drive headlong, and he gnashes his teeth and thunders dreadfully with his arms.
As huge as Athos, or as huge as Eryx, or he himself with his quivering
holm-oaks when he roars, and as huge as he rejoices with his snowy
peak, father Apennine lifting himself to the breezes.
Gluttony.
The sixth, devourer of things, as a swift whirlpool swallows in the sea,
so he is filled with old wine and rich venison,
and taking up bowls of unmixed wine, not sluggishly he drains
the foaming bowl, and drenches himself from the brimming gold:
And from the appearance of men, as the cruel goddess with potent herbs
Circe of old, changes us into the features and faces of wild beasts.
Hence are heard groans, and the rage of lions
refusing their chains, and roaring late in the night,
and bristly swine, and bears in their pens
raging, and the shapes of great wolves howling.
Such as, and as huge as, Polyphemus was in his hollow cave;
who, as soon as he was glutted with the feast, and buried in wine,
laid down his drooping neck, and lay sprawled through the cave
immense, belching gore, and gobbets with bloody
mixed with wine in his sleep, soon on every side around
he is surrounded, and his eye is bored through with a sharp weapon
huge, which lay hidden, the only one, beneath his grim brow;
like an Argive shield, or the lamp of Phoebus.
Sloth.
Finally the last, to be placed among the cattle by his sluggishness
is judged to have deserved by his hand; nothing further is granted;
Hence Sloth gives him a name fitting his deserts;
For the kindly light never rouses this idler,
nor the morning songs of birds beneath the roof,
accustomed as he is to snore, until Aurora with her rosy four-horse chariot
has crossed the middle of the sky in her heavenly course.
Under his leadership, often in the furrows to which we entrusted barley,
wretched darnel and barren wild oats hold sway,

div.note: Gluttony and drunkenness bring this metamorphosis upon us, as may be seen in men buried in wine.

lg.l: Instead of the soft violet, instead of the purple narcissus,
the thistle, and the Christ's-thorn rises with sharp spines.
Relying on this omen, the son of Hyrtacus, at the same time with his sword the proud
Rhamnes he attacks, who by chance on high carpets
propped up, was breathing out sleep from his whole chest,
himself a king, and an augur most pleasing to King Turnus:
but he could not drive away destruction by his augury.
Three attendants nearby lying at random among the weapons,
the armour-bearer of Remus he crushes, and the charioteer under the very
horses having found, and with his sword he severs their hanging necks;
Then he takes the head from the master himself, and leaves the trunk
heaving with black blood; warmed by the gore
the earth and the beds are drenched: and also Lamyrus and Lamus,
