and the youth Serranus, who on that night very much
had played, distinguished in face, and was lying with much
his limbs overcome by unmixed wine, happy if continuously that
game he had made equal to the night, and carried it into the light.
LEADER.
Would the enemy therefore be unequal to our encounters?
MUSE.
We have a greatest leader, most renowned in arms,
powerful in war, alone he would stand against a thousand ranks,
the heavenly armour-bearer would overcome a thousand Camillas;
The peak on his head burns, and from his crests and top a flame
is poured forth, and his golden shield-boss vomits vast fires;
Not otherwise than if ever in the clear night comets
blood-red glow mournfully, or the blazing Sirius:
he, bringing thirst and diseases to sick mortals,
rises, and saddens the sky with his ill-omened light.
At the sight of him, the bravest Hector is a boy:
Aegaeon is a boy, who they say had a hundred arms,
and a hundred hands, and from fifty mouths fire
and chests to have blazed, when against the thunderbolts of Jove
he clashed with as many matching shields, and drew as many swords.
The battle-lines of the winged ones have approached, so many thunderbolts of war:
Finally, a thousand phalanxes are a help to us,
the force of the Christ-born, and the flower of men, the chosen youth.
Meanwhile, with such great forces, victory by an idle
hand is to be won by no one, but by brave deeds.

div.n: De septem virtutibus vitiis capitalibus oppositis.

lg.l: There a grim battle is joined under an ill-starred omen,
where strength is great, and fear has lent wings to the feet:
Thus when a people is bereft of fear, the watch the night
whiles away sleepless in play, and, sprawled across the grass,
young men with crimson crests, gleaming with gold,
indulge in wine and tip up the bronze mixing-bowls.
Even one mighty in war, if he too greatly despises the enemy,
will fall before evening returns with Olympus closed.
Hence the need that the sentinels' watches dangers from the citadel
drive away, and also, trembling with dread, the gates
inspect, and join the bridges and the ramparts,
bear arms: let keen Fear and Love of the Thunderer press on:
whom the almighty Father (should adversity ever call)
appointed to be rulers of the young and masters of affairs.
Let every legion along the walls, having drawn its danger by lot,
keep watch, and then take turns at what each must guard.
But if battle, or to undertake some great deed long since
the mind stirs, and is not content with calm repose,
and if anyone has a spirit that scorns the light, and that
who believes the honour it strives for is well bought with life;
the squadrons of the seven virtues, turned against them, to clash
with the opposing Captains of the vices, roused and eager,
O would that it made them: for they would rush ready into wars.
On the seven virtues opposed to the capital vices.
The virtue whose name is Submission heard this,
and willing Obedience (though she herself by fear of praise
is heavily smitten), in her zeal for seeking the lofty heights above,
freely offers herself. To join herself as ally in the highest affairs
the bountiful giver of goods, whose care is gifts, was burning.
God adds this ardour to the minds of the rest,
who dig their spurs into the shoulders of the foaming horse;
the hoof shakes the crumbling plain with four-footed thunder.
Chaste devotee of purity and of snow-white modesty,
and, resplendent in slender fare and moderate dress,
Virtue's rule advances, and follows her sister;
with equal steps the gentle heroine hastens hither,
Humility.
Liberality.
Chastity.
Temperance.
Kindness.
Patience.
Devotion, or diligent piety.
where, willing to die, she may present herself at the threshold of the Heavenly Ones.
Patience alike hastens on, rejoicing in hardships.
But diligent Piety joins herself to these as a comrade in arms,
Leading a column of horsemen, and troops gleaming with bronze,
A warrior, she not to the distaff, or the baskets of Minerva
Her feminine hand accustomed, but as a virgin battles
Hard to endure, and to outstrip the winds with the swiftness of her feet:
She might even fly over the topmost blades of an untouched crop
Of grass, and would not have harmed the tender ears of grain in her course;
Or suspended over the swelling wave through the midst of the sea
She would make her way, and not wet her swift soles in the water.
All the youth, pouring out from houses and fields,
And the crowd of mothers marvels at her, and watches her as she goes,
Gazing with astonished minds: how royal with purple
Honor veils her smooth shoulders, how a clasp her hair
Binds with gold. How she herself carries a Lycian quiver,
And a pastoral myrtle staff tipped with a spearhead.
In these there is one love, to destroy the plagues of vices,
Yet first they kindle the altars with chaste gifts.
Come then, spare your fear, hope for certain salvation,
While Piety, while hoary faith, and invincible in war
Breasts fight it out, ready to conquer the rebels.
GUIDE.
Is rest to be obtained, once these enemies are defeated?
MUSE.
There are other plagues sprung from the jaws of Erebus.
Which, against the gentle Zephyr of the breeze of the divine Godhead,
Betray themselves by various names as six monsters of crimes.
On the six sins against the Holy Spirit.
First. Presumption.
This one loosens too much the reins of God's mercy,
And presses those of justice more than is just, drawing back the bridle,
Inasmuch as the confidence of our race has begotten it:
Hence the name Presumption is deservedly given to it.
It is right for anyone to trust in the Gods against their will:
Often the mind of men, imbued with this sweet poison,
Considers these things with itself, counterfeiting the color of truth:
If it is our lot to live in the manner of an overturned tree,
For producing various trees there is a varied nature:
For some, with no men compelling them, of themselves
come up of their own accord, and far and wide the plains and rivers
curving they occupy, like the soft osier and pliant brooms,
the poplar, and the willow-groves whitening with glaucous leaf.
Others need no root, and the pruner
does not hesitate, returning it to the earth, to entrust the topmost shoot:
Nay even, when the trunks are cut, wonderful to tell,
an olive root is pushed forth from the dry wood;
And thus we see the branches of one harmlessly
turn into those of another, and grafted apples the changed
pear-tree bear, and stony cornels redden with plums.
But I, a wild olive, to the trunk of a long-lived olive
grafted, could I not hope for wholesome offspring?
Should none of the woods the pressed-down arches of a layer,
expect, nor living nurseries in their own earth?
Those which raise themselves of their own accord into the breezes of light,
unfruitful indeed, but lush and strong they rise;
for nature lies beneath the soil. Yet these too, if anyone
should graft them, or entrust them, transplanted, to well-worked trenches,
will shed their wild spirit, and with no labor,
into whatever arts you wish, not slowly will they follow.
And also the barren one which comes forth from the lowest roots,
will do this, if it be distributed through empty fields.
Therefore what need is there of many things, and frequent cultivation?
* Go far away, cares; let me pursue leisure as good Daphnis.
Let it be in vain through more, what can be done through fewer.
Second. Despair-
A plague opposed to this, to which the name Diffidence
is given; this one rages fiercely with monstrous deeds,
rolling her bloodshot gaze, and with spots her trembling
cheeks flecked, and pale with the death to be endured.
Almighty God does not drive so many with his thunderbolt to the shades,
the pale ghosts of Erebus, and the deep night,
as this one has caused to break off their burdensome life as soon as possible,
instigating to slaughter; this one, that on a bloody blade himself
he might impale, and drive the cruel sword through his ribs:
that one, that he might throw himself headlong from high towers,
Let him rush onto cliffs or rocks, or drown himself in the waves,
Or by some other kind of death to free himself from these cares
Let him find a way: deceit or valor, who would ask in an enemy?
He sings this to ears not deaf, that for the accursed man there will be
One safety for the conquered: to hope for no safety.
Third. The attack on acknowledged truth.
But leading a third troop, dread Celaeno joins herself to these,
And the other Harpies, whom horrid Orcus vomits forth.
No monster is grimmer than they, nor any fiercer
Plague and wrath of God has raised itself from the Stygian waves:
The faces of the birds are virginal, most foul the discharge
Of their belly, and hooked hands, and faces ever pale
With hunger: but indeed they have left their former tables;
Hence, when we feast on delicacies and rich banquets,
Soon they are suddenly present with a horrifying swoop from the mountains,
The Harpies, and they beat their wings with loud clangor,
And they plunder the feast, and befoul everything with their filthy
Touch; then a dread cry amid the foul stench:
Whom might this breed of foul monster, and the most foul discharge
Of the belly signify? Whom shall I believe to be marked by this filth?
Those infected with the heretical plague, to whose heart impious
Pursuits are dear, always like a Fury common to their country.
These have willingly left the sumptuous tables of truth,
So that they might spread false meanings under the image of truth:
Thus, while they fill their black gullet with foul filth,
Bitter hunger presses them, nor is their love of eating appeased—
Hence, when we are refreshed with the delights of truth at the altars,
Soon, from the opposite quarter of heaven and from hidden lairs,
A screeching throng flies round the prey with hooked feet,
Defiles the feast with its mouth, mingling sacred things with profane,
Whose zeal it is to confound the known words of truth.
O would that our comrades might attack and try new battles,
To maim with the sword the obscene birds of the sea;
But neither any force upon their feathers, nor wounds upon their backs †
Do they receive, and, gliding off in swift flight beneath the stars,
They leave the half-eaten prey and foul traces.

div.note: For formally, heretics have reached such a pitch of obstinacy that, when they are refuted by the force of arguments, they refuse to be convinced that they are wrong: hence they turn to evasions.

lg.l: Fourth, envy of fraternal charity.
Hostile men will never be lacking, whom the glory of their brothers
Sidelong Envy will drive with bitter goads,
When heavenly matters succeed well for them, and to Christ
From thence honour accrues, and a great name, and glory.
The force of that envy compels deep silences
To break, and to publish in words their covered grief.
The fourth fierce beast has given us such offspring,
Whom she leads armed with her into hostile battles.
Fifth, Obstinacy.
Here too join themselves those whom, from hard crags, bristling
Caucasus fashioned, to whom savage tigresses their udders
Hyrcanian offered; these, nourished by the milk of wild beasts,
It is no wonder if they are of wild morals and heart.
Sooner would you thrust Cacus down into his dark cave,
And shut in the hollow rock, and bellowing unaccustomed things,
Would Alcides press from above with weapons, and all arms
Expend, pressing on with branches and vast millstones,
Than you could relieve this race of men from their stiff neck,
And lead them down into the right path by warning.
Sixth, Impenitence.
The last race follows, more savage than the remaining troops,
A race hard from its root, cruel, merciless, proud.
The boys stay awake in hunting, and weary the woods:
Their sport is to turn horses, and aim arrows from the bow,
To carry off plunder swiftly and to live on what is seized;
To break off all right and wrong with the monstrous sword;
To take no account of the eternal Deity,
To speak with a sacrilegious mouth, and thrice pour out impious words:
Thus to pass their life, and never remember the Thunderer.
Would that them, pressed in mind by wavering dread,
It were permitted to see, and to look up to heaven from time to time!
Who, assisted by such arms, would not despair?
Should a hostile battle-line equipped with these attempt battles?
It is deceived if it expects the palm with this savage soldiery.
On sins crying out to heaven.
CATECHIST.
Who before the front line, things fit and unfit to be told
strides shouting? Is it Ulysses, contriver of speech?
Whither does the roaring call, and the shout raised to the sky?
The shout goes to heaven: never, roused by a mural
MUSE.
engine, do rocks roar so, nor from a thunderbolt do such great
crashes burst apart, as the great crashes the dreadful voice
arouses of unspeakable crimes, which of the high Judge
demand the avenging right hand, the fierce, I say, of the Judge,
punishments upon the guilty, on account of the offended wrath of the Godhead.
1. Does not the very blood give voice, poured out at the altars,
of innocent Abel, slain by a brother's murder?
There are those recently who to see the death of a son before a father
have made, and have defiled a father's face with death.
How many has grievous ambition, how many the dire lust of possessing
secretly overcome with the sword when off their guard? The flooding blood
has sounded in the ears of Christ. 2. Strikes the lofty heaven
the oppression of the underage boy, and of the widowed mother.
3. The all too foul of the lust of the Sodomites, known to the lands,
overflow, where has a mournful song not re-echoed?
4. How many labours are defrauded of their just wage?
Know that so many breezes resound with deep lamentations.
With this terrible sound of the trumpet the Jerichoan to be overturned
walls can, would you deny? What opposing force could resist?
On the sins of others, which are nine in number.
TEACHER.
What are the sins of others?
MUSE.
In these thrice three ways we are held by another's stain:
These are nine weapons. Not any will the right hand in vain
hurl against comrades, without the horror of a wound falling upon them.
First, that which is committed by wicked counsel.
Counsel, a flying spear, pierces through the bronze of the shield
of many, and bursts the breastplate together with the breast.
Would not Achitophel (had fate not been adverse to him)
without delay, have prepared the Jessean camp with savage slaughter
to rout? Such resolute breasts would not have borne such spirits.
The second is done by Command.
But what a woman can do by a mad command,
how fierce those weapons are to men, that the Trojan hero
learned well enough, tossed about so much on lands and on the deep,
by the power of the gods, on account of the unforgetting wrath of cruel Juno.
And that I may sing of sure things, best known to the whole world:
When once the Baptist opens to future fates
his mouth at God's command, sometimes believed by the cruel
king of the sons of Isaac, what the slippery woman can do by her command
Herodias attests by the grim stroke of the blade,
by which the light of the Christ-born race, and its most faithful hope,
lies dead, the outstanding herald by divine gift,
refusing to prolong any further a life cut short.
The third is done by Assent,
But with the striking storm of Saul's harsh assent,
what bristling hail of stones does not rush rattling down
upon the head of the innocent? (Men of old called him Stephen.)
This man, distinguished in piety, gazing on the heights above,
as Saul harries him by the hands of twice a thousand of his own,
thirsting for death in his heart, he also defiles his right hand with a wound,
and overwhelms the holy man with a savage shower of hail.
The fourth, by Provocation.
But we are assailed by another bitter cast of a weapon:
There are those whose pursuit is this, whose will bears this in the heart,
to goad virtue thus with haughty words:
You, a man? But with what voice shall I bear it? Why cold in war
is your right hand? Is sloth to your heart's liking? You, always fresh
does it please to gather spoils, and live on plunder?
You have garments embroidered with saffron and gleaming purple,
and your tunics have sleeves, and your turbans have ribbons:
O true Phrygian women (for you are not Phrygian men), go over the heights
Dindyma, where the pipe gives its two-holed song to those accustomed,
the timbrels and the Berecynthian luxury of the mother call you,
of Ida: leave arms to men, and yield to the sword.
With such words they burn to mock the gentle,
by instigating them to dare worse by fierce Mars.
Fifth, by praise, or by flattery.
Not seeming to have sharpened rabid furies enough by these things,
should Wickedness cease? With no gentle goads angers
she incites, and to ply tricks and Pelasgian arts
having undertaken, she drives at this, that glory may give praise to vice,
lest anyone refuse to attempt for such great hope,
whatever of the six crimes the dire one holds out to the perpetrator.
Sixth, by the concealment of another's fault.
But those whom she has perceived to be held by a heavier plague,
she refuses for them to be betrayed, and to uncover the hidden crime,
Not however (as is certain) lest to oppose foul shame
Rumor might be able, and lest the good name the badly slippery of the tongue
Darts pierce through, and the iron remain in the breast;
But so that every wickedness may rule with loose reins,
And the evil may creep further, if it is borne with impunity.
Seventh, by connivance, or indulgence.
Busied also, by indulging, with the cares of the wicked,
By whatever means she is able, to descend to all entreaties
She strives, so that she may avert the just wrath of the Judge,
Which neither the virtue of men, nor piety itself could mitigate,
And scarcely, broken by the command of God or by the fates, does she fall silent.
So utterly without reason does the wicked mind rage, always
Closing its eyes, and fearing to catch the sun with its sight:
Yet there is no more efficacious remedy for troubles,
Than if someone were able to cut open with a blade the top
Mouth of the ulcer. The poison is nourished and lives by being concealed.
Eighth, by the wicked defense of another's deed.
But the black night of crimes hovers around with its hollow shade,
Unspeakably urging to defend the wicked deeds committed,
Asserting that this rightly seems to it to be no crime.
Ninth, by sharing in another's property.
To admit the stolen share of a pilfered thing,
Would Wickedness not know? Is it burdened by another's fraud?
From all sides, O companions, by what arms are we surrounded?
My mind is foolish enough, that to succumb to my own fault
I might think I am able: depart far from here, you plagues of another:
I must act, lest the foreign night of crimes dominate me.
Kindly Spirit, I ask, by your divine power our steps
Direct, strengthening the faltering ones with the strength of virtues.
On the works of the flesh.
GUIDE.
What wedge-formations do I see here, and hearts heated by tumult?
MUSE.
Behold, the noble phalanx of the Heavenly Ones sends itself into battle,
And the Leaders of the virtues, and the whole army of cavalry,
Arranged by number into squadrons, over the whole plain roars
The prancing steed, and fights against the tightened reins,
Turning this way, and that: then far and wide with iron spears
The field bristles, and the plains blaze with raised weapons.
† Here on the opposite side the Cyprian leader, Cupid smooth of face,
And with her brother the sister, the ruinous Pleasure of Venus,
And ill-advising hunger, and the frantic love of possessing,
Then fickle Ambition, and Glory drenched in deceit,
Whom the Elation of an inflated mind joins as allies,
Appear opposite on the plain, and the spear with drawn-back
Right hands they stretch forth far, and brandish their darts,
And the approach of men, and the roaring of horses grows fierce:
And now each side, having advanced within the throw of a weapon,
Had halted: suddenly they break forth with a shout, and raging
They urge on their horses, at the same time they pour weapons from all sides
Thickly, in the manner of snow, and the sky is covered with shadow.
Immediately from opposing camps Modesty, and Cupid
Straining charge with spears, and first deal ruin
With a mighty sound, and the shattered [chests] of the galloping steeds

div.note: The army of both sides is introduced, namely of the virtues of the spirit, and of the carnal vices,
† Three kinds of enemies, of which St. John says: Whatever is in the world, is either the concupiscence of the flesh, or the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life.

lg.l: They crash breast against breast: the adulterer, shaken off,
in the manner of a thunderbolt, or of a weight driven by a catapult,
falls headlong far away, and scatters his life into the breezes;
To attempt this outcome of war is then for Chastity
lawful, when by no running now to escape from the fight
she sees she is able, nor to turn away the pressing Cytherean:
For a virgin who an eternal love of virginity
undefiled cultivates, if she had not been caught up
in such warfare, would rather have prepared to turn her back;
but hostile force compelled her three times to take up arms in her hand.
Wicked Pleasure, impatient at the slaughter of her brother,
having begun to turn over wiles in her counsel, to Chastity
begins these words: What is so outstanding, if you, a woman, in a strong
horse trust? dismiss flight, and yourself hand-to-hand on level
ground entrust with me, and gird yourself for a battle on foot,
soon you will know to whom windy glory brings praise.
She spoke; but the other, raging, and inflamed with fierce grief,
Is it thus, plague, she says, that Chastity to be violated by fraud
you think can be? whether deceit or valor, who would ask in an enemy?
You thunder with your mouth, since you are always more ready to deceive;
Go far from here, to turn over your wiles, bringing back ample spoils,
both you, and your boy, Cupid, changed in his face.
It holds no virtue to decide the matter with you by the sword,
sooner would it be an honor, either to withdraw myself from the fight,
by casting off delays, or to fall to certain death.
Fear proves degenerate minds, not the immense love
of the virginal flower, and of protecting snowy beauty.
To hand over my horse to a companion, and to stand in equal arms,
on foot with a bare sword, and undaunted with a blank shield,
I would dare, about to clash with two thousand other Camillas;
But with you, just reason forbids it, nay rather for wings to be bound
to my feet it wishes; the will stands in my heart to have conquered by flight.
This constant opinion rises in our mind.
Scarcely had she said these things, fleeing she is carried away with turned reins,
and wearies the swift quadruped with her iron spur:
Thus the virgin is rescued from danger, with a safe warfare.
Immediately the battle lines are disturbed, and the guilty ones, turned,
throw back their shields, and turn their horses to the walls:
The stronger one pursues, and drives the squadrons against the enemy.

div.note: The strong horse, in this place, is flight from the occasions of sin.
Against the onset of lust, take to flight, if you would win the victory. So St Augustine, Sermon 250 de tempore (printed '5c').

lg.l: And now they were approaching the gates, and again the fleeing ones
raise a shout, and bend back their supple necks:
these flee and are carried far back, with the reins let loose.
Just as when the sea, rushing forward with alternating surge,
foaming, and drenches the farthest sand with its swell;
now rapid backwards, and sucking back, rolled back by the tide,
the rocks, it flees, and leaves the shore with gliding shallow.
Twice the just drove the routed guilty to the walls,
twice repulsed by arms they look back, covering their backs:
But after, having engaged in the third battle, whole
they entangled lines among themselves, and man picked man,
then indeed both the groans of the dying, and in deep blood,
both arms, and bodies, and mixed with the slaughter of men,
half-dead horses are rolled: a fierce battle arises.
Vain Superstition, to whom is dear the false of the Gods
Religion (who once to join over a slaughtered pig
treaties was accustomed, and equipped with Stygian poisons,
to arm the prophetic seers of the race for battle)
is slain: for her, struck off at close quarters with a single blow,
the head lay far away with its helmet; this slaughter to itself
the Ardor of Justice (lest the distinguished glory of the deed
be suppressed) attributed, with Christ as the heavenly avenger.
But hoary Faith, which is the shield of the great Thunderer;
the Sect of unspeakable heresy, with its hamstring cut,
she catches, and hid her dire sword up to the hilt
into its back (Christ supplies strength and courage)
Thence fall Disagreements, Dissension, and the Rival right hand:
Drunkenness collapses; he felt Achilles found,
he who as victor bent the yokes with vine-shoot reins,
Liber, driving tigers from the lofty peak of Nysa.
While the middle forehead for him with the sword, between the twin temples,
Sobriety, and at the same time the jaws with a huge wound
cleaves, the earth was shaken by the huge weight;
his collapsed limbs, and arms bloody with brains
he strews on the ground dying: and for him in equal parts
the head hung hither and thither, from each shoulder.
When Zeal the ally of Venus, and of impure Lyaeus
saw prostrated, and deceit withdrawing from the line,
and the leaders disturbed, suddenly he burns fervent with hope

div.note: The uncertain outcome of war, especially in the matter of chastity: which is most clearly demonstrated by an applied simile, drawn from the flow and ebb of the sea.

lg.l: He calls for horses, and arms at the same time, and, proud, with a leap—
He springs into the chariot, and works the reins with his hands,
Flying about, with his hand he gives many brave bodies to death,
He sends many rolling half-dead, or with his chariot
Tramples the ranks, or hurls seized spears at those who flee.
Just as when, roused beside the streams of icy Hebrus,
Bloody Mars clashes on his shield, and, stirring up raging
Wars, lets loose his horses: they on the open plain
Fly before the South and West winds: furthest Thrace groans, struck
By their feet: and around, the faces of black terror—
And Wraths, and Ambushes, the retinue of the God, are swept along.
Such an eager victor in the midst of battles his horses
Smoking with sweat shakes, (a pitiable sight) the slain
Enemies trampling: the swift hoof scatters dews—
Bloody, and gore is trampled with the mixed sand.
And now he has given Cypris to death, and three thousand monsters—
Of foul crimes, to be roasted in Stygian furnaces;
And those whom the madness for gold, and the love of possessing tormented,
He destroyed them all, and plunged them in bitter death,
Ambition is laid low, to whom the Glory of vain praise
Is added; hence the limbs of the rest are loosened with cold,
And life with a groan flees, indignant, beneath the shades.
But although by this poured-out strength of war the forces
Of the hostile army are broken, no peace will follow;
For the plagues roar such things with their mouth, the Deity despised:
Why should we no longer place hope in our arms?
Are we so deserted? and once the army is turned
Do we fall utterly? and does fortune have no return?
We have both wealth, and youth still untouched,
And various cities and peoples remain for our help.
But to the party of the Gods above glory came with much
Blood, they have their own deaths, and equal through all
The storm: why, unseemly, on the first threshold
Do we fail? why does trembling seize our limbs before the trumpet?
Many a day, and the varying labor of changeable time,
Has brought things back to better; revisiting many alternately
Fortune has mocked, and placed them again on solid ground.
Therefore let them renew arms. Let it be that no peace follows:
For that would be too shameful. Shall virtue, corrupted,

div.note: Our enemy always hopes to carry off the victory over us.

lg.l: Can it be? Let him first seek arms, to clash in war
Let him choose, and let it occur to him that it is beautiful to die in arms:
Glory will always be subject to envy, and vice to shame-
Will not the greatest part of the earth be a help to glory?
But Christ will be the great King of ethereal Olympus:
With the protections of the Gods above then surrounding us, and those whom
So many peoples have sent as Leaders; and no small will follow
Glory those chosen from Latium, and the Laurentian fields:
Few in number, but their valor is lively in war.
CHAPTER VI.
GUIDE.
Is it enough to flee evil, and to turn away from sin?
MUSE.
It is right for everyone to undertake the sacred commands of the highest Father:
And it is not enough to have fled evil; the other part remains:
To learn Justice, and to extend virtue by deeds;
For to know what is right, and to tread on a crooked path,
That is worthy of double punishment, as the sacred explains
Page, which is the sure interpreter of the great Thunderer.
GUIDE.
How many kinds of good works are there?
The exhortation of Maro's Muse to the three kinds of good works.
MUSE.
What are you building? Or with what hope do you waste your leisure on vain things
By delaying? And do you not regard the city given by the fates?
Does no glory of such great things inflame you?
And do you not yourself undertake labor for your own praise?
Chosen race of men, offspring from the high blood of the gods,
Behold, it is perhaps given to you to escape into the upper air
By the rowing of wings: bind the winged sandals to your feet,
The golden ones, which aloft on wings, whether over the seas,
Or the land, may carry you equally with the swift blast.
Not otherwise than he flew between the lands and the sky,
To the sandy shore of Libya, and cut the winds,
The Cyllenian offspring coming from his maternal grandfather,
(As vain poets once fashioned for us)
Indeed, to penetrate the homes of heaven, to hold the high places above,
and there to recline at the joyful tables of the gods,
You are able, relying on this threefold service of deeds.
Which by their merit have made the guilty worthy of heaven:
May it please you to succor the afflicted circumstances of the poor:
And accustom yourself to pray to God with constant vows,
The author of fruits, and the ruler of storms:
Approaches are not to be tested, nor what are the softest for speaking,
Times, what is the right manner for things; more swiftly all
To such an extent does He hear, ready to succor the wretched:
Forbear to shake your faith, and persist in frequent prayer,
For He will grant pardon to your prayers, and will let go of His anger.
Finally, let it be to calm the stirred waves of the flesh
Your greatest care, by the strict laws of fasting.
With these three you calm the swelling seas of an afflicted heart,
And you put to flight the gathered clouds, and bring back the sun
of justice, and calm weather to the mind.
There is no need that Triton, striving with much force, with his sharp
Should thrust the ships from the rock: behold, He lifts them with His trident.
God Himself, rejoicing to alleviate the labors of men,
Both opens the vast Syrtes and calms the sea:
And thus you will glide over the highest waves on light wheels,
Until virtue brings you to the ethereal shores.
On the seven corporal works of mercy.
But if there is so great a love to summon virtue by deeds,
(For indeed it is certain that this consists in practice and zeal)
Dardanian Anchises, known by fame above the heavens,
It will be pleasing here to have recalled the man distinguished for his piety.
While the horns of the moon fill themselves with light for the third time,
Behold, a life in the woods, among the deserted places of wild beasts
Lairs and homes a stranger drags out, wandering off the path, straying:
An unhappy sustenance, berries and stony cornel-cherries
The branches give, and grasses feed him with their torn-up roots.
Out of the woods, I say, consumed by extreme emaciation,
A strange form of an unknown man, and pitiable in his attire,
Advances, and as a suppliant stretches his hands to the shores:
He is looked at: dreadful filth, and an untrimmed beard,

div.note: Virtue consists in action, says Cicero.

lg.l: His covering fastened with thorns, but in all else a Greek;
And once sent to Troy in his country's arms:
Pious Anchises himself, delaying not much,
Gives his right hand to the youth, and strengthens his mind with a present pledge.
1. Piety restores and cherishes him thus exhausted,
And labours to call back his strength with rich feasts:
2. Nor does she deny repeated draughts to his thirsty mouth:
3. And she veils his stripped body with a new garment,
Covering his bare skins. 4. The captive from the cave of the prison
She releases: 5. and the one consumed by disease, or a heavier wasting,
She relieves, with art, with hand, and with the potent herbs of Phoebus.
6. She receives him in hospitality: 7. he dies, she lays him in the earth,
She offers funeral rites to the unknown man and honours him with a tomb.
Earth is heaped up for a mound, altars stand to the Manes
Mournful with dark blue fillets and black cypress,
And around stand the Trojan women, their hair unbound according to custom.
Psalms are sung, and the last farewell is called out with a loud voice.
Let it not irk you to say, who, gentlest of the Trojans,
Taught you this kind of duty? Was it the fierce in arms
Soldier of the Myrmidons, or Dolopians, or of harsh Ulysses?
He was ever a destruction to his enemies, nor ever
To have come to the aid of men, who had the opposing
Dared to follow camp, is it found. But whatever there is everywhere
Of the gentile lot delights to destroy the enemy with the sword.
Therefore innate in you, not implanted by the deeds of anyone,
Made you, of its own accord, spare the Greek enemy,
Outstanding piety, which I would equal to heaven with praises:
But our praise is too small, than that the gratitude for so great a deed
It can be: but what glory of honour can touch you
When absent? It is nothing to be borne above the ether of heaven,
And, being present, to have one's breast scorched by the flames of the Styx.
What reward does virtue have, unknown to Christ?
To whom a mind overcome by decay, and barren of truth, resists?
The gifts of heaven are not owed to such a right hand.
O race of Christians, brought forth by better fates,
To whom it is given by the auspices of the divine Godhead, the high
Seats of the heaven-dwellers, and to bring back much better
Rewards, than are truly owed to our merits;
Inflamed in mind by these things, do not yield to the profane race:

div.note: The seven corporal works of mercy are attributed to Anchises.

lg.l: Would not a great shame convict degenerate souls,
to be called Christians (to whom for so many years have been known
the brave deeds of the Fathers, a very long series of events,
drawn through so many men from the ancient origin of the race)
and that you have not yet followed the illustrious examples of the Saints?
Come now, while the times of the present life demand it.
Let there be one care of the excellent, to kindle virtue by deeds
for you: thus the fates command, let no delay hold you back.
On the spiritual works of mercy.
It is fitting not only to attend to bodily health,
but rather to defend so many injured parts of the soul;
Piety born of God thirsts, and burns in protecting them.
1. This is her duty, and to challenge the guilty with words,
behold, to stir up harsh wars against wickedness with varied warning.
Is it pleasing to build a way? But behold, those who delay
to call back their step from vices. Now with the sun brought back,
here the martial song of hoarse bronze sounds out, and a voice
is heard, imitating the broken sounds of trumpets.
2. To illuminate ignorant minds, and with the night put to flight,
to instruct them with the excellent art of heavenly Pallas.
3. To give counsel, and to weigh all the misfortunes of those who fear,
to say then which better opinion should stand in the mind.
4. By bending the Heavenly Ones, to entreat the salvation of men.
5. To soothe minds, and to turn away cares with words.
6. Let grief not break you, nor the injury of a despised lot,
Nor let wounded patience supply you with arms, as frenzy does,
lest you seem like the places where, with a striking sound, hollow
rocks resound, and the struck image of the voice bounces back.
7. Finally, she wishes it to sit fixed and unmoved in the mind,
that you do not ponder any vengeance in your inflamed heart,
overcoming the wrong with the strength of a tranquil heart.
Thus we shall be an ornament to Christ, nor will our
fame be reported as light, and the glory of so great a deed will grow.

div.note: 1. To correct sinners. 2. To teach the ignorant. 3. To give good counsel to the doubting. 4. To pray to God for the salvation of one's neighbor. 5. To comfort the sorrowful. 6. To bear injuries patiently. 7. To forgive offenses.

lg.l: On the four cardinal virtues.
Weighed down with heavy bronze, it creaks as well on brazen doors,
The fourfold hinge of heaven, which I mark in a twofold verse:
The rule of Justice, Prudence, Strength from on high,
And the power that with measure lets loose balanced reins upon things.
However things shall fall, no force those relying on this hinge,
Disturbed by a sad wound of the mind, from the right,
Will turn away; not if it should pour the earth into the waves
Mixing in a deluge, or send heaven into Tartarus.
That the gates of double-opening Olympus roll on this fourfold
Hinge is well enough known. It remains for sick mortals,
That among these four sisters, by divine law,
Strong covenants be joined in a perpetual bond:
For if by the fate of things a greater prudence to me
Should stand forth, as soon as I should be that most just man
Who was among the Trojans, and most observant of the right,
Nay, pious Aeneas, than whom no other was then more just,
Nor was greater in piety, nor in war and arms;
Unless with the gushing streams of leaping water allays the parched
Mouths with thirst the monstrous gluttony of our palate,
And hunger be taken away, and the love of eating restrained,
Measure will be lacking: but measure is the fairest virtue,
Without which virtue becomes vice, and wounds modesty.
Since measure sets both the bounds and the times of things:
Hence that most famous poet rightly sang:
There is a measure in things, there are, in short, fixed limits,
Beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.
Moreover, when the hinges of high heaven are torn away,
what use are solid doorposts, and what use are brazen thresholds?
There is no need that an enemy, seizing a hard double-axe,
should break through the thresholds, pressing on and straining with his strength,
or hollow them out when cut, battering with a beam the palace's firm
timbers, so that he may prepare a huge window with a wide mouth.
A way must not be made by force, so that thus under the frequent ram totters
the door, until the gate falls forward, its hinge wrenched out:
The house within appears, and the long halls lie open,
whence the serpent of the Styx, hurled down by a thunderbolt to the shades,
with a crash dragged great ruin with him from the orb.
Horace.

div.n: Qua ratione septem dona Spiritus sancti comparantur?

lg.l: Do not, however, believe that, against the will of the heavenly shores,
the doors have stood open, so that violence might be brought to the Thunderer:
For the inner house, splendid with royal adornment,
is thrown open, so that, with destruction shut out from the high seats of the Winged Ones,
it may be entirely free from the Stygian plague.
In the manner of a camp, to be surrounded by battlements and a host
the palace does not need, but indeed far from there the terrors,
the tyrants of Cocytus, broken in adverse war,
the almighty Father has already hidden away in black caverns.
They, indignant, with a great murmur, of Avernus
roar around the barriers, whose angers are without strength,
however great the Shades sent back from Acheron might be.
Meanwhile the greatest Michael, the lofty right hand of the Thunderer,
and nearby Gabriel, the second hope of our race,
lead the host, and at the same time fill the places far and wide with soldiery,
both outstanding in courage, both in surpassing arms,
from wherever the enemies might clash with arms, they will beware of arms.
By what means are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit obtained?
Snatching your body from the bed, soon stretch your upturned
hands to heaven with your voice, and pour offerings
undefiled upon the hearths: joyful, with the honor completed,
hasten to bear the pleasing work to the highest Thunderer:
See to it that at the same time you adore the great Divinity of Mary with prayer.
How many men has she rendered distinguished by the art
of Pallas, rejoicing to bring aid to the affairs of men?
Gladly sing her vows, and the powerful mistress
overcome with suppliant vows: O this band, she says,
O my chosen band, let no foreign band from your undertaking,
nor whatever of monsters Erebus, and in its vast lakes
brings forth, and belches from the dire jaws of Orcus,
divert you; since He Himself to His own, so that strength in their breast
may stand solid, breathes an impregnable vigor,
the King of the Gods above, and strengthens their minds, and supplies weapons.
He, with the ethereal art of divine Pallas, the mind
strengthens, instructing His children to look upon the high heavens,
and to decide their affairs by the highest cause of things.
Increasing the powers of the intellect by the gift bestowed,
Heaping up the glory of counsel from heaven's lofty citadel,
And sending forth from the sky the sublime gifts of Minerva;
Of heavenly strength, and the distinguished paternal shield,
And the veil woven round with saffron acanthus,
The ornaments of divine piety: the gifts of the fear
Of the eternal Godhead. What gifts, in short, with such great
Love for his mother would the royal offspring not bestow?
These things the Virgin briefly speaks, her face cast down,
So that from this you may easily see that nothing is more powerful than she
For bending her offspring by prayer, and to be won over by a nod.
Gifts for the beloved race, and for the flocks of her own,
To the bands chosen for their piety after the manner of a sodality.
Hence let devotion to Mary, the venerable mother, be your care.
What are the fruits of the Holy Spirit?
He whom the Spirit adorns with the sevenfold gift of the divine ones,
Him He inflames with a wondrous love of the highest virtue.
Therefore, burning in spirit, he urges himself on, and every
Pattern of the virtues matching with mighty deeds,
As though he had achieved nothing yet, and for doing deeds
Time were slipping away, he toils the more, and all arms
He summons, and even now about to increase the honor of the heavenly ones,
He shapes himself to the manner of the heavenly ones by zeal and practice.
And at the same time joys thrill his mind,
And makes him be borne ever tranquil in divine order,
Cherishing with abundant peace one tossed by so many chances of life:
Training him with a brave heart to endure all labors:
To hold out, and to keep himself for better fortunes:
To relieve wretched men with signal piety:
To check the waves of anger: duly a quiet
Spirit to receive toward his companions, and a kindly mind.
He grants hearts that know not how to be bent to grow suddenly gentle,
And strengthens with greater light those unshaken in faith:
Ordering the acts of the human body, He tempers them,
And grants them to be modest in the manners of a lowly mind:
To preserve virginal grace and, of snowy modesty,
An outstanding pattern, and to keep a chaste bed.
Exhortation to take care of salvation.
If I should have such great selection for the equine herd,
That just those whom I have decided to rear for the hope of the race,
I should expend special labor from their tender years onward,
And with all zeal the ice, and snowy winds
I should avert, and bring as food the most pleasing of oats
Fodder, and not close the haylofts all winter long,
How much better care must be applied to the salvation of the soul!
It is right to rouse sluggish minds, and hearts unaccustomed to things
Sacred, to the study, and weary of the high Deity;
It is right the sluggish by warning, and the inert of mind with a resounding
Mouth to rouse the men, and to kindle Mars with the voice.
Or because there is some grace in unplowed land,
Will you suffer the sluggish field to harden with neglect?
Why, Tityrus, do you seek idleness, at ease in the shade?
Rest must be indulged to perishable things, I concede,
(For lacking all rest, it is not durable)
Yet leisure must be fled, the Lerna of evils.
Do not the fields rest with changed crops?
Hence there yellow Ceres, with changed name, spelt,
From where previously the gathered legume, with shaking pod;
Or the slender offspring of the vetch, and of the bitter lupine
You will have removed the fragile stalks, and the rustling forest.
For labor is easy with alternating crops: only the dry
Soils let it not shame you to saturate with rich dung, or
To scatter foul ash through the exhausted fields.
The mind, its cheeks bathed in tears, suffused with shame,
The avenging punishments of crimes, fasts to whips
Added, with a groan, and breasts beaten thrice with fists,
Are to be likened to the rich dung, and the ash of the farmers
Suited for the fields of the Gods, to whom heavenly things are a care:
And because, as I said, the fields rest with changed
Crops, you should bear there the ample seeds 1. of rich praise,
From where previously 2. the slender vetches, and bitter lupines,
Nay rather 3. burrs, caltrops, and the bristling forest of vices
Were coming forth, there now let Gargara marvel at the harvests
Of virtues, and of the sacred crop, now with the filth from the lowest
Root torn away, thus the mind in a sound body
May he flourish through the long years of long-lived Nestor.
TO THE GUIDE
What are called the Evangelical Beatitudes?
I. BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.
MUSE
How discordant are the desires of men with the word of Christ!
Some trouble the blind seas with oars, and rush
onto the sword, they penetrate the courts and thresholds of kings,
This one assails a city and its wretched homes with destruction,
that he may drink from a jewelled cup, and sleep on Tyrian purple.
The royal offspring, on the contrary, spoke thus with his mouth:
Happy is he who has been able to despise the treasures of the rich,
and all fears, and inexorable fate
has cast beneath his feet, and the roar of bitter Acheron.
Him neither the fasces of the people, nor the purple of kings
has swayed, nor discord driving faithless brothers,
or the Dacian descending from the conspiring Danube;
not Roman affairs, and kingdoms doomed to perish: nor has he
either grieved pitying the destitute, or envied the one who has:
What fruits the branches, what the willing fields themselves
have borne of their own accord, he has plucked, nor the iron laws,
or the mad forum, or the archives of the people has he seen:
Rather, his will stands fixed in his mind to inhabit humble cottages
and the roof of a poor hut heaped up with turf.
To such it is granted to hold the heavenly kingdoms.
II. BLESSED ARE THE MEEK, etc.
When the sun has varied its rising dawn with spots,
hidden in a cloud, and has retreated in the middle of his disk;
let showers be suspected by you, for from the deep presses
the South wind, sinister to trees and crops and the flock.
Or when toward dawn, among dense clouds
scattered rays break forth, or when pale rises
Aurora, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus,

div.note: The rich seeds of praise are the love of God and of neighbour, the root of good works.
The slender vetches and bitter lupines are morally good works.
The burrs and caltrops are evil and harmful works.

lg.l: Alas, then the vine-leaf will poorly shield the ripe grapes,
So thick the bristling hail leaps crackling on the roofs;
But the grapes of the heavenly vine, which the vine-leaf protects,
And to which heavenly gifts have given mild spirits,
These the harsh hail will not gather, nor the crueler breeze.
The savage madness of tyrants, and the striking storm,
The dire edge of iron, and the burning desire of shedding blood,
The hostile force of men, but the insatiable breast
Of exercising hatred against the venerable name of Christ,
These are to be held in the place of a pruning-hook, the use of which is needed by
The half-pruned leafy vine for God on the elm:
The begun matter must be completed in this way; and thus with full abundance,
Cultivated, very rich in Bacchus, will pour forth its wealth
The vine; on the sunny rocks the vintage is baked.
As many harvests as Gargara has, as many clusters as Methymna has,
So many stony hearts of the harsh tyrant press together
The purple crops of the grape: the wave flows from the presses,
The foaming vintage overflows with full brims.
The victim which rises for Christ does not fall about to die,
For whom it is right now to rise again to the eternal realms of life;
Nor will he have left the borders of his fatherland, nor the sweet fields,
For whom the hall of heaven is a home, in a throne, and the crown of a kingdom
To whom it is given to rejoice: these owed to the Just man for his merits
Rewards are rendered, whom mild hearts make serene;
And not only the gentle man to look upon the convexities of heaven
Worthy, but also to hold his scepters on earth.
For just as the man fierce of mouth exasperates angers with his speech,
So on the contrary, a pious man with soft speech placates the fires of anger,
And just as in a great people, when, as often, there has arisen
Sedition, and the ignoble mob rages in their minds,
And now torches and rocks fly, madness supplies weapons,
Then if by chance some man heavy with piety and merits
They have caught sight of, they are silent, and stand by with raised ears;
He rules their minds with his words, and soothes their breasts.
Rightly therefore I shall declare gentle, for both earth and heaven
Breasts happy for the empire. (but with Christ as guide.)
The ungentle man is driven from his throne, and from his paternal realms,
Who has deserved the punishments of his fatherland, and the hatred of his own people,

div.note: The usefulness of persecutions to the Church. On the witness of Justin Martyr, for the Church to suffer persecution is nothing else than for a vine to be spurred to fruitfulness by pruning.

lg.l: to have himself surrendered his guilty soul through all deaths.
But the meek man does not bound his empire, his fame, by the stars.
III. BLESSED ARE THEY THAT MOURN, etc.
In its own way, mingling joys with vain cares,
let the world exult with applause, celebrating its own feasts.
Let Bacchus, the giver of gladness, be present, mixing all things;
let him set up great mixing-bowls, then crown the wines;
let this man drain the bowl, and drench himself in the full gold,
and after him the lords of the world. Let long-haired Iopas
resound on his gilded one, what greatest Atlas taught:
let some beat out dances with their feet, and sing songs,
and also let the Thracian priest with his long robe,
sound in harmony here the seven distinct notes in rhythm,
and let him strike the same now with his fingers, now with his ivory plectrum.
Meanwhile, in the midst of the applause, death, of life the final
line, hastened on, soon draws near before the doors,
and first, before the day's end, before Evening closes Olympus
and lays the day to rest, bids these men fall by a swift doom.
Ah, how much better it had been for them, if the fates had allowed,
afflicted, their life in darkness and mourning through the years
to have dragged out, and to have indulged in sorrowful grief for their sins,
than, for so little a time of gladness, to punishments
to be condemned to eternal, and to be shut in a dark prison.
IV. BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HUNGER, etc.
O how happy the souls, in whose veins a fiery
thirst, driven through all, unable to be quenched by the fruit
of justice, and at the same time an equal hunger is implanted in the mind,
by which it would wish its life poured out with all its blood,
so that it might extend the empire of Christ, and from deceitful altars
vain Superstition, which turns itself into so many faces,
might depart conquered, and savage rites and fierce peoples
might give their necks to the pleasant yoke, and with darkness driven away
might behold the ethereal light, and through all lands
the Roman Father might give laws, the impious race from the whole
world might be plucked up, and a golden race might grow in the whole world.
Now enough does this ardor turn itself in our bones,
Christ, enough. Shall never your, great King, with blood
Would it be right to ratify our faith? To what end such great desire,
to what end this zeal in our souls, if all things fail, and all
labor is lost? Behold, we have not yet come to wounds here:
we have stood in the battle without blood: great things, we confess,
we ask, undeserving: grant, you, grant that we may be able to merit,
what is given to hope for through you, you being the author of the gift.
V. BLESSED ARE THE MERCIFUL, etc.
But how happy are they for whom to show mercy is a firm
and immovable zeal of the soul: for with the Supreme as witness,
who have tears, and whose minds mortal sorrows touch,
these Almighty God pities from high heaven.
While there comes to mind the image of Christ's pity,
whom, when he pities the fallen, to undergo so many labors
this pity drove, so that with all his blood his life
he might lay down, innocent, dying guiltless for the guilty,
Ah, with what cares did he groan, with what fires did he burn?
As this pity enters the mind, to show mercy with great
flames I am compelled. Moved by the love of Christ,
and I am resolved in my mind to extend virtue by outstanding deeds.
VI. BLESSED ARE THE PURE IN HEART, etc.
Let the priest sing from a divine mouth in the manner of prophets.
The faith is manifest by greater auspices: he
is deemed born under an exceedingly happy star,
whose inner lights of the soul shine with the Divine Presence:
Just as when the Morning Star, bathed in the wave of the Ocean,
whom Venus loves before the other fires of the stars,
will raise his sacred face to the sky, and will dispel the darkness,
and clinging in his gaze, fixed upon the One God above,
he will stand rejoicing, until he is summoned by joyful Heaven.
VII. BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS, etc.
Happy also, with strife laid aside, are the minds
which have joined treaties of peace among companions;
but the souls against the flesh, with victorious arms taken up,
thus the boxers fight, both striving with their strength
so that the succumbing flesh may be laid low in the middle of the arena,
worthy both to be called, and to be considered, the sacred offspring of God.
VIII. BLESSED ARE THEY WHO SUFFER PERSECUTION, etc.
MUSE.
The illustrious glory of the eighth lot is hidden from me:
In your own manner, even though with a horribly grating Muse,
* Teach this, I pray, while I stand by with attentive ears.
CATECHIST.
The approaches to heaven are not easy, nor are the gates wide open,
One must struggle along a narrow path, and seek it by a straight
Track, where the path points out a small threshold.
But yet, there must be no stepping back, nor failing in courage:
Steep, but worn by the feet of many men,
Whom the eternal Father has adorned with deserved honour,
Is the way that leads to the seats and joys of those above.
This way, of course, God, when seized by eternal love,
He, not forgetful of himself and of our salvation,
Took on human form and countenance on earth,
And, pierced through, poured out his soul through very cruel wounds:
This way, I say, God himself, so that confidence might spur the brave
More, and so that shame might chastise the sluggish,
Goes first, flying ahead: weighed down by an immense mass,
Although the cross is a burden to his shoulders; whom the rest of the youth
Follows, wherever he swiftly marks his footsteps,
And is not able to equal his mighty strides by following.
I myself, for your sake, since the series of events is very long,
And it is enough to recount the punishments and deaths briefly,
Will proceed to tell only the highest peaks, following them,
You, turn your two eyes, wherever I, teaching,
Shall turn my finger, and store these things in your mindful mind.
This one's eyes were gouged out: this one's teeth were torn from his mouth.
This one lacked his two ears: this one his right thumb;
This one's hands fell off, and his nostrils by an unjust wound:
This one was shorn with a stone: this one thrown down from a high watchtower.
This one suspended on a straight beam, and turned by the hands,
And entangled in his feet, by the weight of a clinging mass
Is stretched, and, distended in his whole body, grows.

div.note: The Muse of Maro, concerning the eighth Beatitude, acknowledges her ignorance, and desires to be more exactly instructed by her Guide, even if he must use his own effort.

lg.l: That one perished, consumed by hunger and by wretched toil,
With eyes stripped of the defense of their tender rampart:
This one falls amid the cracking of rods: that one to the axe
Meeting the two-edged blade, falls forward on the yellow sand.
This one, with tongue thrust out, and hamstring cut, maimed
In body, the executioners did not mock him grieving,
But they grieved at him laughing at his pains with a lofty mind.
Through the middle of this one a wedge, to this one a pole with a point fixed in front
And an iron-shod stake went through: to that one a sword was driven
Through the side, and streams flowed with warm blood:
To this one goads were applied: torn on all sides with severed limbs
This one lies, that one given as prey to wild birds and wolves,
Still alive hung aloft from a twisted rope.
And what you may marvel at more, plants footsteps with equal
Pace, woman and man, and having imitated the course of men,
Supported by virgin choirs, rivaling virtue flies,
And do men hesitate to imitate these deeds, and the men?
And does piety not drive goads? nor to the senses fire
Entwine, the illustrious spread ardor of virtues?
Does heaven not kindle strength, nor glory the mind
Raise with hope? Warned, ah, let us at last follow better things:
Let toil and constancy conquer the journey: let rewards the mind
Urge, and the will for the right struck into our souls.
A way is made by force: God Himself comes to share the toils.
May He bring us to ancient virtue, and manly spirits;
May the father himself, leader of the choir, and the hero Xavier rouse us.
Too happy, twice and thrice and four times blessed,
Those whom before the faces of a grim Tyrant by a cruel blade
It befell to perish, and whom this one care gnaws.
For these, it is certain, the heavenly kingdoms will await.
On the Three Evangelical Counsels.
Now to you, and your counsels, great Father, I return.
The royal offspring slipped down from the serene sky,
By manifold example, by deeds, and by frequent warning
Gave these counsels. To whom He promised the heavenly citadels,
By His judgments, and wished them to hold the high heavens with Himself:
To prefer poverty of mind to the treasures of Croesus,
To avoid permitted beds, and marriage torches,
In the pursuit of virtue, as if the foul weapons of Cupid,
Always prepared to depend on the nod of another.
Yet that this is the way of counsel; nor is it conscious of fault,
The undefiled mind keeping the commands of God the Father.
Unless, after it has vowed, it slackens the reins of its vows.
The Vow of Poverty.
By this counsel of the Heavenly Ones a rich poverty is produced for you,
By which, stripped of its own goods, the mind, rough to the world,
Is clothed in ethereal splendor, heaped up with the heavens'
Hundredfold interest, until it gains possession of Olympus:
Let it not be enough for you to have heard these things, let it please you to linger constantly,
And to walk side by side, and to tread in the footprints of Christ.
The first seat for God was a stable, a manger His bed.
Alas! So cheap a palace held the King of the Heavenly Ones.
Dare, O guest, to despise riches, and fashion yourself also worthy
Of God, and come not harsh to needy circumstances:
Enter beneath the gables of a narrow roof,
And suffer yourself to be placed on humble hay and bedding.
The Vow of Chastity.
Let it be fixed in the mind not to give birth, so that the womb of a fruitful birth
You may surpass with a virgin offspring, and of snowy modesty
With the adornment, nor will you make yourself like the barren oat.
Lo, I would pray that either the lowest earth gape open for me first,
Or the almighty Father drive me with a thunderbolt to the shades,
The pale shades of Erebus, and the deep night,
Before, O Modesty, I violate you, or break your laws;
Having called Mary to witness, and those whom the temples of heaven receive,
The happy souls, to You, O greatest Ruler of the Heavenly Ones,
That I have vowed once, content with poor attire,
And without a marriage bed, without foul crime; my life
But if perchance I could succumb to such a fault,
That I should wish to ally myself to someone in the marital bond,
He who first joined himself to me, my loves
Has taken away, let him have them with him, and keep them forever.
Do not seek to ally your soul in profane marriages,
O sacred offspring, and do not trust in loose marriage beds;
Virgin men will come who by blood our
They will bear their name to the stars, and the descendants from their lineage,
all things under their feet, where the returning sun
looks upon either Ocean, they will see both turned and ruled:
Hence also the innocent, having set out from their earthly seat,
the golden palace of the starry heaven now on its throne
receives, and they increase the number of the Saints at the altars.
The Vow of Obedience.
King Iarbas is said to have set up a hundred altars to God,
and more than a hundred temples, immense in his broad realms,
the eternal watch-fires of the gods, and with the blood of flocks
the rich soil, and the thresholds blooming with various garlands,
and to have consecrated the wakeful fire; and with all these, to the single
vow of obeying he will be judged unequal in merits,
nor will it be granted that he equal himself to the praises of so great a bond.
And not only the profane gifts of the gentile Iarbas,
when, with bullocks slain according to the law by ancient rite,
yield to this vow: loosening the covering and the fillets
of the consecrated head, from the divine mouth the priest
of old is surpassed. But even he who pours libations at the altars
of the Christians, is not able to run alongside with equal steps.
For this virtue flies above all things in its merits,
by which all the renowned saints more swiftly to divine
commands gladly obey, and execute the orders.
Behold the three counsels of the great Father, as I have learned them,
I teach: and what purpose now stands firm in my mind:
See to it that these things are fixed in your inmost marrow:
MUSE. These things, believe me, will remain fixed and immovable in my mind.
It is not in our power, O guide, nor of whatever there is anywhere
of the purified race, which is scattered through the great world,
to pay worthy thanks for so great a gift.
May Christ, if any divine powers regard the pious, if there is any
justice anywhere, and a mind conscious of right,
bring just rewards, and grant that we may follow these counsels.

div.note: Of this kind are the blessed Father Francis Xavier, our blessed Aloysius, Blessed Stanislaus, etc.
Obedience is better than sacrifice, 1 Kings 15.

lg.l: On the Four Last Things.
Soon you will make every kind of sin succumb to death,
if, with your gaze fixed on any one of these four,
you have lingered, and have grown used to pondering the last fates.
The First of the Last Things: Death.
Hence let Death come to mind, the final boundary of life,
which makes royal sceptres equal to iron mattocks,
by which, as you struggle, your limbs will be loosened with cold,
and life with a groan will flee to be tormented beneath the shades.
Turn this over in your mind with yourself, and turn it over again often.
Behold, God himself, with evenly balanced beam, two scales
holds up, and places in them the differing fates of the two,
whom the struggle condemns, and to which side death sinks with its weight,
the outcome itself proves, when death has taken you out of time,
and has set loose the struggling soul and the knit-together limbs.
The Particular Judgment.
There is no need then for Minos anxiously to shake the urn,
and summon a council, and learn of lives and crimes;
nor has Rhadamanthus anything to do, nor to compel confession
what anyone among the living, rejoicing in vain deceit,
has deferred the committed sins until a late death;
There is no need of these, I say, when each one's own deeds lie open.
Yet the eternal abodes are not assigned without a Judge;
but one more just than they, God from the great Godhead,
unlocking every hidden thing of the mind, and laying bare all works,
will come forth as Judge, to render to each his due.
Trojan and Tyrian will be dealt with by him without distinction.
Woe to the wretched guilty one, whose mind is then turned away from God.
O grief, alas, how great a trembling seizes my limbs even now
while I ponder the lot of these with mindful thought.
Hell.
Will the final day, and the inescapable time
of eternal punishment, and the mercilessness of cruel death,
bring you no help? And will it not profit you to remember these things?

div.note: Remember thy last things, and thou shalt never sin. Ecclus. 7.

lg.l: Happy is he whom the perils of others make cautious.
Those pools of Cocytus, O man, and the Stygian marsh,
let it be fixed in your mind to remember, while breath rules these limbs:
draw yourself into the midst of the assemblies, and the throng of the silent;
Go, and climb the mound, from where you may all in a long line
survey face to face, and learn the faces of those who come,
whom once as allies in crimes, while the times permitted,
if you remember, you know: among these are those who death to themselves
brought forth by an unspeakable hand, and, loathing the light,
flung away their lives; how they would wish in the upper air
now to endure both poverty and harsh toils!
The Fates stand in the way, and the Styx, flowing between nine times, confines them.
There are those to whom brothers were hateful, while life remained,
or a parent was struck, and fraud woven against a client;
or who brooded alone over acquired wealth,
and did not set aside a share for their own, which is the greatest crowd;
and those slain for adultery, and those who followed arms
impious, and did not fear to deceive the right hands of their masters.
How dreadfully now the victorious one, girded with a whip,
Tisiphone shakes them, leaping upon them, and with her left hand the grim
brandishing snakes, she calls the savage bands of her sisters:
From here groans are heard, and savage resound
blows, then the grating of iron, and dragged chains.
There they raise dreadful voices to the stars:
Such bellowings as when, wounded, he flees the altar,
a bull, and has shaken the ill-aimed axe from his neck:
Everywhere is grief, and terror, and many an image of death.
A monstrous hydra with fifty black gaping mouths
fiercer still, holds its seat within: then Tartarus itself
yawns sheer downward twice as far, and stretches beneath the shades,
as is the upward view of the sky to ethereal Olympus.
Here the ancient race of the earth, the Titanian youth,
cast down by the thunderbolt, writhe in the lowest depths:
Here too Tityos, foster-child of the omnipotent Earth,
one may see, whose body over nine whole acres
is stretched out, and a monstrous vulture with hooked beak
beating the immortal liver, and the fruitful for punishments
entrails, and probes for a feast, and dwells deep within
in the breast, nor is any rest given to the reborn entrails.
Why should I mention the Lapiths, Ixion, and Pirithous,
over whom a black crag, now, now about to slip, and to one falling
overhangs like? They shine on high festive
golden props for the couches, and feasts prepared before their faces
with royal luxury: the greatest of the Furies nearby
reclines, and forbids them to touch the tables with their hands,
and she rises up, lifting a torch, and thunders with her mouth.
Here are forms terrible to see, and death and toil,
and many monsters besides of various wild beasts:
Centaurs are stabled in the doorways, and two-formed Scyllas,
and hundredfold Briareus, and the beast of Lerna,
hissing dreadfully, and the Chimera armed with flames.
Gorgons, and Harpies, and the form of the three-bodied shade.
Purgatory.
There are those who must pray, out of love for the farther bank,
so that they may be able to be the first to cross the course of the river.
For those whom life has left with their final light,
not for that reason does every evil for the wretched, nor do all entirely
bodily plagues depart, and it is necessary that deeply
many things long hardened become ingrained in wondrous ways.
Therefore they are disciplined with punishments, and of their old evils
they pay the penalties, some are spread out empty
suspended to the winds: for others under a vast whirlpool
the stained-in crime is washed away, or burned out with fire.
Until a long day, with the cycle of time completed,
has removed the hardened stain, and left pure
the ethereal sense, and the fire of simple air.
On the care to be taken for the dead.
Be mindful of what of a funeral you owe to the sad shades
to pay, and let nothing of your duty be rightfully left undone by you:
But not in the human manner of men, to whom only external things
are dear to the heart, and besides processions, and proud arrogance,
they ponder nothing in their mind, whom miserably of sad Avernus,
or of that world, the ruinous error fascinates.
For does it avail at all that lifeless Pallas be raised to the stars
with praise? He sends chosen men from the whole column,
a thousand men, to escort the last honour,
and to share the father's tears, consolations of a grief
small, of a huge one, but owed to the wretched father?
What does it avail to have active men who a soft bier
weave of arbutus rods and oaken wicker,
and shade the raised couch with a canopy of leaves?
What does it avail that the youth is laid on high upon rustic straw,
like a flower plucked by a maiden's thumb,
whether of soft violet or drooping hyacinth,
whose brightness has not yet faded, nor its beauty departed,
though mother earth no longer nourishes it or supplies its strength?
If meanwhile the soul, to the waves of swift Phlegethon,
to atone for its ingrained stain through everlasting ages,
is wretchedly snatched away from here, never to enjoy rest?
What does it avail that twin garments, stiff with purple and gold,
which royal Dido herself once with her own hands
had made, be spread out, and the corpse be veiled in this mantle?
And besides that many prizes of the Laurentine battle
be added? What does it avail that the booty is led at the same time in a long line?
to yoke horses, and weapons of which he had stripped the enemy?
that the hands be bound behind the backs of those whom he would send to the shades
as funeral offerings, to sprinkle the flames with slaughtered blood?
that even trunks clothed in enemy arms,
the leaders themselves carry, and enemy names be affixed?
What does it avail that chariots drenched in Rutulian blood be led?
What does it avail that the warhorse Aethon, his trappings laid aside,
goes weeping and wets his face with great drops?
Others carry his spear and helmet? By ancient custom,
what does it mean, that the mournful phalanx, and the Teucrians follow,
and the Tyrrhenian leaders, and the Arcadians with reversed arms?
What do all these things avail? What has the soul, relying on this triumph,
received of help, unless perhaps it is relieved from elsewhere?
Perhaps these things to a barbarian race buried in the earth
will be granted to be paid by the Teucrians, to be able to seem enough,
as to those ignorant of the faith of things, from whom the light has been taken away;
But Christians, to whom greater grace has been given,

div.note: They are vain consolations for the living rather than aids for the dead.

lg.l: Who would deny that towards the Shades we are bound to much better things?
For them it would be the least of things to lead solemn processions,
For the squadrons, in gleaming arms, thrice around the kindled
To have run around the pyres, thrice the sad fire of the funeral
To have circled on horseback, and to have uttered wails from their mouths:
Such things are worthless to Christians; whose care is for serious things,
The earth is sprinkled by them with tears, and their faces are sprinkled;
They make vows to God, and load the altars with gifts.
Behold here the funeral torches. The way shines from afar
With a line of flames, and marks off the houses far and wide.
We bring in bowls foaming with warm milk,
And bowls of sacred blood, and the soul in the tomb
We lay to rest, and with a loud voice call out the last farewell.
With the mound of the tomb constructed, and the funeral rites discharged,
They cannot be torn away from the tomb, until the damp night
Revolves the sky studded with burning stars:
Nay, the third day removes the cold shadow from the sky,
When next to the deep ash, and the mingled of their loved ones,
Bones, they pour out prayers, mourning from the bottom of their heart:
They add to this succouring the wretched circumstances of the poor,
To calm the untamed motions of the flesh with the sacred
Bridle of fasting, and to tame the wanton senses.
Thus the piety of the ancients, with united strength, once,
Nights and days for souls to be cleansed from stain
Applied itself in two thousand ways, prepared whatever
Help from the heart to decree to the sad shades:
Until gradually a worse and tarnished age,
Oh sorrow, has followed in this our time, when
Impious posterity, and an ungrateful crowd of descendants
Have abandoned their turns of discharging, for the sake of the dead,
Their vows. Alas, a thing to be deplored with just complaints!
From that time ebbed, and slipping backward was carried away
The hope of Belgium, its strength broken, the mind of God turned away.
Meanwhile the enclosed, from the blind cave of the prison,
The Shades cry out, beating their breasts with their palms,
Alas my offspring, the greatest part of our race,
What are you contriving? Or whither has your care for us departed?
Will you not at last look, where a parent weary with age

div.note: By those foaming bowls can be understood devout prayers offered for the dead.

lg.l: Will you leave me? Meanwhile, sad fates have carried me off;
where I am girt with flames, where twice a thousand battle-lines of pains
wander around me; and unless your prayers withstand them,
alas, I linger in punishments, for the hostile blaze to devour me.
Come now, do not at last be loath to remember us,
by bearing pious prayers and sacrifices to the powers of the gods,
lest the Judge demand further penalties by fire.
These duties you must undertake, lest dread Styx torment you,
and to approach the sad sunless homes, the troubled places,
you be compelled, grieving after your sowings, driven by wanderings,
like the shapes that, rumour says, flit about once death is met,
in a hollow cloud, as I have seen, a thin shade without strength,
in the likeness of a spectre (a monster wondrous to behold),
which, gnashing a mindless sound, gives empty words,
and feigns the clapping of hands and the steps of one walking.
May God avert it, and may a better fortune refute these words.
Look, you may spend all the given time on funeral rites:
let night rush on, and for prayers let Aurora in her rosy chariot,
have already crossed the middle of the sky in her ethereal course;
it is right for you to devote three days to this just labour.
Be firmly persuaded of this: whatever goodwill toward brothers
buried in death, while they lived, whatever care of helping them
there always was, that same remains toward them now bereft of light.
Why then do we not spend more hours in weeping?
O shame! Alas, because the deaths of others do not touch us.
This way does not lead to heaven, but the left-hand path of the wicked
exacts punishments, and sends to impious Tartarus.
On eternal life.
O powers above, ward off these threats, and from the Stygian swamp
after death, in your kindness, turn away our shades.
Thunderbolts hurled from the sky, and blind fires from the clouds
do not so terrify our minds as the name of Avernus,
and the lake of Cocytus: O best God, lo, both bones and limbs
sweat, bursting forth, has drenched over the whole body,
and in my companions the cold blood with sudden fear
froze, their spirits failed, and their voice stuck in their throats.
Grant, I pray, O Christ, that I may thus pass the times of my life.

div.n: Colloquium B. Virginis. ad Musam Maronis.

lg.l: So that no delay may stand in the way, but that the mind to the pleasant green places
of the fortunate groves, and the blessed seats,
may arrive, and the joyful places, where to abide forever
may be granted as right to the soul, you have the power, unless you refuse to will it.
But by what reason would the ardor of a breast so kindled
deny to will it to a wretched one seeking the heavenly kingdoms,
who gave it to the unwilling, softening stony with a gentle
hearts with sound? God, gracious God, have pity on us,
whom the greatest anxiety of committed crime gnaws:
O how often to such ones the rewards of the heavenly kingdom,
nay, by your mercy, are the first honors restored?
But if therefore there are such great rewards for those conquered by crime,
(while you pity the fallen) what gifts to the just
will you give that are worthy, who has earned the first crown by praise?
Are you, O father of fathers, once most mild, in vain?
Will such great, such patient compassion of the heart of Christ,
allow us to pray in vain for pardon and heaven?
But you, divine parent, the confidence of our race,
allow us to carry this hope of you, of those calling you into their vows,
always and everywhere to support your companions with prayers:
And since you are the interpreter of the gods, who the divine will of your son,
not the tripods, nor the laurels of the Clarian, but perceive the stars,
I pray you sing, and willingly unbind your voice and lips:
Come now, for has declared all my course prosperous to me
Religion, and all the Saints have urged by their divine will,
to seek Elysium, and to attempt the remote lands,
a few things to me out of many, (so that I may more safely traverse the welcoming
seas, and be able to settle in the ethereal port)
unfold in words, for the Fates forbid the rest
for mortals to know, and the author of heaven forbids to speak.
The Colloquy of the Blessed Virgin to the Muse of Maro.
Here the Mother: O you, more beloved to your parent than the light,
do not doubt: for that you go through the deep under greater
auspices, is a manifest truth: thus the fates the King of the Gods
allots, and has willed the changes, this order revolves.
But Elysium, which you now think is near,
and whose neighboring ports you ignorantly prepare to enter,
a long pathless way separates far off by long lands,
and first the oar must be bent in the Trinacrian wave,

div.note: Dialogue of the Blessed Virgin with the Muse of Maro.

lg.l: And the expanse of Ausonian brine must be traversed by ships,
And the lakes of the underworld, and the Aeaean isle of Circe,
Before you can settle safely in the harbour of heaven.
Do not refuse the windings, nor shudder at the courses to come,
The fates will find a way, and Jesus, when called upon, will be at hand.
* Let the land on the right, and the right be sought by you in a long
Expanse of sea by a circuit: shun the left shore and waves:
† Scylla the left side, the left implacable Charybdis
